PRODSECRM-309.description:
Exception Title: RHOAI 3.6-ea.1/ea.2 Conforma exceptions: extended hermetic/RPM-signature remediation timelines + new RHAI ModelCar stage-registry base image exception
Exception Type: Conforma - Konflux/ EC policy check, blocking release
Business Unit: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
Product: RHOAI
Conforma MR Link: https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/releng/konflux-release-data/-/merge_requests/22104
Exception Reason:
Two related parts, both implemented in MR https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/releng/konflux-release-data/-/merge_requests/22104:
(A) Extends the hermetic_task.hermetic and rpm_signature.allowed exceptions originally approved under https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/PRODSECRM-213#icft=PRODSECRM-213
 (for RHOAI 2.25/3.3/3.4/3.5) to also cover odh-mlmd-grpc-server, odh-openvino-model-server, and odh-vllm-cpu (EPEL RPM signature, 3.6-ea.1 only) for RHOAI 3.6-ea.1 (release 2026-09-23) and 3.6-ea.2 (release 2026-10-14). PRODSECRM-213's approved Proposed Remediation committed to having 'all remediation in place to address 3.6 EA1 and onward' for these components. That has slipped: mlmd-grpc-server offboarding now targets 3.6 GA (https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/AIPCC-18390#icft=AIPCC-18390
); openvino-model-server's AIPCC onboarding/hermetic build now targets 3.6 GA or later (https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHOAIENG-67702#icft=RHOAIENG-67702
); vllm-cpu is being offboarded to RHAII (https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-2304#icft=RHAISTRAT-2304
) before ea.2.
(B) New global exception for base_image_registries.base_image_permitted covering 5 RHAI ModelCar images (modelcar-redhatai-all-minilm-l6-v2, -en-core-web-lg, -nltk-punkt-tab, -snowflake-arctic-embed-m-long, -ogx-distribution) sourced from registry.stage.redhat.io. The nemo-guardrails and ogx-core components are switching from direct HuggingFace/modelscope downloads to these ModelCar images, but the images are currently only published to the stage registry, not prod. Tracked under https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHOAIENG-88509#icft=RHOAIENG-88509
.
Related Risk Ticket: https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/PRODSECRM-213#icft=PRODSECRM-213
 (part A is a scope/timeline extension of that risk; part B is a new, related gap surfaced in the same MR).
Risk of Approving Exception:
Reduced ability to prove what's inside the image. Two components still pull some build ingredients over the network at build time instead of through Red Hat's locked-down process, so if a source were tampered with during that window, we'd have a weaker paper trail to catch it.
Slower, less predictable patch timelines for a handful of packages. A few OS packages are signed by outside vendors (Intel, CentOS/EPEL) rather than Red Hat, so a future fix would depend on their release schedule instead of our own fast CVE-turnaround process.
An availability risk, not a breach risk, on five small AI-model images. These are temporarily served from Red Hat's internal staging registry, which isn't built for production-grade stability, so a release depending on them could break or silently pick up an unreviewed version if that content changes.
No known vulnerability exists today - this is a bounded, temporary trade-off through October 21.
Impact if Exception NOT Approved:
(A) RHOAI 3.6-ea.1 and 3.6-ea.2 releases would be blocked for odh-mlmd-grpc-server, odh-openvino-model-server, and odh-vllm-cpu.
(B) The nemo-guardrails and ogx-core spikes (https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHOAIENG-85372#icft=RHOAIENG-85372
, https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHOAIENG-85373#icft=RHOAIENG-85373
) could not adopt RHAI ModelCar packaging, blocking any release depending on it.
Proposed Remediation:
mlmd-grpc-server offboarding: https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/AIPCC-18390#icft=AIPCC-18390
, targeting 3.6 GA.
openvino-model-server AIPCC onboarding/hermetic build: https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHOAIENG-67702#icft=RHOAIENG-67702
, targeting 3.6 GA or later.
vllm-cpu: offboarded to RHAII, tracked under https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-2304#icft=RHAISTRAT-2304
.
ModelCar prod-registry publication: RHAI model validation team to publish images to the production registry; currently tracked under https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHOAIENG-88509#icft=RHOAIENG-88509
 pending a dedicated tracking ticket from that team.
Approving VP Email: jofernan@redhat.com
Exception Expiration: 10/21/2026
Additional Watchers: ckodama@redhat.com, rhartman@redhat.com
Related Risk Ticket: N/A

third party rpm keys, unsupported base image exceptions, and not building from source - main risk here is supportability, especially if we need to turn around a CVE fix in a package from one of these rpm repos, or a CVE in the unsupported base image
permissive mode exception - this means the cargo lockfile needs to be regenerated during the build process, impacting the ability for the build to be reproductible
hermetic exceptions - non-hermetic builds negatively affect several aspects of SLSA, for example software provenance, ability to produce SBOM, and reproductibility.

Delays in the upcoming RHOAI 3.5-ea.1, ea.2, and GA releases, as well as the subsequent z-stream releases for RHOAI-2.25, 3.3, 3.4, and 3.5. It will also require code changes and potential instabilities in these z-stream releases far beyond the normal scope of CVE bugfixes, etc.
This will also delay our ability to implement CVE fixes for CVE-2026-42271 by the June 16th deadline.
Proposed Remediation:
We plan to have all remediation in place to address 3.6 EA1 and onward. Please refer to the google document for details.

comments.author: Imran Khalidi
comments.body:
Feasibility Analysis: Hermetic Build for OVMS
Summary
A hermetic build for OVMS is not feasible today. The primary blocker is the upstream Bazel-based build system, which relies heavily on external dependency fetching at build time — incompatible with Konflux's hermetic build model (Cachi2 does not support Bazel).
Technical Findings
Upstream (openvinotoolkit/model_server):
- Build uses Bazel with extensive external dependencies via http_archive, git_repository, and new_local_repository rules in WORKSPACE

- Key external dependencies include: TensorFlow Serving, TensorFlow, MediaPipe, OpenVINO, Azure SDK, AWS SDK, GCS SDK, OpenCV, and many others

- These dependencies are fetched dynamically during the build — not pre-vendored

Downstream (red-hat-data-services/openvino_model_server):
- Dockerfile.redhat / Dockerfile.konflux download additional artifacts via wget and git clone before invoking Bazel

- Pre-Bazel network dependencies: Boost, Azure SDK, OpenVINO components, cpprest SDK

- Current Konflux pipeline (openvino-model-server-push.yaml) does not set hermetic: true

Upstream Roadmap & Path Forward
- TensorFlow Deprecation: Upstream is planning to deprecate the TensorFlow API imminently. This accounts for ~75% of the Bazel complexity. Waiting for this deprecation is a prerequisite.

- MediaPipe: The remaining Bazel complexity is MediaPipe (computer vision / vision modeling). The path forward depends on discussions with Intel to understand their appetite for change and what options are viable.

- bazel-remote: Intel may suggest bazel-remote as a potential solution. This would need to be validated with ProdSec to determine if it meets hermetic build requirements.

Timeline Assessment
- Code Freeze for 3.6 EA1: August 21, 2026

- Assessment: Targeting 3.6 EA1 is ambitious given the dependency on upstream TensorFlow deprecation timeline and MediaPipe research. A more realistic target may be 3.6 GA or later, depending on upstream progress.

Action Items
- Seek approval for hermetic build exception while blockers are resolved

- Track upstream TensorFlow deprecation as a blocker

- Discuss hermetic build feasibility with Intel in next week's telecon

- Evaluate bazel-remote with ProdSec if Intel proposes it

- Reassess timeline and target release after Intel feedback

comments.author: Steven Grubb
comments.body:
The high level plan for the build is located here:

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xB3A7dZp7AEXs2HfEhLz5Ijm40laWpNKF30_FvHb6vo/edit?usp=sharing
In a nutshell, Fedora has an openvino rpm. This would build the foundation layer for everything else. It currently builds 2026.0.0, so there would be some work to bump it up to 2026.3. Looks like some folks at Intel are involved with this. The next phase would be to build openvino-tokenizers and openvino.genai. Then we would need to layer on MediaPipe and then finally the model_server.

comments.author: Steven Grubb
comments.body:
The current status is:
- I have used Fedora’s openvino.spec as the basis for an updated set of openvino rpms.

- I have packaged openvino_tokenizers

- I have packaged openvino_genai

- I have created a detailed plan to tackle MediaPipe and this has always been the big issue.

Currently investigating the best path forward for MediaPipe, Option A is the strongest contender but not a good situation. The MediaPipe plan is here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1vO2OhxGr6TVJMP3usMbNcJKLgBSLxbsyJL2O68taWNM/edit?usp=sharing
 
Google does not want a MediaPipe divorced from bazel. They want a very tight version controlled reproducible build that requires exact versions of bazel, protobuf, and abseil. Changing anything to a system library will lead to something that probably doesn’t work. So, the next step is packaging up MediaPipe. We’ll probably make a bazel cache, tar that up and call that the source code. Then we can use bazel to finish the build from the cache. The main issue would be how to get a blessed version of bazel 6.1.1?

comments.author: Steven Grubb
comments.body:
Current status is that I have all of the non-python parts built as rpms. MediaPipe was and still is a big problem. The current path involves around 113 individual tar files that get built. This gives the most compact build because it does not include cuda, rocm, metal, android, apple, etc. I think I want to investigate method 2 next to compare size and whether that would be easier to maintain in the long run. One problem that was identified is opencv and its dependencies.

The hermetic build is being prototyped on Fedora 44. It is largely using Fedora packages instead of following the Dockerfile which downloads source and builds its own copy of things. Turns out that MediaPipe has a dependency on opencv which in turn pulls in 390 dependencies. So, what I’m doing now is building opencv using the same options that the Dockerfile used to limit the dependencies. With this in place, we have a functioning prototype built on Fedora 44. Also, this cleans up one more issue. When opencv is built in the dockerfile, it also does not pass WITH_IPP=OFF. That downloads and installs Intel IPP which is closed source. By building it ourselves, we turn that off just like Fedora does.

comments.author: Steven Grubb
comments.body:
Current status is I have a completed prototyped container. The 2026.3 release of openvino has not occurred yet. What the next steps are:
- Upstream patches while there is still time

- Create package dependency tree

- Start getting repositories populated

Also, in the last phase of the now closed spike, I found one piece of software that doesn’t have a typical license. It is OouraFFT which is called via MediaPipe. It’s page is here: https://www.kurims.kyoto-u.ac.jp/~ooura/fft.html
  The license is at the bottom. May need legal to assign SPDX identifier for it.

comments.author: Steven Grubb
comments.body:
Also discovered just now that Azure/azure-storage-cpp was retired on March 29, 2025, and archived the repository on April 8, 2025. Legacy Azure Storage C++ repository (https://github.com/Azure/azure-storage-cpp)
 
Microsoft replaced it with the modern Azure SDK for C++:
- azure-storage-blobs 12.18.0

- azure-storage-files-shares 12.18.0

- azure-core 1.16.4

The catch is that it is not a drop-in replacement. OVMS uses the legacy API extensively:
- was/blob.h and was/storage_account.h

- azure::storage::cloud_storage_account

- cloud_blob_client, cloud_blob, cloud_file_client, cloud_file_share, and
related classes

  See repos/model_server/src/filesystem/azurestorage.hpp:32 and repos/model_server/src/filesystem/azurestorage.cpp:55. The affected OVMS adapter is approximately 1,868 lines across its four Azure filesystem files. The new SDK uses unrelated types such as Azure::Storage::Blobs::BlobClient, so adopting it requires an OVMS source migration and corresponding behavior tests.

RHOAIENG-67702.description:
Problem Statement
The OpenVINO Model Server (OVMS) image (odh-openvino-model-server-rhel9) is currently not built hermetically in Konflux. To comply with the ProdSec Security Policy Compliance Directive, all RHOAI components must achieve hermetic builds — ensuring reproducible, isolated builds with no external network access during the build process.
Non-hermetic builds are a security risk and will require VP-level exception approval going forward. Products that do not meet ProdSec security requirements do not ship.
Repository
- GitHub: https://github.com/red-hat-data-services/openvino_model_server

- Image: odh-openvino-model-server-rhel9

Prior Work
- RHOAIENG-31542 - Onboard runtimes to AIPCC workflow (OVMS) - Closed

- RHOAIENG-30979 - Migrate OVMS Dockerfile to Konflux - Closed

- RHOAIENG-34097 - OpenVino Needs Konflux setup - Closed

Scope
- Identify all external dependencies fetched during OVMS Konflux build

- Pin all dependencies with SHA256 hashes for reproducibility

- Use AIPCC base images and AIPCC-provided packages where applicable

- Ensure pre-fetch stage can resolve all dependencies without network access

- Support both x86_64 and aarch64 architectures

- Validate hermetic build passes Conforma policy checks

Acceptance Criteria
OVMS Konflux build completes successfully in hermetic mode (no network access during build)All dependencies are pinned with SHA256 hashesBuild uses AIPCC base images and approved package sourcesMulti-arch support (x86_64, aarch64) is maintainedConforma policy checks pass without exceptionsBuild is reproducible — same inputs produce identical image digestNo new security policy exceptions required for OVMS

Reach = 3 (Small user group) IBM Power (ppc64le) and IBM Z (s390x) customers represent a small, specialized segment of the RHAII/RHOAI user base. The x86 CPU variant already exists, and GPU variants (CUDA, ROCm, Gaudi) serve the majority of inference users. This feature delivers architecture parity for a limited customer segment — strategic for IBM partnership but narrow in breadth. Comparable to RHAISTRAT-1714 (Xeon Model Discoverability, R=3) and RHAISTRAT-1492 (AutoML Advanced Settings, R=3) — hardware-specific features serving named but small customer populations.
Impact = 8 (Major new capability) For the customers it reaches, impact is high: Power and Z users currently have NO supported path to deploy vLLM CPU inference through RHAII. The RFE explicitly states "customers on Power and Z cannot use RHAII for LLM serving." This goes from impossible to possible — a complete capability unlock, not an incremental improvement. Not I=13 because this is platform parity, not a strategic differentiator or compliance mandate. Comparable to RHAISTRAT-1377 (RHAII MaaS on xKS, I=8) and RHAISTRAT-1742 (Deploy agent images from AI Hub, I=8) — platform expansion features that open new deployment targets.
Confidence = 75% Supporting evidence: Approved RFE (RHAIRFE-2136) with PM + engineering sign-off. Hard dependency RHAIRFE-1926 (prebuilt wheel packages) is now Closed/Done — the biggest risk is resolved. Strategy review passed at 7/8. Technical approach is well-grounded: existing Dockerfile, existing runtime templates, existing AIPCC base image. Priority is Critical. Not 100% because: testability scored 1/2 with unresolved gaps (no model test matrix, no failure-mode criteria), feasibility reviewer flagged the effort estimate as optimistic (AIPCC base migration more complex than a FROM-line change), prior s390x build failures (torch 2.11.0), and open questions remain (TP vs GA support level, AIPCC index package availability for all dependencies). Per rubric: "Approved RFE with some customer evidence, strategy review passed 7-8/8" = 75%.
Effort = 5 (PM-set, validated) Respecting PM Selbi Siddiqi's assessment: "high level of collaboration/work across teams and is a new product offering at RHAII." Five impacted teams require coordination. The feasibility reviewer independently corroborated this, noting the strategy's S-size estimate (1-2 sprints) is optimistic — AIPCC base migration involves different venv layout, user identity, and package manager conventions beyond a FROM-line swap. Prior architecture- specific build failures (torch 2.11.0 on s390x) suggest debugging overhead. E=5 matches rubric: "Multiple unknowns, multiple teams, will likely require feature story mapping."
Calibration context: At RICE=3.6, this lands below the "standard moderate feature" cluster at 9.375 (R=5, I=5, C=75%, E=2) and near RHAISTRAT-1492 (AutoML Advanced Settings, RICE=3.75). This feels right: it is a high-impact feature for a small audience with significant cross-team effort. comments.author: Edward Arthur Quarm Jnr
comments.body:
RHAISTRAT-2304 status update —    RED
Release decision:
- RHAII CPU Power/Z slips from 3.6-EA1 to 3.6-EA2. A Z-specific (s390x) torch runtime failure could not be resolved within the EA1 code-freeze window. RHOAI will ship the existing 3.5 GA Power/Z CPU image for 3.6-EA1/Fast-1 per proposal (https://docs.google.com/document/d/1071_U6WckqaATHvTVO3dnzuAiDY4jYOY-KhRwVbsIts/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.9f9fm28fdv4
 ). AIPCC, midstream, and IBM agreed to slip to EA2.

Root cause:
- vLLM CPU on s390x fails at runtime during torch.compile when vllm serve runs (wheel build succeeds; Power and x86 work). The differentiator is VXE (s390x vector ISA) enablement — upstream PyPI torch is built without VXE (that path is dead code and never triggers), while AIPCC torch is built with VXE enabled. torch.compile therefore exercises the VXE path and hits a compile bug. Confirmed fix: upstream pytorch#173072.

EA2 fix decision:
- Apply upstream pytorch#173072 (currently blocked downstream by ADR-0081; IBM/Joseph Groenenboom pushing) or rebuild s390x torch. Both options have a large blast radius (all CPU torch-consuming wheels and spyre on torch 2.11). Routed to the pytorch call.

- File a blocker JIRA for the s390x runtime torch.compile/VXE issue.

cc: @Selbi Siddiqi @Imran Khalidi @Erwan Gallen @Alessandro Lazarotti @Joseph Groenenboom

RHAISTRAT-2304.description:
Business Need (from RFE)
The full business need is maintained in the source RFE: RHAIRFE-2136

Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)
TL;DR
Build and publish a supported vLLM CPU container image for IBM Power (ppc64le) and IBM Z (s390x) within Red Hat AI Inference, by migrating the existing Dockerfile.konflux.cpu and architecture-specific build scripts in the red-hat-data-services/vllm-cpu repository to AIPCC base images, onboarding prebuilt wheel packages, and establishing Konflux pipelines for multi-arch builds. The image integrates with RHOAI via the existing vllm-cpu-power-runtime-template and vllm-cpu-z-runtime-template platform templates.
Components: vllm-cpu, odh-model-controller (runtime templates), rhods-operator (CSV relatedImages)
Technical Approach
Container Image Build Architecture
The red-hat-data-services/vllm-cpu repository already contains the essential build infrastructure for ppc64le and s390x. The Dockerfile.konflux.cpu implements a two-stage build that dispatches to architecture-specific build scripts: build_vllm_ppc64le.sh compiles OpenBLAS, Apache Arrow, and numactl from source, while build_vllm_s390x.sh compiles OpenBLAS, Apache Arrow, and LLVM. The vLLM wheel is then built with uv build --wheel and installed into a Python virtual environment at /opt/vllm.
The primary technical gap is that the Konflux Dockerfile currently builds on registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal and installs Python packages from upstream PyPI, the PyTorch CPU index, and IBM DevPI. This must be migrated to the AIPCC CPU base image (quay.io/aipcc/base-images/cpu), which supports aarch64, ppc64le, s390x, and x86_64. The AIPCC base provides Python 3.12 pre-configured with the RHEL AI Python Package Index, eliminating the need for direct upstream package index access and enabling hermetic builds.
Once RHAIRFE-1926 delivers prebuilt wheel packages, the architecture-specific build scripts can be simplified: native library compilation from source (OpenBLAS, Arrow, LLVM) would be replaced by installing prebuilt wheels from the AIPCC index. Some native dependencies (numactl, OpenMP) will still need to be installed via microdnf from RHEL repositories available in the AIPCC base.
Konflux Pipeline Configuration
A Konflux pipeline must be configured to produce multi-arch images for ppc64le and s390x. The existing Dockerfile.konflux.cpu already targets these architectures, but the pipeline configuration in .tekton/ must be validated to trigger builds for both. Each architecture requires its own Tekton PipelineRun since the build scripts compile architecture-specific native code. The resulting images are published to registry.redhat.io/rhaii/odh-vllm-cpu-rhel9 under architecture-specific manifests, then assembled into a multi-arch manifest list.
Platform Integration
No changes are required to the KServe, odh-model-controller, or Dashboard components. The platform templates (vllm-cpu-power-runtime-template and vllm-cpu-z-runtime-template) already exist in odh-model-controller/config/runtimes/. These templates reference the vLLM CPU image via SHA256 digest from the operator CSV relatedImages. Once the image is published, the image reference in the CSV is updated by Release Engineering and the templates work automatically. The HardwareProfile webhook handles resource injection and the Dashboard discovers templates via annotation scanning -- no code changes needed from those teams.
The image exposes the OpenAI-compatible REST API on port 8080 via vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server, consistent with all other vLLM OOTB templates. gRPC is not exposed in platform templates (REST-only per platform convention).
Affected Components
- vllm-cpu (IBM Power/Z teams): Migrate Dockerfile.konflux.cpu to AIPCC base image; update build scripts for prebuilt wheel consumption; configure Konflux pipeline for ppc64le and s390x

- odh-model-controller (Model Runtimes team): Update runtime template image digests once new images are published (routine image bump, no logic changes)

- rhods-operator (Release Engineering): Add ppc64le and s390x image references to CSV relatedImages for disconnected deployment support

Impacted Teams
- IBM Power team (vllm-cpu ppc64le build): Build, validate, and maintain the ppc64le container image

- IBM Z team (vllm-cpu s390x build): Build, validate, and maintain the s390x container image

- RHAIIS/AIPCC team (AIPCC base images, wheel packages): Deliver prebuilt wheel packages (RHAIRFE-1926) and support AIPCC base image consumption

- Release Engineering (Konflux pipelines, CSV): Configure Konflux pipelines for multi-arch builds and update CSV relatedImages

- Model Runtimes team (integration tests): Validate image works end-to-end with KServe on Power and Z clusters

High Level Requirements
- [P0] vLLM CPU container image builds successfully for ppc64le architecture on AIPCC CPU base

- [P0] vLLM CPU container image builds successfully for s390x architecture on AIPCC CPU base

- [P0] Image serves LLM inference requests via OpenAI-compatible REST API on port 8080

- [P0] Image is published to registry.redhat.io with SHA256-pinned digests

- [P0] Konflux pipeline produces multi-arch image manifests for ppc64le and s390x

- [P1] Image supports disconnected/air-gapped deployment via RELATED_IMAGE pattern in operator CSV

- [P1] Image passes RHOAI integration tests using existing vllm-cpu-power and vllm-cpu-z runtime templates

- [P1] Build uses prebuilt wheels from AIPCC index (hermetic build, no upstream PyPI access)

- [P2] Image size is within acceptable limits for air-gapped deployment (comparable to x86 CPU variant)

Dependencies
- RHAIRFE-1926 — Prebuilt vLLM CPU wheel packages for Power and Z (internal, needed): Hard prerequisite. Without prebuilt wheels for ppc64le and s390x, the image build cannot use AIPCC hermetic builds. Currently blocks image production.

- AIPCC CPU base image (internal, exists): quay.io/aipcc/base-images/cpu already supports ppc64le, s390x, x86_64, and aarch64. Available for consumption.

- RHEL AI Python Package Index (internal, exists): Must include all vLLM CPU dependencies for ppc64le and s390x. Package availability depends on RHAIRFE-1926 completion.

- Konflux build infrastructure (internal, exists): Multi-arch build support exists in Konflux. Pipeline configuration needed for this specific component.

- Power and Z test infrastructure (internal, unknown): CI/CD test clusters with ppc64le and s390x nodes must be available for integration testing.

Non-Functional Requirements
- Security: Image must be built on AIPCC CPU base image (quay.io/aipcc/base-images/cpu) which provides UBI9 / RHEL 9.6 foundation with FIPS-compliant system OpenSSL. Python application inherits FIPS compliance from the base image. (architecture context: vllm-cpu.md, overlay 0017)

- Backwards Compatibility: No backwards compatibility concerns. This delivers new architecture support that does not exist today. Existing x86 vLLM CPU image is unaffected.

- Build Hermeticity: All Python packages must be sourced from the AIPCC pip index with no direct access to upstream PyPI, PyTorch CPU index, or IBM DevPI at build time. This is a security directive for all RHOAI serving runtime images. (architecture context: overlay 0014, overlay 0017)

Out-of-Scope
- Prebuilt vLLM CPU wheel packages for ppc64le and s390x -- tracked in RHAIRFE-1926

- GPU-accelerated vLLM variants (CUDA, ROCm, Gaudi) -- owned by RHAII team, separate images

- IBM Spyre accelerator support -- separate fork (red-hat-data-services/vllm-spyre), separate strategy

- vLLM engine feature development (multimodal, tool calling, speculative decoding) -- RHAII scope

- gRPC protocol support for vLLM -- not exposed in RHOAI platform templates (REST-only)

- x86 vLLM CPU image -- already exists at Tech Preview, tracked separately

- llm-d integration on Power/Z -- depends on this image but is a separate feature scope

Acceptance Criteria (Proposed -- requires PM/Engineering validation)
- Given an OpenShift cluster running on IBM Power (ppc64le) with KServe and odh-model-controller deployed,

   when a user creates an InferenceService referencing the vllm-cpu-power-runtime-template with a compatible LLM model stored in S3,    then the vLLM CPU container starts, loads the model, and responds to /v1/chat/completions requests with valid inference output,    measured by HTTP 200 response with non-empty choices[].message.content matching expected keywords.
- Given an OpenShift cluster running on IBM Z (s390x) with KServe and odh-model-controller deployed,

   when a user creates an InferenceService referencing the vllm-cpu-z-runtime-template with a compatible LLM model,    then the vLLM CPU container starts, loads the model, and serves inference via the OpenAI-compatible REST API,    measured by HTTP 200 response to /v1/completions with valid generated text.
- Given a disconnected OpenShift cluster with mirrored images,

   when the operator CSV relatedImages includes the vLLM CPU ppc64le/s390x image digests,    then oc-mirror successfully mirrors the images and the runtime template deploys without external registry access,    measured by successful pod creation using only mirrored image references.
- The vLLM CPU container image for ppc64le and s390x is built on the AIPCC CPU base image with all Python dependencies sourced from the RHEL AI Python Package Index,

   measured by Dockerfile FROM directive referencing quay.io/aipcc/base-images/cpu and no pip install commands using external indices.
- The /health endpoint on port 8080 returns HTTP 200 after model loading completes,

   measured by readiness probe succeeding within the configured initial delay (120s for readiness).
Effort Estimate
Size: S (1-2 sprints)
The core work is container image build configuration, not new feature development. The Dockerfile and architecture-specific build scripts already exist. The primary effort is: (1) migrating the base image to AIPCC CPU and updating dependency installation to use the AIPCC index (~0.5 sprint), (2) configuring and validating Konflux pipelines for ppc64le and s390x builds (~0.5 sprint), (3) integration testing on Power and Z clusters (~0.5 sprint). This is gated on RHAIRFE-1926 (prebuilt wheels) which is tracked separately. The estimate assumes prebuilt wheels are available when this work begins.
Risks
- Prebuilt wheel availability delay (RHAIRFE-1926): If prebuilt wheels for ppc64le/s390x are not available, the image cannot be built hermetically on AIPCC base. -- Mitigation: Track RHAIRFE-1926 as a hard gate. If delayed, evaluate whether a non-hermetic interim build on ubi9/ubi-minimal (current approach) can be promoted as Tech Preview while hermetic migration proceeds separately.

- Architecture-specific native compilation failures: OpenBLAS, Arrow, and LLVM builds from source may fail on specific architecture/toolchain combinations during the AIPCC migration. The rhoai-3.5-ea.2 branch already experienced s390x build issues requiring torch 2.11.0 fixes. -- Mitigation: IBM Power/Z teams maintain architecture-specific build scripts and have direct access to test hardware. Surface failures early by running test builds during sprint 1.

- AIPCC index missing dependencies: Some vLLM CPU dependencies (e.g., intel_extension_for_pytorch is x86-only, IBM DevPI packages for ppc64le) may not yet be in the AIPCC index. -- Mitigation: Cross-reference requirements/cpu.txt against AIPCC index availability during planning. Initiate AIPCC package onboarding (1-3 week lead time) for any missing packages before build work begins.

- Test cluster availability: Integration testing requires OpenShift clusters on Power and Z hardware, which may have limited availability. -- Mitigation: Reserve Power and Z test cluster time during sprint planning. Coordinate with IBM teams who maintain test environments for these architectures.

Assumptions
- RHAIRFE-1926 will deliver prebuilt wheel packages for ppc64le and s390x before this work begins -- needs validation

- The AIPCC CPU base image (quay.io/aipcc/base-images/cpu) remains stable and available for ppc64le and s390x -- confirmed (overlay 0017)

- IBM Power and Z teams will continue to own and maintain the architecture-specific build scripts -- confirmed (overlay 0014, overlay 0015)

- Existing vllm-cpu-power and vllm-cpu-z runtime templates do not require modification beyond image digest updates -- needs validation

- The vLLM CPU image on Power/Z will serve the same models and API endpoints as the x86 variant -- needs validation (model compatibility may vary by architecture)

Open Questions
- When will RHAIRFE-1926 prebuilt wheels be available? (Owner: AIPCC/RHAIIS team) -- Blocks all work on this strategy; timeline determines sprint planning.

- Which models are validated for ppc64le and s390x? (Owner: IBM Power/Z teams) -- The existing tests use Falcon3-7B, Llama-3.2-1B, Phi-4, Mistral-7B, and Granite-3.1-8B with bfloat16 dtype. Need to confirm which models will be in the GA support matrix.

- What is the target support level: Tech Preview or GA? (Owner: Product Management) -- vLLM CPU for x86 is currently Tech Preview. Should ppc64le/s390x launch at the same level or does the RFE imply GA support?

- Are all vLLM CPU Python dependencies available in the AIPCC index for ppc64le and s390x? (Owner: AIPCC team) -- Must be verified before sprint 1. Missing packages require 1-3 week onboarding lead time.

Supporting Documentation
- Source RFE: RHAIRFE-2136

- Prerequisite RFE: RHAIRFE-1926 (prebuilt wheel packages)

- Architecture context: vllm-cpu.md, kserve.md, odh-model-controller.md, PLATFORM.md (RHOAI 3.5-ea.2)

- Overlay 0014: Model Runtimes team architecture

- Overlay 0015: vLLM variant architecture

- Overlay 0017: AIPCC base images

- Design doc: _To be created_

Prerequisites & Process Gates

- ODH/RHOAI Build Onboarding: _Pending human review_

- Accelerator/Package Support: _Pending human review_ -- AIPCC wheel availability for ppc64le/s390x must be confirmed

- Documentation Support: _Pending human review_

- UXD Support: _Pending human review_ -- No UX changes expected (existing templates, no new UI)

- Performance Team Support: _Pending human review_ -- Performance baseline for CPU inference on Power/Z may be needed

Staff Engineer / SME Input
Add technical corrections, architectural direction, component preferences, or domain expertise below. Write in declarative, cumulative form — statements that remain valid across refinement iterations. This input takes priority over architecture context when they conflict. After review: address findings, then remove the needs-attention label from Jira.

RHAISTRAT-2046.description:
Problem Statement
Current Challenge
Specific AIPCC processes currently exhibit severe non-compliance with core Red Hat Product Security requirements. Multiple critical security and compliance gaps have been identified across the build pipeline, artifact provenance, dependency management, and release gating processes.
The primary drivers of this non-compliance stem from the proprietary nature of certain affected upstream artifacts (which limits visibility) and insufficient engineering runway allocated to address these gaps prior to the upcoming release cycle. This RFE aggregates the consolidated business risks and outlines a structured remediation roadmap requiring immediate executive alignment.
Identified Security Gaps
#
Exposure
Impact
Severity
1
Shipping pre-built third-party binaries without source code visibility.
Zero Patch Capability: Red Hat cannot analyze or remediate vulnerabilities in these binaries. Customers are exposed to unmitigable CVEs.
Critical
2
Missing Legal sign-off for redistribution of libtpu.
Immediate Legal Liability: Potential breach of Google commercial redistribution terms. Risk of legal action or forced product recall.
Critical
3
Non-hermetic builds pulling unverified upstream elements.
Malware/Injection Risk & Lack of Provenance: Vulnerable to upstream dependency poisoning. Inability to verify chain of custody.
Critical
4
End-of-Life (EOL) Python 3.11 base image for KFTO.
Permanently Unpatched Vulnerabilities: Python maintainers do not backport security fixes for EOL releases. Core runtime remains exposed.
High
5
Internal CI/CD systems operating without Security Operating Approvals (SOA/ESS).
Privileged Credential Exposure: Unverified credential/token storage for automated repository-write bots. Compromise could poison downstream builds.
Critical
6
Automated security gates intentionally disabled for RHAI & RHOAI disk/container images.
Compliance Failure: Absence of SBOMs violates upcoming regulatory frameworks. Suppressed cve.cve_blockers parameters.
Critical
7
Suppressed CVE blocker release gates.
Blind Shipping: Shipped images lack SLSA provenance, CVE scan results, and SAST analysis. No verifiable security posture exists.
Critical
8
Pre-compiled packages pulled directly from third-party vendor repositories (Mellanox, AMD, Intel, CentOS, EPEL).
Supply Chain Risk: Vendor supply chain compromises propagate directly to Red Hat. Artifacts cannot be signed with approved Red Hat keys.
High

Risk Classification
- Severe Technical Vulnerability: 5 of 8 identified gaps are ranked Critical. These represent scenarios where Red Hat cannot patch software, cannot prove provenance, or is actively bypassing release-gate verification.

- Regulatory Exposure: 2 gaps carry direct regulatory penalties. The upcoming EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) mandates Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) and strict vulnerability handling. Non-compliance carries severe global financial penalties.

- Immediate Legal Exposure: 1 gap carries immediate legal risk. The libtpu redistribution issue could trigger legal action or injunctions from Google regardless of our overall security posture.

Why This Matters Now
- Regulatory Timelines: EU CRA enforcement structures are tightening. SBOM generation gaps (Gap #6) must be resolved before artifacts are distributed into European markets.

- Escalating Supply Chain Vectors: Recent high-profile compromises (e.g., XZ Utils, SolarWinds) demonstrate that non-hermetic builds and unvetted third-party binary pipelines (Gaps #1, #3, #5, #8) are high-priority target vectors.

- Enterprise Customer Procurement: Government, financial, and healthcare sectors increasingly enforce SLSA provenance, signed SBOMs, and CVE transparency as baseline procurement requirements.

- Compounding Technical Debt: Retrofitting security compliance into post-release software architectures is significantly more expensive and disruptive than building compliance into the active release gate.

⚠️ Executive Decision Required
This RFE requests that the Accountable VP formally select and sign off on one of two courses of action:
- Option A: Accept the Risks — Formally document risk acceptance with a designated business owner, defined mitigation parameters, and an explicit review cadence. Ship the next release with acknowledged gaps.

- Option B: Delay the Release(s) — Pause upcoming release milestones until the identified Critical gaps are fully remediated to meet Product Security standards.


2. Business Alignment
Business Value
- Risk Reduction: Eliminates zero-patch-capability exposure, restores standard CVE remediation SLA capabilities, establishes explicit chain-of-custody provenance, and brings internal infrastructure under corporate security governance.

- Compliance Readiness: Achieves baseline readiness for the EU Cyber Resilience Act and provides the necessary artifact compliance requirements (FedRAMP, SOC2, ISO 27001) demanded by partners.

- Legal Protections: Resolves libtpu redistribution liabilities proactively before becoming a matter of active legal dispute.

- Customer Trust: Ensures enterprise and regulated-industry customers can validate Red Hat's security claims against industry standard software attestations.

Quantifiable Impact (Unmitigated Risk Materialization)
Scenario
Estimated Business Impact
CVE in unpatched 3rd-party binary (Gap #1)
Inability to patch. Red Hat must issue a public advisory stating "No Fix Available," resulting in significant customer erosion.
Google legal action on libtpu (Gap #2)
Immediate legal defense costs, potential product injunctions, and forced product withdrawal from the market.
Supply chain compromise via build pipeline (Gap #3)
Intensive incident response overhead, brand damage, and mandatory data breach notification cycles.
EU CRA Non-Compliance Fine (Gap #6)
Up to 2.5% of global annual turnover or EUR 15M (whichever is higher).
Compromised CI/CD credentials (Gap #5)
Full pipeline isolation and rebuild requirements. All downstream artifacts become suspect.

Remediation Cost vs. Incident Cost: Remediating these gaps requires targeted engineering resources over 1–2 quarters. Conversely, a single unmitigated security or legal incident is estimated to exceed remediation costs by 10x to 100x in financial and brand liability.

Alignment to Red Hat AI Outcomes
This initiative directly underpins the following corporate pillars:
- Product Security & Trust: Maintains the foundational enterprise promise of Red Hat software.

- Regulatory Compliance: Aligns development output with global legal and security standards.

- Operational Excellence: Implements secure, deterministic, and scalable automated pipelines.

RHOAISTRAT-631.description:
Feature Refinement Document: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1JZGeFz_dlLf2ajZnn2NFK9ak_Dfjh0Z3BBAAnlXRujY/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.9ravvzwdbl5t
The current platform's model experimentation metrics are distributed across various components, catering to both predictive and generative use cases. This feature will enhance existing experiment tracking capabilities to better support Generative AI (GenAI) use cases.
Initially, the goal is to establish experiment tracking as a centralized service for managing experiments and storing performance metrics, and evaluations. This will enable systematic tracking of foundation model performance as they get customized, ensuring reproducible validation and evaluation across all Red Hat AI components and services by storing all relevant data and artifacts.
Goals
- Develop visualizations that enable AI engineers and researchers to correlate run parameters and configurations with evaluations and key performance metrics. For the Minimum Viable Product (MVP), the following use cases should be included:
- Model compression

- Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

- Document preprocessing

- Evaluation of Models performance


- Enhance the usability of experiment tracking capabilities through:
- A single-page  summarized visualization of runs with filtering options and user-friendly configuration of metrics of interest.

- An interactive run comparison page.


- Support diverse run types for experiment tracking, including:
- Pipelines

- Notebooks

- Distributed Workloads (KubeFlow Trainer)


- Support low effort integration with the tracking service. With auto-logging of metrics customers just start a job that is tracked by default as an experiment.

- Enhance the metadata stored for a run
- User that started the run 

- environment metadata

- Infra specs{*}*


- Support various hardware profiles.

- Instrument a subset of Red Hat OpenShift AI (RHOAI) components for metric tracking:
- KubeFlow Pipelines

- Notebooks

- KubeFlow Trainer (collect the metrics and checkpoints from the distributed nodes/jobs).


- Provide MLFlow equivalency and support migration scenarios from MLFlow to facilitate adoption of RHOAI

Out of Scope
- Developing a new experiment tracking system from inception.

 
Requirements Functional
- Decouple metrics and evaluation tracking from AI pipelines. Experiment tracking should function as an independent service, compatible with various RHOAI components such as workbenches, training SDKs, and external components.

- Introduce new visualizations to facilitate improved comparisons of:
- Input parameters

- Metrics and evaluations

- Forecasting of metrics


- Implement filterable categories on the experiment runs page (MVP), including:
- Run type: (e.g., Workbench, Pipeline, Training job, Script)

- Run name: (e.g., Compressor, RAG)

- Owner

- Metrics


- Ensure filters are interactively applicable with dynamic updates to search results upon selection (MVP).

- Establish default sorting of search results and unfiltered lists by metrics (descending).

- Display metadata corresponding to filterable categories for each experiment listed in the catalog.

- Support queries on experiment data.

- Support the ability to publish to Model Registry the metadata and artifacts of the champion run

Data & Integration
- Integrate with Model Registry for storing metrics and evaluations.

Done - Acceptance Criteria
- A new left navigation option for experiments is available within RHOAI UI.

- Users are presented with a landing page displaying a table of available experiments (including runs and metrics) with filtering capabilities.

- The metrics displayed in the table are configurable, and the table is interactive.

-  Users can create a new experiment, then create a new run, select its type, and be directed to the specific run flow (e.g., pipelines).

- Upon selecting an experiment, users can view a table containing only the runs for that specific experiment.

- Users can compare multiple runs and view an interactive visualization of parameters and metrics of interest.

- Users can select different metrics or parameters for comparison.

Documentation Considerations
- Update RHOAI documentation with a new section on experimentation, encompassing metrics and evaluations, to explain the new capabilities.

Background & Strategic Fit
A significant challenge for customers adopting AI in production environments is the comprehensive evaluation and metric tracking. This process must consider the entire system, not solely the models. Therefore, a centralized service dedicated to systematically tracking and versioning this data is crucial. Currently, customers experience fragmented metric exploration across various AI components, with support limited to pipelines. This feature aims to expand support to include more components capable of tracking metrics and evaluations within a single, unified service.
Furthermore, this service will align with the new RHOAI GenAI Studio, contributing to the strategic objective of simplifying and centralizing the GenAI experience for Red Hat AI customers.

comments.author: Doug Hellmann
comments.body:
https://github.com/openvinotoolkit/model_server
  is a C++ application which could conceivably be built in the image instead of as a package.

comments.author: Lance Barto
Steven Grubb
comments.body:
Well, there’s a lot to this C++ application. It goes through several phases where it is building dependencies. Then it pulls some of them together at the end. There is a model_server component which is the API that our users interface with. It uses drogon for the API and tensorflow for the predictive part. But tensorflow is being removed in the 2026.3 release. Then there is a C++ library which then has python bindings. There is a very tight dependency loop between openvino, nncf, optimum-intel, and transformers. They all have to be in sync and sometimes to an exact git commit. This changes every release.

I am looking at how to disassemble the whole thing. There are 4 different git repos that we mirror that make up this application. model_server, openvio, openvino.genai, openvino-tokenizers. Model_server has the Dockerfile that builds the whole project by cloning the other repos into the tree.

We do not need the final app on-boarded. But we’ll have to see how to break this all down so it compiles it’s part and links.

RHAIRFE-2136.description:
Feature Overview
Red Hat AI Inference (RHAII) customers on IBM Power (ppc64le) and IBM Z (s390x) cannot deploy vLLM CPU inference workloads because no supported vLLM CPU container image exists for these architectures. Without a container image, customers on Power and Z cannot use RHAII for LLM serving, creating a platform support gap compared to x86.
On x86, RHAII ships a vLLM CPU container image that provides a supported, production-ready serving runtime. The equivalent image is missing for Power and Z, meaning customers on these platforms have no supported path to deploy vLLM-based inference through RHAII.
Business Justification
IBM Power and IBM Z represent strategic platform investments for RHOAI and RHAII. Customers deploying on these architectures expect feature parity with x86, including a supported container image for vLLM CPU inference. Delivering the image completes the stack: once the prerequisite wheel packages (RHAIRFE-1926) are available, the container image enables end-to-end LLM serving on Power and Z through RHAII.
Desired Outcome
A supported vLLM CPU container image is available for IBM Power (ppc64le) and IBM Z (s390x) within Red Hat AI Inference, enabling customers to deploy LLM serving workloads on these architectures with a production-ready, supported container runtime.
Prerequisites
Prebuilt vLLM CPU wheel packages for Power and Z (RHAIRFE-1926) must be available before the container image can be built.
Scope
- Build and publish a vLLM CPU container image for ppc64le and s390x architectures

- Image must be compatible with RHAII serving runtime and RHOAI deployment model

- CI/CD pipeline for multi-arch image builds including Power and Z

Out of Scope
Prebuilt wheel packages — tracked separately in RHAIRFE-1926.

RHAIRFE-1926.description:
Feature Overview
RHOAI components on IBM Power (ppc64le) and IBM Z (s390x) require prebuilt CPU-only wheel packages for vLLM and its dependencies. Today, these packages must be compiled from source, which introduces dependency management issues (e.g., SciPy, NumPy toolchains), longer build times, and increased failure rates.
RHOAI hermetic builds require all dependencies to be available as prebuilt wheel packages. This is not currently supported for ppc64le and s390x, which blocks llm-d integration in RHOAI on Power and Z — llm-d depends on vLLM CPU wheels for its KV caching and tokenizer components.
Business Justification
IBM Power and IBM Z represent strategic platform investments for RHOAI. Customers deploying on these architectures expect feature parity with x86, including supported LLM serving capabilities. The absence of prebuilt vLLM wheel packages is the first prerequisite gap that must be resolved before RHOAI can deliver LLM serving on Power and Z.
Desired Outcome
Prebuilt CPU-only wheel packages for the components listed in scope are available for IBM Power (ppc64le) and IBM Z (s390x), enabling RHOAI hermetic builds to include vLLM CPU dependencies without compiling from source.
Scope — Packages Requiring Prebuilt Wheels
Common (ppc64le and s390x): numactl llvmlite opencv opencv-python-headless rust torch-vision hf-xet outlines-core-builder numba pytorch pyarrow
Additional ppc64le packages: lapack openblas torchaudio blake3 cbor2 llguidance  openai-harmony outlines_core xgrammar
Out of Scope
vLLM CPU container image for Red Hat AI Inference — tracked separately in RHAIRFE-2136.

links.summary: Xeon Model Discoverability: Labeling, Catalog Refresh, and HuggingFace Collection
Xeon Model Discoverability

RHAISTRAT-1714.description:
Summary
Customers deploying on Intel Xeon need a clear way to discover which Red Hat AI models are validated and optimized for Xeon hardware. Today, validated Xeon models lack the appropriate label in the model catalog, there is no curated Xeon collection on Hugging Face, and models already shipped have not been rescanned to surface Xeon compatibility metadata. This limits discoverability for Intel joint customers and undermines a published blog that references the Xeon collection URL.
Problem Statement
Red Hat AI has completed validation of a set of models for Intel Xeon (documented in the "Model-List-April-9th-2026" spreadsheet, "Validated Models - Yes Only" tab). However, customers cannot currently identify these models as Xeon-validated through the model catalog because:
- The Xeon label has not been affixed to the validated models.

- Models that have already shipped were not scanned for Xeon compatibility, so the catalog does not reflect their Xeon readiness.

- There is no curated Xeon collection on Hugging Face (the expected URL https://huggingface.co/collections/RedHatAI/intel-xeon-compatible-models
  does not resolve), which breaks a published blog post that links to it.

Affected Customers
- Intel partnership: Joint go-to-market customers deploying RHOAI on Intel Xeon infrastructure who need to identify compatible, validated models.

- Red Hat AI users on CPU-based deployments: Users running inference on Intel Xeon who need confidence that selected models are validated for their hardware.

Business Justification
This is driven by the Red Hat–Intel partnership. Xeon model discoverability is a joint go-to-market commitment. A published blog post references the Hugging Face Xeon collection URL, which currently does not resolve — creating a broken experience for customers and partners following the blog's guidance. The validated model list is ready; the catalog and collection need to reflect it.
Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Validated models from the final provided list have the Xeon label affixed in the model catalog

- [ ] All previously shipped models from the validated list are rescanned so the Xeon label is pulled into the catalog

- [ ] A Xeon collection exists on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/collections/RedHatAI/intel-xeon-compatible-models
 containing the validated models

- [ ] The final model list is attached to or referenced in this ticket before work begins

Success Criteria
- Customers browsing the Red Hat AI model catalog can filter or identify Xeon-validated models by label.

- The Hugging Face Xeon collection URL resolves and displays the curated set of validated models.

- The published blog post's link to the Xeon collection functions correctly.

Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)
TL;DR
Add the "Xeon" label to validated Intel Xeon models in the Red Hat AI model catalog by updating the model-metadata-collection indexes and triggering a catalog rebuild, rescan previously shipped models for Xeon compatibility metadata, and create a curated Xeon collection on HuggingFace at the published URL.
Components: model-metadata-collection, odh-dashboard (catalog consumer), HuggingFace (external)
Technical Approach
This strategy delivers Xeon model discoverability through three coordinated workstreams: catalog labeling, rescan of shipped models, and HuggingFace collection creation.
1. Xeon Label in Model Catalog. The model-metadata-collection component generates YAML catalogs (validated-models-catalog.yaml, models-catalog.yaml) from model index files and HuggingFace metadata enrichment. To affix the "Xeon" label, update the validated-models-index.yaml (and models-index.yaml if applicable) to include a xeon tag on each validated model entry from the provided model list spreadsheet ("Model-List-April-9th-2026", "Validated Models - Yes Only" tab). The model-extractor CLI already supports tags and labels on model entries (tags such as validated, featured, lab-teacher). Adding a xeon tag to validated entries follows the existing labeling pattern. After index updates, a CI rebuild of the model-metadata-collection container image will produce updated catalog YAML files. The odh-dashboard then consumes these updated catalogs via volume mount at /app/data and can surface the Xeon label for filtering.
2. Rescan Previously Shipped Models. Models already shipped to registry.redhat.io/rhelai1/ that are on the validated Xeon list but were originally scanned without Xeon metadata need to be rescanned. The model-extractor CLI fetches OCI manifests and model card metadata from the registry, then enriches with HuggingFace data. Running the extractor against the full validated index (with the newly added xeon tag) will regenerate catalog entries for these models, picking up the Xeon label. This is part of the normal catalog rebuild pipeline -- no code changes to the extractor are needed, only index file updates and a rebuild.
3. HuggingFace Xeon Collection. Create a curated collection at https://huggingface.co/collections/RedHatAI/intel-xeon-compatible-models containing the validated Xeon models. The model-metadata-collection component already includes a HuggingFace client that discovers RedHatAI validated model collections (internal/huggingface/collections.go). However, collection creation on HuggingFace is a manual/API operation performed through the HuggingFace Hub interface or API, not through the model-extractor build pipeline. This is a one-time setup task that adds the validated models to the collection. Once the collection exists, future runs of the model-extractor can discover it if the collection is added to the HuggingFace collections configuration.
The dashboard UI (odh-dashboard) reads catalog YAML files and displays model metadata including tags. If the dashboard does not currently support filtering by hardware compatibility tags like xeon, a minor UI enhancement may be needed to expose this tag as a filter option. This should be validated during implementation.

Non-Functional Requirements
- Backwards Compatibility: Adding a new tag to model catalog entries is additive and does not break existing catalog consumers. Dashboard versions that do not recognize the xeon tag will ignore it. (architecture context: model-metadata-collection.md -- catalog is consumed via volume mount, additive fields are safe)

- Performance: Catalog rebuild is a CI/CD-time batch operation, not a runtime concern. No runtime performance impact. (architecture context: model-metadata-collection.md -- "Egress connections are only made during build-time CI/CD catalog generation, not at runtime")

- Security: No new security surface. HuggingFace collection creation uses existing org credentials. Catalog data flow is read-only at runtime via volume mount. (architecture context: model-metadata-collection.md)

Out-of-Scope
- Adding Xeon-specific inference optimization or runtime changes to vllm-cpu or OVMS

- Automated Xeon hardware detection or auto-labeling based on cluster hardware

- Performance benchmarking or certification of models on Xeon hardware (validation is already complete per the RFE)

Acceptance Criteria (Proposed -- requires PM/Engineering validation)
- Given a validated model from the provided Xeon model list, when a user browses the Red Hat AI model catalog, then the model displays a "Xeon" label, measured by the presence of the xeon tag in the generated validated-models-catalog.yaml for each model on the list.

- Given a model that was previously shipped to registry.redhat.io before Xeon validation, when the catalog is rebuilt after index updates, then the model's catalog entry includes the xeon tag, measured by comparing the model's tags in the regenerated catalog YAML.

- The HuggingFace collection at https://huggingface.co/collections/RedHatAI/intel-xeon-compatible-models resolves and contains all models from the validated list, measured by HTTP 200 response and model count matching the validated list.

- The published blog post's link to the Xeon collection returns a valid page (not 404), measured by HTTP response code.

- Given a user viewing the RHOAI dashboard model catalog, when filtering or browsing models, then Xeon-validated models are identifiable by label, measured by the Xeon tag being visible in the dashboard model catalog UI.

Effort Estimate
S (Small, 1-2 sprints). The work involves updating YAML index files in model-metadata-collection (data changes, no code changes to the extractor), triggering a standard CI rebuild, and creating a HuggingFace collection via their API. The dashboard verification is a minor validation task. Cross-team coordination is limited to confirming the final model list with Intel and verifying dashboard rendering.

Platform refinement review [RHAISTRAT-1492] - AutoML Advanced Experiment Settings - Preset Support & Evaluation Metric Override

parent.summary: [Outcome] Enable AutoML

RHAISTRAT-1492.description:
Problem Statement
Current experiment configuration (AutoML KFP pipeline input parameters) relies primarily on system-selected defaults for:
- Training configurations (e.g., model quality vs. speed trade-offs)

- Evaluation metrics used for optimization

While this simplifies the experience for new users, it introduces limitations.

Business Justification
Strategic Value: Provides advanced experiment control in AutoML through presets and metric override. Enables power users to optimize for specific business objectives (accuracy vs speed, custom evaluation metrics) while maintaining AutoML ease-of-use.
Customer Use Case: Enterprises have diverse optimization goals - some prioritize model quality for critical decisions, others need fast turnaround for rapid experimentation. Regulated industries may require specific evaluation metrics aligned to compliance requirements. Without presets, users waste time manually tuning configurations to achieve common trade-offs. Custom metric override enables domain-specific evaluation (e.g., false negative cost weighting in fraud detection).
Value Delivered:
- Common optimization presets (quality vs speed)

- Custom evaluation metric override for domain-specific needs

- Faster configuration for common use cases

- Flexibility for regulated industry requirements

Sovereign AI Alignment: User-controlled experiment configuration ensures training objectives align with business requirements without external constraints.
Pain Points
Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)
TL;DR
Expose two new KFP pipeline input parameters (eval_metric and preset) in the AutoML pipeline and surface them in the AutoML Dashboard UI with predefined value lists. This gives power users control over optimization targets and training speed/quality trade-offs while preserving defaults for new users.
Components: data-science-pipelines (AutoML pipeline), odh-dashboard (automl-ui plugin)
Technical Approach
The PM assessment (Lukasz Cmielowski, 2026-04-23) confirms the approach: the AutoML KFP Pipeline exposes two new input parameters (eval_metric and preset), and the AutoML Dashboard allows setting values based on a predefined list.
1. Pipeline Parameter Exposure: The AutoML KFP pipeline component adds two new optional input parameters. eval_metric controls which metric AutoGluon optimizes during training (e.g., accuracy, f1, roc_auc, log_loss, rmse, mae). preset enforces runtime constraints that trade off model quality against speed (e.g., best_quality, high_quality, good_quality, medium_quality). Both parameters have sensible defaults matching current behavior (system-selected metric and no preset constraint), ensuring backwards compatibility. The parameters are passed through to the AutoGluon TabularPredictor.fit() call within the training component.
2. Dashboard UI Integration: The AutoML UI micro-frontend (port 8643, federated via Module Federation into odh-dashboard) adds form controls for both parameters. eval_metric is rendered as a dropdown populated from a predefined list of supported metrics, grouped by task type (classification vs regression). preset is rendered as a selectable option set (e.g., radio buttons or dropdown) with descriptive labels explaining the quality/speed trade-off. Both controls show the default value when no override is selected. The UI communicates these parameters to the KFP pipeline via the existing pipeline submission flow.
Affected Components

Change
Owner Team

Add eval_metric and preset input parameters to AutoML KFP pipeline component

Non-Functional Requirements
- Performance: No runtime performance impact from adding pipeline parameters. Preset selection may change training duration by design (e.g., best_quality trains longer than medium_quality), but this is user-intended behavior. (Source: RFE — presets control speed vs quality trade-offs)

- Security: Dashboard controls are protected by existing kube-rbac-proxy authentication on odh-dashboard. No new RBAC resources needed — parameter submission follows existing pipeline execution authorization. (Source: architecture context — odh-dashboard.md)

Reach: 8 (Large group)
MaaS on xKS is the foundational enabler for RHAII's primary target market — non-OpenShift Kubernetes (AKS, CKS, EKS, GKE). RHAII is defined to run on "any Kubernetes," and MaaS is explicitly listed as part of the RHAII MVP. This reaches all future RHAII xKS deployments: enterprises needing multi-tenant inference API management on managed Kubernetes. Scoring R=8 rather than R=13 because this is Dev Preview (functional demonstration, not production-ready), so immediate direct reach is a large but not universal segment. Comparable to RHAISTRAT-1527 (Multimodal Support in Gen AI Studio, R=8) and RHAISTRAT-1547 (MaaS Self-Service Subscription Page, R=8) — platform features targeting the core MaaS/inference user base.
Impact: 8 (High — major pain point solved)
Without this feature, xKS users have zero MaaS capability — no validated deployment path, no user management strategy, no subscription management or rate limiting. The status quo is "completely blocked" (no workaround exists). MaaS on xKS is a blocking dependency for Dashboard/UI scope decisions and was required for Summit 2026. Per the Impact checklist: pain severity is maximum (blocked entirely), alternatives are nonexistent, and it unblocks downstream features and product positioning. Scoring I=8 rather than I=13 because Dev Preview scope limits the depth of per-user value delivered — core CRUD and OIDC auth, but no operator integration or production-readiness. Comparable to RHAISTRAT-1547 (MaaS Self-Service Subscription, I=8) — similarly critical MaaS enablement.
Confidence: 75% (Some evidence, some assumptions)
Evidence supporting R and I estimates:
- Approved RFE (RHAIRFE-1236, Critical priority) with clear business alignment

- Strategy review passed 6/8 (APPROVE) with human sign-off

- MaaS explicitly listed as RHAII MVP component in product definition

- Parent Outcome (RHAISTRAT-1077) is Blocker priority

Reasons not to score 100%:
- RHCL official xKS support commitment status was "Unknown" at strategy time — if

  Kuadrant cannot deploy on xKS, the auth/rate-limiting story collapses
- The feasibility reviewer flagged "critical dependency statuses are unvalidated"

- No telemetry data on actual xKS user demand (business case is strategic projection)

Per rubric: "Approved RFE with some customer evidence" and "strategy review passed" supports 75%. The 6/8 review score is slightly below the 7-8/8 benchmark but still APPROVE. Uncertainty about dependencies affects Effort more than R/I estimates, but the unvalidated RHCL commitment introduces enough R/I uncertainty (if no auth, the delivered value drops significantly) to cap at 75%.
Effort: 5 (High — multiple unknowns, multiple teams)
The strategy estimates M (3-5 sprints). Three teams involved: MaaS (primary), xKS Platform (secondary), and RHCL/OpenShift (critical external dependency). Key effort drivers:
- Helm chart packaging for maas-api, maas-controller, payload-processing

- OIDC configuration plumbing (Authorino config, configurable group claim paths)

- Validation on CKS (priority) then AKS — deployment, auth, rate limiting, observability

- Cross-team coordination overhead with RHCL and xKS Platform teams

- Unresolved: RHCL xKS support commitment, Kuadrant installability on CKS

Scoring E=5 rather than E=8 because: the core MaaS codebase exists (adaptation, not greenfield), the architecture review scored 2/2 (sound approach), and the OIDC integration is primarily configuration change (Authorino already supports OIDC). Fallback paths exist for the RHCL dependency (standalone Authorino+Limitador, direct Envoy ext_authz). Comparable to RHAISTRAT-1267 (Perses Dashboard Patterns, E=5) and RHAISTRAT-1527 (Multimodal Support, E=5) — cross-team platform features with multiple unknowns.
Calibration
RICE = (8 × 8 × 0.75) / 5 = 9.6
This lands exactly at the same score as RHAISTRAT-1527 (Multimodal Support in Gen AI Studio, 9.6) and RHAISTRAT-1758 (Agent Deployments View, 9.6). This feels right — all three are significant platform-enabling features with broad reach, high per-user impact, moderate confidence, and substantial cross-team effort.
Re-scoring Triggers
- RHCL confirms official xKS support → Confidence could increase to 100%, Effort could

  decrease to 3 (removing the largest dependency unknown)
- Kuadrant fails to install on CKS → Effort increases to 8 (fallback paths add work),

  Confidence drops to 50%
- Scope expands beyond Dev Preview to GA → Effort increases to 8+

- Summit deadline missed and product strategy shifts → Re-evaluate Reach and Impact

RHAISTRAT-1377.description:
Problem Statement
Red Hat AI Inference (RHAII) targets non-OpenShift Kubernetes environments (AKS, CKS, EKS, GKE), but MaaS - a key component of the RHAII product definition - has no validated deployment path or user management strategy for xKS.
Current State:
- MaaS is in Dev Preview on RHOAI 3.0 with OpenShift-specific dependencies

- No validated deployment of MaaS on xKS environments exists

- User management relies on Kubernetes RBAC identity mapping - unavailable on xKS

User Scenario: A platform team wants to deploy RHAII on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) with MaaS capabilities for multi-tenant inference API management. They need user authentication, subscription management, and rate limiting - but these depend on identity infrastructure that doesn't exist on xKS the way it does on OpenShift.
—
Business Alignment
What is the Business Value and/or Impact?
- Enables RHAII adoption on xKS - the primary target platform for the new product

- MaaS is explicitly listed as part of RHAII MVP (Dev Preview)

- Blocking dependency for Dashboard/UI scope decisions

- Required for Summit (May 2026) product announcement

Red Hat AI Outcome Alignment:
- Customer Success: Enables MaaS capabilities for xKS customers

- Competitive Positioning: Enterprise-grade inference API management on any Kubernetes

—
Proposed Solution/Rationale
Validate MaaS deployment on xKS and define user management strategy for non-OpenShift environments.
Solution Components:
- User Management Strategy for xKS:

  - Define authentication approach without k8s identity mapping   - Evaluate OIDC/OAuth2 integration options   - Document user identity flow for xKS deployments
- MaaS xKS Deployment Validation:

  - Deploy current MaaS on AKS/CKS test environment   - Document what works vs. what breaks   - Identify engineering delta to make it functional
What Gets Delivered (Dev Preview):
- Validated MaaS deployment on at least one xKS platform (AKS or CKS)

- User authentication solution (external OIDC)

- Core MaaS functionality: subscription/tier management, token rate limiting, API access

What Users Must Do:
- Provide their own identity provider (OIDC-compatible)

Key Assumptions:
- Dev Preview = functional demonstration, not production-ready

- Significant scope reduction from RHOAI MaaS GA (see below)

—
Scope Reduction from RHOAI MaaS GA
RHAII MaaS xKS Dev Preview is explicitly scoped down from RHOAI MaaS 3.4 GA. The following table clarifies what's included vs. excluded:
Included in xKS Dev Preview:
Feature
Notes
Token rate limiting
Core RHCL/Kuadrant functionality
Tier/subscription management
Basic tier/subscription CRUD both are acceptable
External OIDC authentication
Required
API access control
As usual

Excluded from xKS Dev Preview (Defer to future releases):
Feature
Reason
Operator Integration
xKS uses Helm-based installation

—
Acceptance Criteria
Deployment Validation:
- [ ] MaaS successfully deployed on at least on xKS platform (AKS AND CKS)

- [ ] Core functionality validated: subscription management, rate limiting

- [ ] Known limitations documented

User Management:
- [ ] User authentication strategy defined and documented

- [ ] External OIDC integration validated (or alternative approach)

- [ ] User identity flow documented for xKS deployments

—
Affected Customers/Partners & Scope
Current/Potential Customers:
- All RHAII xKS deployments (AKS, CoreWeave, EKS, GKE)

- Enterprises requiring multi-tenant inference API management

- Partners deploying RHAII on managed Kubernetes services

Scope:
- Impact: All RHAII xKS deployments requiring MaaS

- Timeline: Required for RHAII Tech Preview (Summit May 2026)

—
Reference Documents/Links
- RHAISTRAT-1077 - Red Hat AI Inference Outcome

- RHAIRFE-1056 - RHAII Dashboard/UI (blocked by MaaS xKS clarity)

- Red Hat AI Inference Product Definition - Naina's product definition deck showing MaaS as MVP component

- MaaS GA Scope Definition - RHOAI MaaS 3.4 GA scope

- Slack: #topic-redhat-ai-inference-xks - Jan 26 discussion on MaaS xKS ownership

- Slack: #forum-rhaii - Jan 23 discussion on user management dependency

—
Open Questions
User Management:
- What authentication approach should we use for xKS? (External OIDC? BYO identity provider?)

- Can we leverage existing MaaS AuthPolicy with external OIDC, or are changes needed?

- How do we map external identities to MaaS subscriptions/tiers?

Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)
TL;DR
Deploy MaaS (Models as a Service) on non-OpenShift Kubernetes environments (xKS: CKS, AKS, EKS, GKE) as a Dev Preview for RHAII, using MaaS 3.4 GA as a baseline with Helm-based installation and external OIDC authentication replacing OpenShift-specific identity infrastructure. CKS (CoreWeave Kubernetes Service) is the priority platform per Staff Engineer Input. This is scoped to Dev Preview — functional demonstration, not production-ready. Observability (metrics, logging, tracing) is a core value proposition per Staff Engineer Input.
Components: models-as-a-service (maas-controller, maas-api, payload-processing BBR ext_proc), Kuadrant/RHCL (Authorino, Limitador), Gateway API, PostgreSQL, observability (Prometheus, Perses dashboards, structured logging)
Technical Approach
MaaS on RHOAI 3.4 GA relies on three OpenShift-specific dependencies: (1) OpenShift's built-in OAuth/OIDC for user identity (KubernetesTokenReview against the OpenShift API server), (2) OLM-based operator installation for the maas-controller and Kuadrant components, and (3) the openshift-default GatewayClass with Istio data plane for the MaaS gateway. For xKS Dev Preview, each of these must be replaced or adapted to work on non-OpenShift managed Kubernetes (CKS, AKS, EKS, GKE).
User Management Strategy for xKS
The MaaS architecture (architecture context: models-as-a-service.md) consists of three primary components: (1) maas-controller (operator managing 5 CRDs: Tenant, MaaSModelRef, MaaSAuthPolicy, MaaSSubscription, ExternalModel), (2) maas-api (REST service for OpenAI-compatible model listing, API key lifecycle management, subscription selection), and (3) payload-processing BBR ext_proc server (Envoy external processor for request transformations). Authentication enforcement is handled by Kuadrant Authorino via AuthPolicy CRs that the maas-controller generates and aggregates per model.
On RHOAI, Authorino uses KubernetesTokenReview to validate Bearer tokens against the OpenShift API server's identity mapping. On xKS, managed Kubernetes services do not expose the same identity infrastructure. The proposed approach (RFE comment from Lindani Phiri: "Utilize OIDC work planned for 3.4 for authentication") is to configure Authorino to use external OIDC validation instead of KubernetesTokenReview.
The customer provides their own OIDC-compatible identity provider (Keycloak, Entra ID, Google Identity Platform, Cognito, or other standards-compliant OIDC providers). The MaaS AuthPolicy resources (architecture context: deployment/base/maas-api/policies/auth-policy.yaml) would be updated to use Authorino's oidc identity source with the customer's OIDC issuer URL and JWKS endpoint. The Tenant CRD already supports external OIDC configuration (architecture context: Tenant CRD spec includes oidcIssuerURL, oidcClientID, oidcAudience), so this is a configuration change rather than a code change for basic OIDC integration. API key authentication (the sk-oai-* flow) requires no changes — it already uses the maas-api callback validation path (/internal/v1/api-keys/validate endpoint via Authorino HTTP callback), which is OIDC-agnostic.
The MaaSSubscription controller maps rate limiting tiers to user groups via CEL predicates on auth.identity.groups (architecture context: maas-controller/pkg/controller/maas/maassubscription_controller.go). On xKS, user group claims must be sourced from the OIDC token's group claim rather than Kubernetes RBAC groups. OIDC group claim formats vary across identity providers: Entra ID uses groups, Cognito uses cognito:groups, Google Identity Platform may use custom claims. The controller MUST support configurable claim path mapping to extract groups from different OIDC token formats. Implementation approach: add a groupClaimPath field to the Tenant CRD (default: auth.identity.groups) that is passed through to the MaaSSubscription controller's CEL predicate generation. This allows the claim path to be configured per deployment without code changes. If the Tenant CRD is frozen in MaaS 3.4 GA, the fallback is to document the required claim format and push IdP configuration burden to customers.
Deployment Strategy
xKS uses Helm-based installation (no OLM). The MaaS components (maas-api, maas-controller, payload-processing) must be packaged as Helm charts with configurable values for: gateway class name (not openshift-default), OIDC issuer configuration (issuer URL, client ID, audience, group claim path), TLS certificate source (cert-manager instead of OpenShift service-CA auto-generated certificates), PostgreSQL connection (may be shared with other RHAII components or dedicated), and group claim path mapping.
The MaaS gateway must use a GatewayClass available on the target xKS platform. CKS-specific validation (priority platform per Staff Engineer Input): CoreWeave deploys with Istio service mesh; the MaaS Helm chart must support istio GatewayClass with appropriate TLS and mTLS configuration for Istio's control plane integration. The architecture context confirms MaaS uses Gateway API HTTPRoutes (models-as-a-service.md: Ingress section documents HTTPRoute-based routing), which are GatewayClass-agnostic. Other validated options for future platforms: envoy-gateway (multi-platform), azure-application-gateway (AKS).
Kuadrant (RHCL) Deployment on xKS
RHCL (Red Hat Common Libraries) provides Kuadrant (Authorino + Limitador) for MaaS authentication and rate limiting. On RHOAI, RHCL deploys via OLM. On xKS (Helm-only), official RHCL xKS support must be confirmed with the OpenShift team — this is a strategic dependency.
Deployment options (priority order):
- Primary: RHCL Helm charts (requires OpenShift team commitment)

- Fallback: Standalone Authorino + Limitador via Helm

- Contingency: Direct Envoy ext_authz integration

Sprint 1 validation: Confirm RHCL xKS support commitment. If not committed, escalate to product leadership.
Observability Strategy
Observability is a core value proposition for MaaS on xKS. The xKS implementation must deliver:
- Metrics (P0): Token usage, rate limiting enforcement, API key lifecycle, inference latency. Requires Prometheus metrics instrumentation in maas-api (/metrics endpoint) and Perses dashboards.

- Logging (P1): Structured JSON logs for authentication decisions (Authorino), rate limit enforcement (Limitador), API key validation (maas-api). Integrate with CKS Grafana Loki.

- Tracing (P2): Distributed tracing through gateway → Authorino → Limitador → payload-processing → backend using OpenTelemetry.

Validation Approach
Deploy MaaS 3.4 GA codebase on CKS first (priority platform per Staff Engineer Input: "CKS (CoreWeave Kubernetes Service) is the most important and initial flavor of Kubernetes to support for RHAII MaaS on xKS. Validation, deployment strategy, and initial Helm chart work must prioritize CKS before AKS, EKS, or GKE."). Then validate on AKS (satisfies "AKS AND CKS" acceptance criterion from RFE). Document what works, what breaks, and the engineering delta (code changes, configuration changes, Helm chart packaging).
Known risk: MaaS 3.4 GA code freeze was late March 2026 per RFE comment from Jonathan Zarecki; it is now early May 2026, meaning the stable build should be available but integration timeline is tight for Summit (May 2026). Mitigation: obtain MaaS 3.4 RC build by April 27 (latest); begin CKS validation (priority platform) in parallel with RC testing; pre-identify MaaS 3.4 features that can be deferred if validation reveals blockers; maintain fallback demo using RHOAI 3.3 MaaS as proof-of-concept if 3.4 integration fails.
