Non-Functional Requirements
- Security: Authentication must use external OIDC with JWT validation via Authorino (RFE). API key validation flow remains unchanged -- maas-api validates keys internally (architecture context: models-as-a-service.md).

- Backwards Compatibility: No changes to RHOAI MaaS GA -- xKS changes must be additive or configuration-driven.

- Observability: Metrics must include token usage per user/subscription, rate limiting enforcement events, API key lifecycle events (creation, validation, revocation), and inference request latency, exposed via Prometheus-compatible endpoints (Staff Engineer Input: observability is a core value proposition). Logging must include structured authentication events, rate limit enforcement (429 responses with exceeded quota), and subscription selection decisions, formatted for aggregation in CKS Grafana Loki (Staff Engineer Input). Distributed tracing (P1) must capture request flow from gateway ingress through Authorino/Limitador/payload-processing to model backend (Staff Engineer Input).

Out-of-Scope

Acceptance Criteria (Proposed -- requires PM/Engineering validation)
Happy Path Criteria:
- Given a CKS cluster (priority platform) with RHCL/Kuadrant and Gateway API (Istio) installed, when MaaS is deployed via Helm chart with OIDC configuration, then the maas-api and maas-controller pods are running and healthy, measured by pod readiness checks passing.

- Given an AKS cluster with RHCL/Kuadrant and Gateway API installed, when MaaS is deployed via Helm chart with OIDC configuration, then the maas-api and maas-controller pods are running and healthy, measured by pod readiness checks passing.

- Given a deployed MaaS instance on CKS with OIDC configured, when a user authenticates with a valid OIDC JWT token and creates an API key, then the API key is persisted in PostgreSQL and can be used for model inference, measured by a successful inference request using the generated API key.

- Given a MaaSSubscription with token rate limits configured, when a user exceeds the rate limit, then Limitador returns HTTP 429, measured by monitoring the response status codes.

- Given an OIDC deployment with a non-standard group claim format and groupClaimPath configured to match that format, when a user with group membership authenticates, then the MaaSSubscription controller correctly maps the user to the appropriate subscription tier, measured by successful tier-based rate limiting enforcement.

- A document exists listing all known limitations of MaaS on xKS versus RHOAI MaaS GA.

- Given a deployed MaaS instance on CKS with Prometheus integration, when a user creates an API key, makes inference requests, and exceeds a rate limit, then Prometheus metrics include maas_api_key_created_total, maas_inference_requests_total{user, model, subscription}, and maas_rate_limit_enforced_total{user, model, exceeded_quota}, measured by querying the CKS Prometheus instance.

- Given a deployed MaaS instance on CKS with structured logging enabled, when an authentication event occurs (success or failure), then the log entry includes timestamp, user identity, authentication method (OIDC/API key), decision (allow/deny), and reason (if denied), measured by querying CKS Grafana Loki with label filters.

- Given a deployed MaaS instance on CKS with Perses dashboards installed, when an admin navigates to the MaaS observability dashboard, then the dashboard displays token usage per subscription, rate limiting enforcement events, and API key lifecycle metrics over the last 24 hours, measured by dashboard rendering with live data.

Failure Mode Criteria:
- Given a deployed MaaS instance, when the OIDC provider becomes unavailable (network partition or IdP downtime), then inference requests using valid API keys continue to succeed (API key validation is OIDC-independent), while OIDC-authenticated requests fail with HTTP 503 and a descriptive error message, measured by response status and error body.

- Given a MaaS deployment with Limitador pod terminated, when a user makes an inference request, then the request is denied with HTTP 503 (rate limiting enforcement unavailable), measured by response status and Envoy logs showing upstream connection failure.

- Given a deployed MaaS instance on xKS with cert-manager-issued TLS certificates, when the certificates are rotated (renewal before expiration), then active inference requests continue without interruption and new requests succeed with the new certificate, measured by zero connection errors during the rotation window and successful TLS handshake validation post-rotation.

- Given a MaaS deployment, when the PostgreSQL database becomes unavailable (network partition or pod restart), then API key creation requests fail with HTTP 503, existing API key validation requests fail (cache miss scenario), but OIDC token-based authentication continues to succeed (OIDC validation does not depend on PostgreSQL), measured by response status and error logs.

RHAI-706.description:
vLLM CPU on IBM Z (s390x) fails at runtime torch.compile when `vllm serve` runs. The wheel build succeeds; Power (ppc64le) and x86 are unaffected. This blocks RHAII CPU Power/Z delivery for 3.6-EA1; work slips to 3.6-EA2.

Root cause:
The differentiator is VXE (s390x vector ISA) enablement, not the compiler (AIPCC and IBM both build torch with gcc11).
- Upstream PyPI torch-2.11.0+cpu is built without VXE, so the VXE header code path is dead code and the bug never triggers.
- AIPCC torch is built with VXE enabled, so vLLM's runtime torch.compile exercises the VXE path and hits a compilation bug.

Confirmed fix: upstream pytorch#173072 (fixes the VXE code path), validated on the AIPCC build.

Fix options (3.6-EA2):
- pytorch#173072 - only confirmed fix; blocked downstream by ADR-0081 (no downstream patches for RH-maintained packages). Path forward: upstream it (IBM / Joseph Groenenboom pushing); AIPCC consumes once merged.
- Rebuild s390x torch with gcc-14 - unproven; the issue is the VXE code path, not the compiler. Needs validation before being considered.

Both carry a large blast radius (all CPU torch-consuming wheels + spyre, both on torch 2.11). CPU torch ownership moves to the pytorch team in EA2; decision routed to the pytorch call.

Interim: RHOAI ships the existing 3.5 GA Power/Z CPU image for 3.6-EA1/Fast-1.

- Pipeline produces architecture-specific image manifests for ppc64le and s390x

RHAI-119.description:
Migrate vllm-cpu containerfile from RHOAI to AIPCC for s390x
Description
Migrate the vllm-cpu container image build for s390x (IBM Z) from the current ubi9/ubi-minimal base to the AIPCC CPU base image. This includes updating the s390x-specific build script (build_vllm_s390x.sh) to consume prebuilt wheel packages from the RHEL AI Python Package Index instead of compiling native libraries (OpenBLAS, Apache Arrow, LLVM) from source, and eliminating direct access to upstream package indices at build time. The shared Dockerfile.konflux.cpu FROM directive migration is coordinated with the ppc64le AIPCC migration work.
Scope
- Update build_vllm_s390x.sh to install prebuilt wheels from the AIPCC index rather than compiling OpenBLAS, Apache Arrow, and LLVM from source

- Coordinate with the ppc64le AIPCC migration on shared Dockerfile.konflux.cpu changes (FROM directive, package index configuration)

- Remove or replace references to external package indices with AIPCC index configuration for s390x

- Verify all s390x Python dependencies in requirements/cpu.txt are available in the AIPCC index; initiate package onboarding for any missing packages

- Validate that the s390x container image builds successfully and produces a working inference server

- Validate inference serving on s390x hardware using OpenAI-compatible REST API on port 8080

Acceptance Criteria
- Dockerfile.konflux.cpu FROM directive references AIPCC CPU base image (quay.io/aipcc/base-images/cpu)

- build_vllm_s390x.sh uses prebuilt wheels from the AIPCC index instead of compiling native libraries from source

- No pip install or uv commands use external package indices (upstream PyPI, PyTorch CPU index) at build time

- Container image builds successfully for s390x architecture

- Image serves LLM inference requests via OpenAI-compatible REST API on port 8080 on s390x hardware, with HTTP 200 responses to /v1/completions with valid generated text

- /health endpoint on port 8080 returns HTTP 200 after model loading completes (within 120s readiness probe initial delay)

- Build pipeline green (Konflux pipeline produces successful s390x build)

- Image size is within acceptable limits for air-gapped deployment (comparable to x86 CPU variant)

- Validated model support matrix for s390x is documented, confirming which models (from the candidate set: Falcon3-7B, Llama-3.2-1B, Phi-4, Mistral-7B, Granite-3.1-8B) produce correct inference output on Z hardware

HLR Traceability
- [P0] vLLM CPU container image builds successfully for s390x architecture on AIPCC CPU base

- [P0] Image serves LLM inference requests via OpenAI-compatible REST API on port 8080

- [P0] Image is published to registry.redhat.io with SHA256-pinned digests

- [P1] Image passes RHOAI integration tests using existing vllm-cpu-z runtime template

- [P1] Build uses prebuilt wheels from AIPCC index (hermetic build, no upstream PyPI access)

- [P2] Image size is within acceptable limits for air-gapped deployment

Risks
- Prebuilt wheel availability (RHAIRFE-1926): This epic is gated on RHAIRFE-1926 delivering prebuilt s390x wheel packages. If delayed, evaluate non-hermetic interim build on ubi9/ubi-minimal as Tech Preview.

- Architecture-specific compilation failures: The rhoai-3.5-ea.2 branch required torch 2.11.0 fixes for s390x and llguidance restoration. Surface failures early with test builds in sprint 1.

- AIPCC index missing dependencies: Some vLLM CPU dependencies may not be in the AIPCC index for s390x. Cross-reference requirements/cpu.txt against AIPCC index availability and initiate onboarding for missing packages.

- Test cluster availability: Integration testing requires OpenShift clusters on IBM Z (s390x) hardware, which may have limited availability. Reserve Z test cluster time during sprint planning and coordinate with IBM teams who maintain test environments.

Assumptions
- RHAIRFE-1926 will deliver prebuilt s390x wheel packages before this work begins

- The AIPCC CPU base image remains stable and available for s390x

- IBM Z team continues to own and maintain build_vllm_s390x.sh

AIPCC-29662.description:
Summary:
GCC 14 (via gcc-toolset-14) needs to be installed in the CPU base image for Power (P) and Z architectures. This is required for torch.compile when a model is served using vLLM at runtime — the default gcc-11 toolchain is not supported on P11, causing runtime failures.
Background:
- vLLM builds successfully with the standard gcc, but serving fails on P11 because gcc-11 is not supported on that platform.

- GCC 14 does not need to be enabled at compile time — it only needs to be available and enabled at runtime for the specific inference mode (torch.compile).

- P/Z uses the same AIPCC base image as CPU x86, so this should be added at the base image level (not per-Dockerfile) so both architectures benefit.

- Reference for a similar install pattern: context/spyre/app/dnf-install-spyre.sh.

Acceptance Criteria:
- gcc-toolset-14 is installed in the CPU base image for P/Z.

- Package is available and can be enabled at runtime in downstream containers (e.g., vLLM image) without additional install steps.

- Confirm no regressions to existing gcc-11-based build/compile steps.

- Document how to enable gcc-14 (e.g., scl enable gcc-toolset-14) for consumers of the base image.

Priority/Timeline:
Needed before August 15 to unblock vLLM P11 runtime testing.

ADR-0081.description:
One of the core concepts used in ConsoleDot is the token-agnostic identity object, also known as the x-rh-identity header. This concept abstracts away various authentication mechanisms and provides a standard way to propagate information about a principal.
In its current form, the identity object as implemented in ConsoleDot lacks certain security features, which makes it problematic as we aim to implement https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/SDSTRAT-189#icft=SDSTRAT-189

Define a way of addressing these gaps, specifically:
- the authenticity of the object should be cryptographically verifiable

- the object should have an expiration time

- a mechanism should exist to exchange the identity object for an opaque token and back so that it can be passed through external systems

Considerations:
- the implementation should be backward compatible with the way the identity object is used currently (i.e. validation of signatures and expiration date should be opt-in)

[RFE Creator] Split child 1 of 6: Third-party Artifact Provenance and CVE Remediation Capability for RHOAI
---
rfe_id: RFE-006
title: Third-party Artifact Provenance and CVE Remediation Capability for RHOAI
priority: Undefined
status: Draft
size: M
parent_key: RHAIRFE-2440
original_labels: null
---
## Summary

Enterprise customers in regulated industries require that Red Hat can analyze and remediate vulnerabilities in all software shipped as part of RHOAI. Currently, RHOAI ships pre-built third-party binaries without source code visibility and pre-compiled packages from third-party vendor repositories (Mellanox, AMD, Intel, CentOS, EPEL), which means Red Hat cannot patch these components and customers are exposed to unmitigable CVEs with "No Fix Available" advisories.

## Problem Statement

RHOAI currently ships two categories of third-party artifacts without adequate provenance:

1. **Pre-built third-party binaries without source code visibility**: Red Hat cannot analyze or remediate vulnerabilities in these binaries. When CVEs are discovered, customers receive "No Fix Available" advisories because Red Hat has no ability to produce patches.

2. **Pre-compiled packages from third-party vendor repositories**: Artifacts pulled directly from Mellanox, AMD, Intel, CentOS, and EPEL repositories cannot be signed with approved Red Hat keys and propagate vendor supply chain risk directly to Red Hat customers.

Customers deploying RHOAI in regulated environments cannot accept software components with unverifiable provenance or components for which the vendor cannot provide timely CVE remediation.

**Split from**: RHAIRFE-2440

## Affected Customers

Enterprise customers in regulated industries (government, financial services, healthcare) that require:
- Verifiable provenance for all shipped software components
- Timely CVE remediation SLAs without "No Fix Available" gaps
- SLSA-compliant artifact attestation for procurement evaluation

## Business Justification

- **CVE Remediation SLAs**: Red Hat's enterprise value proposition depends on the ability to provide timely CVE patches for all shipped software. Components without source visibility break this promise.
- **Supply Chain Risk**: Vendor supply chain compromises (e.g., XZ Utils) propagate directly to Red Hat customers when artifacts lack provenance verification. Recent high-profile incidents have elevated customer scrutiny of third-party artifact handling.
- **Regulatory Compliance**: EU Cyber Resilience Act, FedRAMP, SOC2, and ISO 27001 frameworks increasingly require documented provenance for all software components.
- **Procurement Barriers**: Government and financial sector procurement processes enforce SLSA provenance and signed artifacts as baseline requirements. Without provenance for third-party components, RHOAI cannot meet these evaluation criteria.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All third-party binaries shipped in RHOAI have either source code visibility enabling Red Hat to produce CVE patches, or formal vendor attestation agreements ensuring timely upstream fixes
- [ ] Pre-compiled packages from vendor repositories (Mellanox, AMD, Intel, CentOS, EPEL) are either built from source through Red Hat's build system or accompanied by signed provenance from the vendor
- [ ] No RHOAI release includes components for which Red Hat must issue "No Fix Available" CVE advisories due to lack of source access

## Success Criteria

- Red Hat can produce CVE patches for all shipped binaries within standard SLA timelines
- All third-party artifacts have verifiable provenance documentation
- Regulated-industry customers can validate the provenance of all RHOAI components during procurement evaluation

comments.author: rhoaieng automationbot

[RFE Creator] Split child 2 of 6: Hermetic Build Pipeline with Verified Provenance for RHOAI Components
---
rfe_id: RFE-029
title: Hermetic Build Pipeline with Verified Provenance for RHOAI Components
priority: Undefined
status: Draft
size: M
parent_key: RFE-007
original_labels: null
---
## Summary

Enterprise customers in regulated industries need assurance that RHOAI software artifacts are built through hermetic, tamper-resistant build pipelines with verifiable chain of custody. Currently, some RHOAI components use non-hermetic builds that pull unverified upstream elements at build time, making it impossible for customers to verify artifact provenance and creating risk in their own compliance audits.

## Problem Statement

RHOAI ships 126 container images built from 57 components. Some of these component builds pull unverified upstream elements at build time, making them vulnerable to upstream dependency poisoning attacks. Customers receiving these artifacts cannot verify chain of custody, which creates risk in their own compliance audits and blocks deployment in security-sensitive environments.

The Konflux build ecosystem already supports hermetic builds (some components like MLServer already use hermetic Tekton pipelines), but coverage is not uniform across all RHOAI components. Without hermetic builds, valid SLSA-level provenance attestations cannot be generated, leaving customers unable to verify that the software they deploy meets supply chain security standards.

**Split from**: RFE-007

## Affected Customers

Enterprise customers in regulated industries (government, financial services, healthcare) that require:
- Verifiable build provenance for deployed software
- Compliance with supply chain security frameworks (SLSA, NIST SSDF)
- Auditable build provenance as part of their own security assessments and procurement evaluations

## Business Justification

- **Supply Chain Attack Mitigation**: Recent high-profile supply chain compromises (XZ Utils, SolarWinds) demonstrate that non-hermetic build pipelines are high-priority attack vectors. Customers are acutely aware of this risk and increasingly evaluate vendor build practices during procurement.
- **Provenance Verification**: Regulated-industry customers require SLSA-level provenance attestation for software they deploy. Non-hermetic builds cannot produce valid provenance attestations, blocking adoption in these segments.
- **Compliance Requirements**: FedRAMP, SOC2, ISO 27001, and the EU Cyber Resilience Act frameworks require verifiable software provenance. Customers distributing RHOAI artifacts need compliant provenance data to meet their own regulatory obligations.
- **Incident Cost Avoidance**: A build pipeline compromise would require full pipeline isolation and rebuild, with all downstream artifacts becoming suspect. Remediation costs exceed prevention costs by estimated 10x-100x.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All RHOAI component builds are hermetic, pulling no unverified upstream elements at build time
- [ ] Build provenance attestations are generated for all RHOAI artifacts, enabling customers to verify chain of custody

## Success Criteria

- All RHOAI artifacts have verifiable build provenance that customers can validate
- No RHOAI build process pulls unverified dependencies at build time

[RFE Creator] Split child 3 of 6: Security Operating Approval Compliance for RHOAI CI/CD Build Infrastructure
---
rfe_id: RFE-030
title: Security Operating Approval Compliance for RHOAI CI/CD Build Infrastructure
priority: Undefined
status: Draft
size: S
parent_key: RFE-007
original_labels: null
---
## Summary

Internal CI/CD systems that have automated repository-write access to RHOAI build pipelines operate without formal Security Operating Approvals (SOA/ESS). Credential and token storage for automated build bots has not been verified under corporate security standards, creating privileged credential exposure risk. A compromise of these credentials could poison downstream builds, impacting all customers receiving RHOAI artifacts.

## Affected Customers

- Internal security and compliance teams responsible for build infrastructure governance
- Enterprise customers in regulated industries whose own compliance audits require documentation that vendor build infrastructure meets enterprise security governance standards

## Business Justification

- **Privileged Credential Exposure**: CI/CD systems with automated repository-write access store credentials and tokens that, if compromised, could be used to inject malicious code into RHOAI builds. Without SOA verification, credential management practices are unaudited.
- **Compliance Requirements**: FedRAMP, SOC2, and ISO 27001 frameworks require documented, governed build infrastructure. CI/CD systems operating outside security governance create compliance gaps that propagate to customers.
- **Incident Prevention**: A compromised CI/CD credential would require full pipeline isolation and rebuild, with all downstream artifacts becoming suspect. SOA governance provides the verification and controls to prevent such incidents.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Internal CI/CD systems with repository-write access operate under Security Operating Approvals with verified credential management

## Success Criteria

- CI/CD infrastructure passes Security Operating Approval review
- Credential and token storage for automated build bots meets corporate security standards

[RFE Creator] Split child 4 of 6: Release Gate Compliance — SBOMs and CVE Blocker Enforcement for RHOAI Artifacts
---
rfe_id: RFE-008
title: Release Gate Compliance — SBOMs and CVE Blocker Enforcement for RHOAI Artifacts
priority: Undefined
status: Draft
size: M
parent_key: RHAIRFE-2440
original_labels: null
---
## Summary

Enterprise customers in regulated industries need RHOAI release artifacts to include Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs), SLSA provenance, and CVE scan results so they can meet their own regulatory obligations and verify the security posture of deployed software. Currently, automated security gates are intentionally disabled for RHEL AI disk/container images and CVE blocker release gates are suppressed, meaning shipped images lack the compliance artifacts customers require.

## Problem Statement

RHOAI's release process currently has two related compliance gaps:

1. **Disabled security gates**: Automated security gates for RHEL AI disk/container images have been intentionally disabled. SBOM generation is not active for these artifacts, which will violate upcoming regulatory frameworks including the EU Cyber Resilience Act.

2. **Suppressed CVE blocker release gates**: Release gate parameters (e.g., `cve.cve_blockers`) are suppressed, meaning shipped images lack SLSA provenance, CVE scan results, and SAST analysis. Customers cannot verify the security posture of images they deploy.

The underlying Konflux build system supports SBOM generation and security scanning. These gates were suppressed as a policy decision, and re-enabling them requires resolving the underlying issues that led to their suppression.

**Split from**: RHAIRFE-2440

## Affected Customers

Enterprise customers distributing or deploying RHOAI artifacts in:
- European markets (EU Cyber Resilience Act compliance)
- Government environments (FedRAMP, NIST requirements)
- Financial services and healthcare (SOC2, ISO 27001, HIPAA security requirements)

## Business Justification

- **Regulatory Compliance**: The EU Cyber Resilience Act mandates SBOMs and strict vulnerability handling. Non-compliance carries penalties of up to 2.5% of global annual turnover or EUR 15M (whichever is higher). Customers distributing RHOAI artifacts in European markets may face their own regulatory exposure due to missing SBOMs.
- **Procurement Requirements**: Government, financial, and healthcare sectors enforce SLSA provenance, signed SBOMs, and CVE transparency as baseline procurement requirements. Without compliant release artifacts, RHOAI cannot pass security evaluation.
- **Security Posture Verification**: Customers in security-sensitive environments cannot deploy images whose security posture cannot be independently verified. Suppressed CVE gates block deployment in these environments.
- **Market Access**: Removing compliance barriers enables RHOAI adoption in regulated sectors that represent significant enterprise revenue opportunities.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All RHOAI release artifacts (including RHEL AI disk and container images) include generated SBOMs
- [ ] CVE blocker release gates are enforced, ensuring shipped images include CVE scan results and SLSA provenance attestations
- [ ] Customers can independently verify the security posture of shipped RHOAI images using standard compliance tooling

## Success Criteria

- All RHOAI release artifacts pass security gate verification with SBOMs, CVE scans, and provenance attestations
- Regulated-industry customers can use RHOAI compliance artifacts to satisfy their own audit and procurement requirements

## Summary

RHOAI redistributes `libtpu` without completed legal sign-off for Google's commercial redistribution terms. This creates immediate legal liability -- potential breach of redistribution terms could trigger legal action or forced product withdrawal, leaving customers without a supported product.

## Affected Customers

All customers deploying RHOAI components that include `libtpu`. A forced product withdrawal due to legal action would affect all active RHOAI deployments relying on TPU-accelerated workloads.

## Business Justification

- **Legal Risk Mitigation**: Missing legal sign-off for `libtpu` redistribution represents immediate legal liability. Potential breach of Google commercial redistribution terms could result in legal action or injunctions regardless of the product's overall security posture.
- **Customer Continuity**: A forced product withdrawal due to legal action would leave customers without a supported product, causing disruption to production deployments.
- **Proactive Resolution**: Resolving redistribution licensing proactively before it becomes a matter of active legal dispute avoids significantly higher costs and customer impact.

**Split from**: RHAIRFE-2440

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Legal sign-off for `libtpu` redistribution is obtained, or an alternative packaging approach is implemented that eliminates redistribution liability
- [ ] RHOAI can ship components that depend on `libtpu` functionality without legal risk from Google's commercial redistribution terms

[RFE Creator] Split child 6 of 6: EOL Python Runtime Remediation for RHOAI Components
---
rfe_id: RFE-010
title: EOL Python Runtime Remediation for RHOAI Components
priority: Undefined
status: Draft
size: S
parent_key: RHAIRFE-2440
original_labels: null
---
## Summary

Several RHOAI components use End-of-Life Python 3.11 as their base runtime. Python maintainers do not backport security fixes for EOL releases, leaving these components permanently exposed to unpatched vulnerabilities. Customers need all RHOAI components to run on actively maintained runtimes to receive timely security patches.

## Affected Customers

Enterprise customers deploying RHOAI in environments that require:
- All software components to run on vendor-supported, actively maintained runtimes
- Timely security patches for runtime vulnerabilities
- Compliance with security policies that prohibit EOL software in production

## Business Justification

- **Permanently Unpatched Vulnerabilities**: Python 3.11 EOL means no security backports from upstream. Affected components (KFTO, lm-evaluation-harness, pipelines-components, llm-d-planner) have a core runtime that is permanently exposed to new vulnerabilities.
- **Customer Security Policies**: Enterprise customers in regulated industries enforce policies prohibiting EOL software in production environments. Components on EOL Python block deployment in these environments.
- **Existing Migration Path**: AIPCC base images have already moved to Python 3.12 for newer components (OGX distribution, MLServer). A proven migration path exists within the platform.

**Split from**: RHAIRFE-2440

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All RHOAI components are migrated from EOL Python 3.11 to an actively maintained Python version (3.12+)
- [ ] Affected components (including but not limited to KFTO, lm-evaluation-harness, pipelines-components, llm-d-planner) receive security patches through the supported Python runtime

## Success Criteria

- No RHOAI component ships on an EOL Python runtime
- All Python-based components can receive timely security patches through the supported runtime

RHAIRFE-2440.description:
Problem Statement
Current Challenge
Specific AIPCC processes currently exhibit severe non-compliance with core Red Hat Product Security requirements. Multiple critical security and compliance gaps have been identified across the build pipeline, artifact provenance, dependency management, and release gating processes.
The primary drivers of this non-compliance stem from the proprietary nature of certain affected upstream artifacts (which limits visibility) and insufficient engineering runway allocated to address these gaps prior to the upcoming release cycle. This RFE aggregates the consolidated business risks and outlines a structured remediation roadmap requiring immediate executive alignment.
Identified Security Gaps
#
Exposure
Impact
Severity
1
Shipping pre-built third-party binaries without source code visibility.
Zero Patch Capability: Red Hat cannot analyze or remediate vulnerabilities in these binaries. Customers are exposed to unmitigable CVEs.
Critical
2
Missing Legal sign-off for redistribution of libtpu.
Immediate Legal Liability: Potential breach of Google commercial redistribution terms. Risk of legal action or forced product recall.
Critical
3
Non-hermetic builds pulling unverified upstream elements.
Malware/Injection Risk & Lack of Provenance: Vulnerable to upstream dependency poisoning. Inability to verify chain of custody.
Critical
4
End-of-Life (EOL) Python 3.11 base image for KFTO.
Permanently Unpatched Vulnerabilities: Python maintainers do not backport security fixes for EOL releases. Core runtime remains exposed.
High
5
Internal CI/CD systems operating without Security Operating Approvals (SOA/ESS).
Privileged Credential Exposure: Unverified credential/token storage for automated repository-write bots. Compromise could poison downstream builds.
Critical
6
Automated security gates intentionally disabled for RHEL AI disk/container images.
Compliance Failure: Absence of SBOMs violates upcoming regulatory frameworks. Suppressed cve.cve_blockers parameters.
Critical
7
Suppressed CVE blocker release gates.
Blind Shipping: Shipped images lack SLSA provenance, CVE scan results, and SAST analysis. No verifiable security posture exists.
Critical
8
Pre-compiled packages pulled directly from third-party vendor repositories (Mellanox, AMD, Intel, CentOS, EPEL).
Supply Chain Risk: Vendor supply chain compromises propagate directly to Red Hat. Artifacts cannot be signed with approved Red Hat keys.
High

Risk Classification
- Severe Technical Vulnerability: 5 of 8 identified gaps are ranked Critical. These represent scenarios where Red Hat cannot patch software, cannot prove provenance, or is actively bypassing release-gate verification.

- Regulatory Exposure: 2 gaps carry direct regulatory penalties. The upcoming EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) mandates Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) and strict vulnerability handling. Non-compliance carries severe global financial penalties.

- Immediate Legal Exposure: 1 gap carries immediate legal risk. The libtpu redistribution issue could trigger legal action or injunctions from Google regardless of our overall security posture.

Why This Matters Now
- Regulatory Timelines: EU CRA enforcement structures are tightening. SBOM generation gaps (Gap #6) must be resolved before artifacts are distributed into European markets.

- Escalating Supply Chain Vectors: Recent high-profile compromises (e.g., XZ Utils, SolarWinds) demonstrate that non-hermetic builds and unvetted third-party binary pipelines (Gaps #1, #3, #5, #8) are high-priority target vectors.

- Enterprise Customer Procurement: Government, financial, and healthcare sectors increasingly enforce SLSA provenance, signed SBOMs, and CVE transparency as baseline procurement requirements.

- Compounding Technical Debt: Retrofitting security compliance into post-release software architectures is significantly more expensive and disruptive than building compliance into the active release gate.

⚠️ Executive Decision Required
This RFE requests that the Accountable VP formally select and sign off on one of two courses of action:
- Option A: Accept the Risks — Formally document risk acceptance with a designated business owner, defined mitigation parameters, and an explicit review cadence. Ship the next release with acknowledged gaps.

- Option B: Delay the Release(s) — Pause upcoming release milestones until the identified Critical gaps are fully remediated to meet Product Security standards.


2. Business Alignment
Business Value
- Risk Reduction: Eliminates zero-patch-capability exposure, restores standard CVE remediation SLA capabilities, establishes explicit chain-of-custody provenance, and brings internal infrastructure under corporate security governance.

- Compliance Readiness: Achieves baseline readiness for the EU Cyber Resilience Act and provides the necessary artifact compliance requirements (FedRAMP, SOC2, ISO 27001) demanded by partners.

- Legal Protections: Resolves libtpu redistribution liabilities proactively before becoming a matter of active legal dispute.

- Customer Trust: Ensures enterprise and regulated-industry customers can validate Red Hat's security claims against industry standard software attestations.

Quantifiable Impact (Unmitigated Risk Materialization)
Scenario
Estimated Business Impact
CVE in unpatched 3rd-party binary (Gap #1)
Inability to patch. Red Hat must issue a public advisory stating "No Fix Available," resulting in significant customer erosion.
Google legal action on libtpu (Gap #2)
Immediate legal defense costs, potential product injunctions, and forced product withdrawal from the market.
Supply chain compromise via build pipeline (Gap #3)
Intensive incident response overhead, brand damage, and mandatory data breach notification cycles.
EU CRA Non-Compliance Fine (Gap #6)
Up to 2.5% of global annual turnover or EUR 15M (whichever is higher).
Compromised CI/CD credentials (Gap #5)
Full pipeline isolation and rebuild requirements. All downstream artifacts become suspect.

Remediation Cost vs. Incident Cost: Remediating these gaps requires targeted engineering resources over 1–2 quarters. Conversely, a single unmitigated security or legal incident is estimated to exceed remediation costs by 10x to 100x in financial and brand liability.

Alignment to Red Hat AI Outcomes
This initiative directly underpins the following corporate pillars:
- Product Security & Trust: Maintains the foundational enterprise promise of Red Hat software.

- Regulatory Compliance: Aligns development output with global legal and security standards.

- Operational Excellence: Implements secure, deterministic, and scalable automated pipelines.

AIPCC-10075.description:
Summary
Red Hat policy is to build distributed artifacts from source wherever possible.
AIPCC currently ships a small number of pre-built Python wheels due to upstream gaps, proprietary components, or timeline constraints. This initiative aims to identify all such wheels and transition them to source builds where legally and technically feasible, while documenting approved exceptions.
This effort reduces long-term technical debt, improves supply-chain transparency, and aligns AIPCC distribution practices with Red Hat build-from-source principles.
Problem Statement
Pre-built wheels in AIPCC indexes/images create:
- compliance and redistributability risk

- limited reproducibility

- unclear ownership

- inconsistent intake process

- technical debt across releases

There is currently no single place tracking:
- which wheels are pre-built

- why they exist

- whether they can be rebuilt

- legal status

Goal
Ensure all Python wheels shipped by AIPCC are built from source wherever possible, with documented and approved exceptions for proprietary or legally restricted components.
Objectives
- Create inventory of all pre-built wheels shipped in AIPCC

- Classify each package:

- 
- build from source possible

- requires engineering work

- proprietary / legal exception

- removable


       3. File epics/tickets to implement source builds
       4. Engage Legal for proprietary redistribution gaps
       5. Define a repeatable exception/intake process
       6. Optionally explore AI-assisted audit tooling
Scope
In scope
- Python wheels in AIPCC indexes

- Wheels in images delivered via RHAIIS/RHEL AI

- CUDA / ROCm / CPU stacks

- Vendor-provided wheels

- Licensing + redistribution review

Out of scope
- RPM packaging unrelated to wheels

- Non-Python artifacts

Deliverables
- Inventory spreadsheet/dashboard

- Classification matrix

- Jira epics per package

- Documented policy for future requests

- Legal exception tracking

- Recommendation for automation

Success Criteria
- 100% of shipped wheels audited

- Source build plan created for rebuildable packages

- Legal status documented for proprietary packages

- No new pre-built wheels added without tracking

- Clear intake workflow defined

Stakeholders
- AIPCC(AE/DP/PyTorch)

- Release Engineering / SP-RHEL

- Legal

- Prodsec

References
1. AIPCC pre-built wheels - 2026-02-02  
2. AIPCC-5621 Package Origin

AIPCC-13013.description:
This initiative aims to improve our supply chain security posture to protect our downstream consumers from compromised packages.
Goals
Goal: Implement measures to improve our resiliency to supply chain attacks on upstream packages we are shipping.
Who benefits: AIPCC Engineers, InfoSec/ProdSec teams, and end-users of RHEL AI/RHOAI who are protected from malicious upstream payloads.
Requirements:
Dependency Cooldowns: Implement a mandatory waiting period for new package versions to mitigate zero-day compromises.
Enhanced Scanning Suite: Integrate vulnerability scanning into the package building process.
PyPI Status Monitoring: Automate tracking of "yanked," "deleted," or "quarantined" statuses via the PyPI JSON API.
SBOM Generation: Generate Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) to improve visibility into what we are shipping.
Rapid Remediation Tooling: Develop a mechanism to quickly restrict versions and yank packages from Pulp bypasssing the slow standard builder process.
and others.
Done - Acceptance Criteria:
- See Acceptance Criteria from the linked issues.

Use Cases - i.e. User Experience & Workflow:
Proactive Prevention: An upstream package is compromised and uploaded to PyPI. The package is blocked before entering our internal mirrors.
Emergency Response: InfoSec notifies the team of a confirmed compromise. An AIPCC engineer can immediately yank the affected version from Pulp without waiting for a full MR/release cycle.
Documentation Considerations:
- Create documentation that describes all of these measures.

EC-1881.description:
Summary
Extend the disallowed_attributes rule data schema to support pattern-based exceptions scoped by PURL qualifier, enabling teams to allow specific disallowed attributes (e.g., hermeto:pip:package:binary) for packages from trusted indexes while still blocking them from untrusted sources.
Background
Multiple products (RHOAI, RHEL AI, RHAII, OpenShift Lightspeed) consume prebuilt Python binaries from the AIPCC (AI Platform Content Catalog) index hosted at console.redhat.com. The AIPCC team handles license compliance and source builds; downstream products consume the resulting binaries.
The disallowed_package_attributes rule (in both sbom_spdx and sbom_cyclonedx) flags these binaries via the following default rule data in rhtap-ec-policy:
disallowed_attributes:
- name: cachi2:bundler:package:binary
  value: "true"
- name: cachi2:pip:package:binary
  value: "true"
- name: hermeto:bundler:package:binary
  value: "true"
- name: hermeto:pip:package:binary
  value: "true"
Today, the only options are:
- Blanket exception on disallowed_package_attributes -- too broad, allows unauthorized PyPI binaries to slip through.

- Per-package exceptions via volatile config terms -- requires listing every individual package PURL, which is impractical given the AIPCC index changes each release.

- Custom rule data that omits the pip binary entries from disallowed_attributes -- requires manual updates when upstream rule data changes, and still doesn't scope the exception to trusted indexes.

None of these options allow expressing: "allow binary packages from AIPCC, but not from PyPI."
How AIPCC and PyPI packages are distinguished
Hermeto (the SBOM generator) reliably sets the repository_url PURL qualifier for packages fetched from non-default indexes. The logic is in hermeto/core/package_managers/pip/main.py:172-176:
- AIPCC package: pkg:pypi/some-lib@1.0?repository_url=https://console.redhat.com/api/pypi/public-rhai/rhoai/3.5/e1/simple/

- PyPI package: pkg:pypi/some-lib@1.0 (no repository_url qualifier -- defaults to pypi.org)

This is deterministic: if the index URL differs from the default PyPI endpoint, repository_url is unconditionally included. The qualifier is tracked from requirements.txt --index-url through resolution to PURL generation with no code path where it gets dropped.
Proposed solution
Extend the disallowed_attributes rule data schema with an optional except_when field that suppresses the violation when a PURL qualifier matches a set of regex patterns:
disallowed_attributes:
- name: hermeto:pip:package:binary
  value: "true"
  except_when:
  - purl_qualifier: repository_url
    patterns:
    - "^https://console\\.redhat\\.com/api/pypi/.*"
    - "^https://packages\\.redhat\\.com/pypi/.*"
- name: cachi2:pip:package:binary
  value: "true"
  except_when:
  - purl_qualifier: repository_url
    patterns:
    - "^https://console\\.redhat\\.com/api/pypi/.*"
    - "^https://packages\\.redhat\\.com/pypi/.*"
- name: hermeto:bundler:package:binary
  value: "true"
- name: cachi2:bundler:package:binary
  value: "true"
Semantics: "disallow hermeto:pip:package:binary EXCEPT when the package's PURL has a repository_url qualifier matching one of these patterns." Entries without except_when (the bundler entries) behave exactly as they do today.
The filtering is fail-closed: if the package has no purl-type external ref, or the PURL has no repository_url qualifier (i.e., default PyPI), the exception does not apply and the attribute remains disallowed.
This follows the same regex pattern approach used by the existing allowed_package_sources and allowed_proxy_url_patterns rule data.
Backwards compatibility
The except_when field is optional. Existing rule data without it continues to work with no behavior change. The ec-policies schema update (adding except_when to the additionalProperties list) must land before anyone adds except_when to their rule data, since the current schema has additionalProperties: false.
Scope
The except_when filter operates at the index level, not the package level. All packages from a matching index are exempted for that attribute. This matches the use case: AIPCC is a trusted index where compliance is handled upstream, so all packages from it should be allowed.
For per-package temporary exceptions (e.g., allowing a specific PyPI binary during onboarding), see the volatile config section below.
Implementation notes
Affected rules (both need the enhancement)
- sbom_spdx.disallowed_package_attributes (policy/release/sbom_spdx/sbom_spdx.rego:228)

- sbom_cyclonedx.disallowed_package_attributes (policy/release/sbom_cyclonedx/sbom_cyclonedx.rego:143)

Rule data schema change
Add except_when to the disallowed_attributes JSON schema in policy/lib/sbom/sbom.rego:249-270:
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "name": {"type": "string"},
    "value": {"type": "string"},
    "effective_on": {"type": "string", "format": "date-time"},
    "except_when": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "purl_qualifier": {"type": "string"},
          "patterns": {
            "type": "array",
            "items": {"type": "string", "format": "regex"}
          }
        },
        "required": ["purl_qualifier", "patterns"],
        "additionalProperties": false
      }
    }
  },
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "required": ["name"]
}
Rego logic change
The disallowed_package_attributes deny rule currently iterates over all externalRefs independently. The enhanced rule needs to:
- Find the purl-type external ref on the package (filter by referenceType == "purl" in SPDX, or use component.purl in CycloneDX)

- Parse the PURL with ec.purl.parse()

- Extract the specified qualifier (e.g., repository_url)

- If the qualifier value matches any pattern in except_when, suppress the violation

Note: the existing rule generates one violation per (externalRef, annotation) combination. If a package has both a PURL ref and a CPE ref, it produces two violations. The except_when logic should check the purl-type ref regardless of which external ref is generating the current violation.
Existing library functions to reuse
- ec.purl.parse() -- PURL parsing (used by allowed_package_sources)

- sbom.url_matches_any_pattern() -- regex matching against URL patterns (used by allowed_package_sources and allowed_proxy_urls)

What about volatile config?
The original request included "volatileConfig support for disallowed_attributes." Investigation revealed that term-level volatile config matching already works in ec-cli (internal/evaluator/filters.go:869-903). A volatile config entry like this already functions today:
{
  "exclude": [{
    "value": "sbom_spdx.disallowed_package_attributes:pkg:pypi/urgent-package@1.0",
    "componentNames": ["my-component"],
    "effectiveUntil": "2026-09-01T00:00:00Z"
  }]
}
This excludes the violation for that specific package PURL, scoped to a component, with an expiration date. This covers the temporary onboarding scenario (a team needs a specific PyPI binary while transitioning to AIPCC) without any code changes.
RHOAI may not be aware this capability exists. We should document it when delivering this story.
Acceptance criteria
- disallowed_attributes rule data supports optional except_when field with purl_qualifier + patterns

- SPDX disallowed_package_attributes rule suppresses violations when qualifier matches

- CycloneDX disallowed_package_attributes rule suppresses violations when qualifier matches

- Violations are still produced when: no purl-type ref exists, qualifier is absent, or qualifier doesn't match any pattern (fail-closed)

- Rule data schema validation rejects malformed except_when entries

- Tests cover: match (violation suppressed), no match (violation produced), missing qualifier (violation produced), multiple patterns, multiple except_when entries

- Documentation updated (rule data format, conforma.dev policy docs)

- Notify RHOAI about existing term-level volatile config capability

Downstream rule data change (rhtap-ec-policy)
After the ec-policies change lands, the upstream rule data in rhtap-ec-policy should be updated to add except_when to the pip binary entries:
disallowed_attributes:
- name: cachi2:bundler:package:binary
  value: "true"
- name: cachi2:pip:package:binary
  value: "true"
  except_when:
  - purl_qualifier: repository_url
    patterns:
    - "^https://console\\.redhat\\.com/api/pypi/.*"
    - "^https://packages\\.redhat\\.com/pypi/.*"
- name: hermeto:bundler:package:binary
  value: "true"
- name: hermeto:pip:package:binary
  value: "true"
  except_when:
  - purl_qualifier: repository_url
    patterns:
    - "^https://console\\.redhat\\.com/api/pypi/.*"
    - "^https://packages\\.redhat\\.com/pypi/.*"
The specific AIPCC URL patterns should be confirmed with RHOAI before merging.
Related
- Support thread: KFLUXSPRT-7872

- Reference story: EC-1824

- Relevant rule data: rhtap-ec-policy rule_data.yml L224-229

- Hermeto PURL generation: hermeto/core/package_managers/pip/main.py:164-192

- ec-cli term-level matching: internal/evaluator/filters.go:869-903

Currently, the steps to meet the requirements for onboarding components as DP, TP, GA are manual, scattered across multiple documents, and hard to verify. This strat tracks developing tooling and automation to simplify integration for all new components and features.

comments.author: Christian Heimes
comments.body:
In Slack thread https://redhat-internal.slack.com/archives/C079FE5H94J/p1758217829339629 we discussed hermetic builds for base images. The base images currently use shell scripts and repo files with additional repo vars. The old approach is incompatible with cachi2 prefetching https://konflux-ci.dev/docs/building/prefetching-dependencies/#rpm and rpm-lockfile-prototype . * We would have to completely redesign how we enable repos and install RPMs. Our shell scripts to configure repositories and to install the RPMs are incompatible with Konflux's hermetic builds.
- We have some complicated logic, e.g. NVIDIA repo modules depend on certain configurations. That would not work.

- The RPM mirroring tool expects repo files. Our repo files depends on additional DNF vars. I don't know if that's supported, probably not.

- The ability to test base image builds locally and in GitLab CI are important features of the developer experience. We may loose these features or have to implement additional tooling to restore the feature.

- Each image has two sets of RPMs: a common set of RPMs from RHEL / RHELAI repos, then a second set of vendor + accelerator-specific packages. The tool only accepts one file.

- The RPM lock file needs to be regenerated every time we update the base image, provide new RPMs, or update an existing RPM. The proess has to be automated and integrated into Renovate.

I estimate that it would take a team with a senior and junior engineer at least one month to rewrite the base image pipeline to support hermetic builds – assuming one of the engineers has a good understanding of RPMs, DNF, and Konflux. There is a good chance that they have to work with Konflux team to extend the features and improve cachi2 to deal with gigantic CUDA and ROCm RPMs. I would not be surprised if it takes until end of calendar year until the new system is stable and fully automated.

comments.author: Doug Hellmann
comments.body:
Preserving an old comment from @Christian Heimes :
Update 2025-10-01
@Christian Heimes 
Hermetic builds in Konflux are not supported. Neither the AIPCC base images nor the production images like RHAIIS can use hermetic sealed builds as of now. Due to technical limitations, internal design decisions, lack of resources, and other reasons, AIPP is not able to implement hermetic Konflux builds in the foreseeable future. It's going to require major redesigns and rewrites of our base images and wheel installations. I see a small chance to deliver hermetic builds by CY26Q1 or Q2, but even that comes with a big if.
Our engineers are under immense pressure to deliver new features and versions in record time. Hermetic Konflux builds are just not as important as delivering new vLLM version, Torch version, or AI accelerator hardware support. (I'm a security engineer by heart and I agree that we need to implement hermetic Konflux pipelines eventually.)
My comment from 2025-09-19 lists some some requirements. The summary:
- Konflux does not have a stable, fully supported tool to generate RPM lock files. rpm-lockfile-prototype is still documented as proof-of-concept without any stability guarantees. Our products have very short release cycles and we are constantly missing our release dates. Even a delay by half a work day can through us of. We need a stable tool with SLAs.

- Our base image builds are heavily parametrized and rely on build args, additional DNF repo args, scripts, and Renovate Bot. rpm-lockfile-prototype may be missing features to be as flexible as we need it to be.

- Wheels for product images are currently hosted on GitLab. GitLab has technical limitations, which forces us to delete and replace wheel files. The approach is incompatible with pip lock files. We are currently moving away from GitLab to Pulp for Python wheels. Pulp may allow us to generate proper pip lock files.

PSRR-20.description:
Risk Summary and Impact
AIPCC ships approximately 50 third-party Python packages as pre-built binaries across RHEL AI, OpenShift AI, and RHAIIS. Roughly 28 are proprietary binaries from 6 hardware vendors (Google, Intel/Habana, AWS, NVIDIA, IBM, AMD) where Red Hat has no source access, no independent vulnerability remediation capability, and no confirmed vendor agreements covering vulnerability disclosure.
This risk compounds the existing executive-level supply chain gap (PSRR-17, Sonatype Nexus Firewall) with AIPCC-specific proprietary binary exposure that Nexus will not fully address — private vendor registries are outside Nexus's architectural scope. The March 2026 LiteLLM compromise validated this attack pattern in the AIPCC ecosystem. VP Product Security assessed that current protections "would be ineffective" against this class of attack.
A confirmed legal finding exists for Google's libtpu library (AIPCC-10599): redistribution is prohibited under current license terms. Shipping continued on verbal go-ahead from an individual contributor (Sr Principal PM), without formal risk acceptance documentation.
CRA Art. 14 reporting obligations (24-hour actively exploited vulnerability notification to ENISA) apply from Sep 11, 2026. CRA Art. 13 manufacturer due diligence obligations are structurally unsatisfiable for opaque proprietary binaries where Red Hat has no source access.
Promoted from PRODSECRM-194. Risk Council endorsed promotion on Jun 2, 2026. Full adversarial-reviewed analysis (4 rounds, 22 challenges, disposition EXHAUSTED): PRODSECRM-194 audit comment (ID 17155718).
Likelihood and Proximity with Justification
Likelihood: Likely. Two populations with different threat models:
- Population B (public registries, ~12 packages): Likely to Almost Certain. LiteLLM compromise (Mar 2026) validated the exact attack pattern for PyPI-sourced packages. 315% increase in malicious packages (Sonatype 2024). Zero pre-build gating currently in place.

- Population A (private vendor registries, ~28 packages): Possible. Compromising Fortune 100 vendor internal registries requires more sophisticated attackers. No prior compromise evidence. However, Red Hat's structural inability to detect compromise in proprietary binaries is an impact amplifier.

Proximity: Imminent. Code freeze Jun 9-19 constrains near-term remediation. CRA Art. 14 reporting obligations effective Sep 11, 2026 — Red Hat may lack the information to characterize vulnerabilities in proprietary components within the 24-hour reporting window.
Existing Mitigations
- AIPCC-10263 (build-from-source initiative): In Progress for Population B only. 4 of ~12 open-source/Bazel packages resolved. Does not address proprietary binaries (Population A).

- Sonatype Nexus Firewall (PSRR-17): Not deployed until Sep 2026. Python onboarding not started. Architecturally cannot cover private vendor registries — proprietary dependencies from Habana GitLab, IBM Pulp, AWS Neuron bypass Nexus entirely.

- Post-build scanning (Snyk/Dependabot): Detects known vulnerabilities after build. Cannot detect novel malware, backdoors, or supply chain attacks within opaque proprietary binaries.

- Dependency lock files: Prevent version substitution but do not prevent initial compromise. Adoption not enforced across all AIPCC teams.

- Legal review for libtpu (AIPCC-10599): In Progress since Feb 2026. Determined redistribution is prohibited; shipping continued without formal risk acceptance.

Decision Requests (Risk Posture)
Request risk acceptance and remediation commitment from AI BU leadership. The following decisions are needed:
- Risk acceptance for the Jun 9 code freeze: AI BU leadership to formally accept shipping pre-built proprietary binaries in the upcoming release, with documented acceptance and a remediation timeline aligned to CRA Art. 14 effective date (Sep 11, 2026).

- Vendor agreement verification: Direct AI BU to confirm vulnerability disclosure SLA coverage exists for all 6 vendor partnerships before the CRA compliance deadline. "Partner Agreement" listed as exception basis in the Pre-built Wheels spreadsheet is not confirmed vulnerability disclosure coverage.

- libtpu legal resolution: Require formal risk acceptance documentation for libtpu redistribution from a director+ authority (current verbal go-ahead is from an IC), or cease redistribution pending legal resolution.

- Nexus scope extension evaluation: Evaluate extending Nexus Firewall coverage to private vendor registries, or document acceptance that Population A will remain ungated indefinitely.

Backing analysis: PRODSECRM-194 Risk Assessment (2026-06-02), adversarial-reviewed (4 rounds, 22 challenges, EXHAUSTED). Action owner: Anna Marie Syed (ProdSec AI Lead).

PRODSECRM-194.description:
Reporter: fcanogab@redhat.com
Risk Type: Technology
Risk Level: Product Security level
Team: PSRD
Severity: High
Likelihood: Likely
Proximity: Imminent - < 1 day
Category: Release
Specific Risk:
The issue is that AIPCC team is not building from source a group of dependencies. They are providing them as binaries to products like RHEL AI, RHAIIS and OpenShift AI. The reasons to not build them from source are two: that they are proprietary and provided to us through a partnership agreement or that they are hard to build. The list of all the dependencies in this situation is in https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1WEYkQoxn3phAI0_NzYdzPT8wiQreJQXsftO6kCLweik/edit?gid=468184110#gid=468184110 (49 packages).
AIPCC team has a plan (https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/AIPCC-10263) in place to prioritize building the dependencies that are hard to build. Although they are hard to build, it is possible to build them, so they are working on it. But they need an exception because there is a release soon and the code freeze starts the 9th of June.
The risk is that because we are using and shipping these dependencies without building them from source, the probability of them including a backdoor or malware is higher. There is also the risk that if these dependencies have security vulnerabilities, the capability of the team of fixing them is lower because they would depend on the current builder. This is especially true in relation to the proprietary ones.
Potential Impact:
If it is discovered that one of these dependencies contain malware, backdoors or malicious code after we have shipped a product which includes them, the customers would have impact. It could hurt the Red Hat brand too.
Existing Mitigation:
The team has a plan in place to build from source some of the dependencies that are open source but hard to build.

RHAISTRAT-122.description:
Refinement Document 
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HL7vm2a8N6pUcubaYWXXkAq83rJsu_fL4IONvrISsSs/edit?tab=t.3mrf1syv46a
Rationale - The “Why”
The integration of MLFlow into OpenShift AI is proposed to address a critical user pain point by delivering centralized ML lifecycle management. MLFlow is slated to become a first-class component of RHOAI.
Currently, data scientists and ML engineers utilizing OpenShift AI components—such as AI Pipelines, Notebooks, Workbenches, custom components, and the Training SDK—require a unified mechanism to track their experiments, parameters, metrics, and artifacts. Embedding MLFlow functionalities within the user's primary OpenShift AI workspace will reduce context switching and improve the overall user experience.
This integration will allow users to track their AI experiments and compare different runs directly within the OpenShift AI platform, enabling informed decisions about model performance.
Business Alignment
- How does this RFE align with Red Hat’s corporate strategy? This project significantly enhances Red Hat OpenShift AI by making MLFlow a first-class component of the platform. The integration facilitates enhanced collaboration and streamlines the path from a tracked MLFlow model to deployment within OpenShift AI.

- To what Red Hat AI Outcome does this Align? (if applicable) This aligns with providing a comprehensive, centralized platform for managing the entire AI lifecycle, ensuring data consistency and security across different tenets in the platform.

- What is the Business Value and/or Impact of this? The integration will enhance the competitiveness of OpenShift AI by providing industry-standard experimentation tracking capabilities directly integrated into core services like Pipelines and SDKs. MLFlow is a well-known experimentation tracking component with a large community of users. Adopting MLFlow will allow us to facilitate adoption by that community with the advantage of providing them scalability through our hybrid cloud support. This improvement will appeal to data scientists and ML engineers, resulting in improved user adoption and satisfaction.

Proposed Enhancement - The “What”
This enhancement focuses on ensuring that the MLFlow tracking capability is fully integrated into the environments and tools used for model training and execution, specifically AI Pipelines, Workbenches, Kubeflow SDK, Kubeflow Trainer and the AI Hub components.
The final result should enable users running training jobs, whether through a Pipeline or directly via a Training SDK within a Workbench or Notebook, to have their experiment runs automatically tracked and logged by a dedicated MLFlow Server instance accessible within their project.
Key deliverables and assumptions for this scope include:
- MLFlow Server Provisioning: Add support for the MLFlow Server provisioning through the operator. This includes defining and implementing support for the storage layer and data policies.

- SDK Availability: Update base images (e.g., notebook images) to include the MLFlow SDK. The integration must ensure that runs generated via the Training SDK and other SDKs from the model customization team are trackable.

- Pipelines Integration: Develop the necessary integrations to allow MLFlow to work with Pipelines for Experiment Tracking. Tighter integration with OpenShift AI’s pipeline tools for automated MLFlow tracking is a future consideration.

- Security and Access: Design and implement RBAC for both in-cluster and off-cluster access to the MLFlow environment.

- Artifact Tracking: Ensure the solution supports the ability for users to log and browse artifacts (e.g., model files, plots) logged during MLFlow runs.

Acceptance Criteria
The enhancement is considered "done" when the following criteria are met:
- The MLFlow Server is successfully deployed and managed by the operator, supporting per-namespace scopes.

- Productized images for MLFlow are built via Konflux.

- Updated base images include the MLFlow SDK, making it readily available for users in Notebooks/Workbenches.

- MLFlow is fully integrated with AI Pipelines, successfully tracking experiment runs generated by pipeline executions.

- MLFlow is fully integrated with the Kubeflow Trainer and the Kubeflow SDK

- Robust RBAC is in place to govern access to MLFlow data, aligning with OpenShift AI's permission model.

- User documentation and onboarding material (e.g., tutorials/examples) are developed to guide users on using MLFlow tracking within Pipelines and SDKs.

- Validation confirms that user stories defined during the refinement phase regarding the MLFlow SDK, Server, and UI are addressed.

For the Dashboard integration 
Proposed Enhancement - The “What”
 
This document outlines the requirements for integrating MLFlow within the RHOAI Dashboard. The primary goal of this integration is to provide users with a unified and enhanced experience for managing the entire AI  lifecycle, from experimentation and model development to deployment and monitoring, directly within the OpenShift AI ecosystem. MLFlow will become a pillar of RHOAI. MLFlow will be a first-class component in the dashboard.
Key deliverables and assumptions for this scope include:
- Embedded MLFlow UI – Integrate the MLFlow user interface directly into the OpenShift AI Dashboard, providing a native, consistent experience aligned with the platform’s visual language (patternfly) and authentication model.

- Cross-Component Deep Links – Enable seamless navigation between RHOAI components and the MLFlow UI. For example:

- From a Pipeline execution, allow users to open the corresponding MLFlow experiment or run view for detailed metrics and artifacts.

- Unified Configuration – The MLFlow server endpoint, credentials, and data policies should be automatically managed and discoverable by MLFlow UI

 
Acceptance Criteria
The enhancement is considered "done" when the following criteria are met:
- The MLFlow UI is successfully deployed and managed by the operator, supporting per-namespace scopes.

- The MLFlow UI is embedded within the RHOAI Dashboard, following as many platform design guidelines as possible.

- Users can navigate from RHOAI components (Pipelines, AI Hub, etc.) directly to the relevant MLFlow experiment or run view.

- Access to MLFlow UI is governed by RHOAI RBAC, scoped to each namespace.

- End-user documentation, quickstarts, and examples are published to guide data scientists and engineers through MLFlow tracking within RHOAI.

comments.author: Ana Biazetti
comments.body: Updated text based on discussion with @Myriam Fentanes Gutierrez

comments.author: Ana Biazetti
comments.body:
- Assessment: Accepted

- Primary component: KubeFlow SDK - devX

- Impacted components: Model Registry, KubeFlow Pipeline, Dashboard, KubeFlow Trainer

- High level architecture plan: 
Beyond the functional requirements, this RFE must address the following non-functional aspects:

- 
- API Generality: The Experiment Tracking API (Kubeflow SDK) needs to be flexible enough to handle not only initial uses (Notebooks, KFP, KFT) but also future experiment tracking needs (see Other related work)


- 
- Disconnected Local Support: The Kubeflow SDK must support completely "disconnected" local operation. This means experiment data should be stored locally without any dependency on a remote Model Registry. Users should then have the option to save preferred local experiments or runs to a remote Model Registry later.


- 
- Flexible Source Model Specification: Users shouldn't be limited to only models available in the Model Registry. The system must allow clients to specify a URL for their source models.


- 
- Scalability and Data Management: Due to the automatic experiment tracking feature capability,  which will automatically generate experiments, runs, and metrics, the design must account for potential scale issues. This includes managing high volumes of data and metadata produced by many users and components. An expiration policy for old experiments is crucial to prevent performance degradation.


- 
- MLFlow Integration Strategy: The design phase must clearly define the approach for MLFlow integration. This includes how MLFlow will plug into the shared Kubeflow SDK and how existing MLFlow data will migrate to RHAI. This strategy needs agreement from both the architecture and business unit teaams


- Other related work: The work getting started for RHOAI 3.0 Gen AI UI mentions "experiments/tests/trials" that the AI Engineer may do as part of playgrounds, prompt tuning, agent building, MCP integration, where "parameters" are changed to improve the solution. Such tests could potentially become experiments that may want to be tracked (with resulting metrics) and compared. While this requirement is not part of RHOAI3.0, the MVP solution for Experiment Tracking should not prevent that it could be expanded to support such scenarios in the future.

comments.author: Anya Kramar
comments.body:
Thanks everyone for working on this! From Kubeflow SDK perspective I have a few clarifications:
- AI engineers might struggle with discovering and connecting to the right Model Registry instance. To address this we've added functionality that let users list available model registries and get MR URIs as part of PoC. I think this complements "low effort integration" goal. I'm curious whether this kind of service discovery should be called out explicitly in the requirements or if it's already covered under the general Model Registry integration scope?

- The requirement states "save preferred local experiments or runs to a remote Model Registry later", is this intended to be limited to local file storage only or could it include publishing from any tracking backedns (existing MLflow servers or databases) to Model Registry? This seems relevant given the MLflow migration scenarios.

- We have both "auto-logging" and "automatic experiment tracking" in the description, but are these referring to the same capability? MLflow's autolog() requires users to call .autolog() in their code, when automatic tracking would create experiments without any code changes when platform components detect job execution and framework used.

cc @Ana Biazetti @Myriam Fentanes Gutierrez

[RFE Creator] Split child 1 of 6: Centralized Experiment Tracking Platform
---
rfe_id: RFE-006
title: Centralized Experiment Tracking Platform
priority: Major
status: Draft
size: L
parent_key: RHAIRFE-124
original_labels: null
---
## Summary

AI engineers and researchers working with Red Hat OpenShift AI need a centralized experiment tracking platform to manually create, manage, compare, and visualize experiment runs and their associated metrics and evaluations. Today, experimentation metrics are fragmented across various RHOAI components with no unified way to track, compare, or reproduce experiments. This RFE establishes the core experiment tracking service, SDK for manual logging, dashboard UI, and Model Registry integration.

**Split from**: RHAIRFE-124

## Problem Statement

Customers using RHOAI for AI experimentation today face fragmented metric exploration across different components. There is no centralized way to:
- Track and version experiment runs alongside their parameters, metrics, and evaluations
- Compare multiple experiment runs side-by-side to identify the best-performing configuration
- Reproduce experiments by reviewing the full context of a prior run (parameters, environment, user, results)

Users must manually piece together information from different tools and components, making it difficult to systematically evaluate model performance as models are customized. This slows down the experimentation cycle and reduces confidence in model selection.

## Affected Customers

Customers adopting AI in production environments who need systematic experiment tracking and reproducible evaluation across Red Hat AI components and services. This capability aligns with the RHOAI GenAI Studio strategic initiative to simplify and centralize the GenAI experience.

## Business Justification

A significant challenge for customers adopting AI in production is comprehensive evaluation and metric tracking. Customers experience fragmented metric exploration across various AI components, with no unified service for experiment management. This capability is critical to the strategic objective of the RHOAI GenAI Studio, which aims to simplify and centralize the GenAI experience for Red Hat AI customers.

## User Scenarios

1. **As an AI engineer**, I need to create an experiment, run multiple configurations, and compare their metrics in a single view so I can quickly identify the best-performing approach for model compression, RAG, document preprocessing, or model evaluation.

2. **As an AI researcher**, I need to view a table of all my experiment runs with filtering by run type, name, owner, and key metrics, so I can find and revisit prior experiments without searching across multiple tools.

3. **As a data scientist**, I need to publish the champion run's metadata and artifacts to Model Registry so the best model from my experiments is available for serving without manual transfer.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Experiment tracking functions as an independent, centralized service compatible with various RHOAI components (workbenches, training SDKs, external components)
- [ ] A new left navigation option for experiments is available within the RHOAI UI
- [ ] Users are presented with a landing page displaying a table of available experiments (including runs and metrics) with filtering capabilities (run type, run name, owner, metrics)
- [ ] The metrics displayed in the table are configurable, and the table is interactive with dynamic updates upon filter selection
- [ ] Default sorting of search results and unfiltered lists is by metrics (descending)
- [ ] Users can create a new experiment, then create a new run, select its type, and be directed to the specific run flow
- [ ] Upon selecting an experiment, users can view a table containing only the runs for that specific experiment
- [ ] Users can compare multiple runs and view an interactive visualization of parameters and metrics of interest
- [ ] Users can select different metrics or parameters for comparison
- [ ] Metadata for each run includes: user that started the run, environment metadata, and infrastructure specs
- [ ] Users can publish the metadata and artifacts of the champion run to Model Registry
- [ ] Users can query experiment data
- [ ] Various hardware profiles are supported for experiment runs

## Success Criteria

- AI engineers can track, compare, and reproduce experiments from a single unified interface
- Experiment data (runs, parameters, metrics, evaluations) is stored centrally and accessible through both UI and API
- Time to compare experiment results is significantly reduced compared to the current fragmented approach

## Scope

### In Scope
- Experiment tracking service/API design and backend
- SDK integration for manual experiment and metric logging
- Dashboard UI with experiment landing page, run comparison, and visualization
- Model Registry integration for storing metrics, evaluations, and publishing champion runs
- Visualizations for model compression, RAG, document preprocessing, and model evaluation use cases
- Enhanced run metadata (user, environment, infra specs)
- Support for various hardware profiles

### Out of Scope
- Automatic/zero-code experiment tracking and platform-level component instrumentation (covered by a separate RFE)
- MLFlow equivalency and migration from MLFlow (covered by a separate RFE)
- Developing a new experiment tracking system from inception
- GenAI Studio experiment integration (future scope, but API should not preclude it)

## Documentation Considerations

Update RHOAI documentation with a new section on experiment tracking, covering the centralized service, UI workflows, SDK usage for manual logging, and Model Registry integration.

[RFE Creator] Split child 2 of 6: Automatic Experiment Tracking for KubeFlow Pipelines
---
rfe_id: RFE-009
title: Automatic Experiment Tracking for KubeFlow Pipelines
priority: Major
status: Draft
size: S
parent_key: RFE-007
original_labels: null
---
## Summary

AI engineers running KubeFlow Pipelines on Red Hat OpenShift AI need pipeline runs to be automatically tracked as experiment runs with metrics logged to the centralized experiment tracking service, so they can review results without adding logging code to their pipeline components.

**Split from**: RFE-007

## Problem Statement

KubeFlow Pipeline users must currently add manual SDK logging calls to each pipeline component to track experiment data. This creates adoption friction and risks incomplete tracking -- any pipeline component that omits logging produces gaps in experiment history. Because the Data Science Pipelines stack already has a structured execution model (Argo Workflows with kfp-driver orchestration), the platform has the information needed to log experiments automatically. Platform-level instrumentation would ensure comprehensive coverage without burdening pipeline authors with instrumentation effort.

## Affected Customers

AI engineers and ML platform teams using RHOAI Data Science Pipelines who run frequent pipeline experiments and need comprehensive tracking without modifying pipeline component code. This particularly benefits teams running many pipeline variations at scale where manual logging across all components is impractical.

## Business Justification

Automatic pipeline experiment tracking removes the primary adoption barrier for centralized experiment management in pipeline workflows. Customers who build and iterate on pipelines benefit from complete, consistent tracking without modifying their pipeline definitions. This supports the strategic objective of simplifying the AI experience by making experiment tracking a platform capability rather than a user responsibility.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] KubeFlow Pipelines runs are automatically tracked as experiment runs with metrics logged to the centralized tracking service
- [ ] Auto-logging requires minimal or zero user code changes -- users submit a pipeline and it is tracked by default as an experiment
- [ ] Automatically tracked pipeline experiments appear in the experiment tracking UI alongside manually logged experiments
- [ ] Auto-tracked pipeline runs are categorized by run type (Pipeline) for filtering in the experiment UI
