[RFE Creator] Split child 3 of 6: Automatic Experiment Tracking for Notebooks
---
rfe_id: RFE-010
title: Automatic Experiment Tracking for Notebooks
priority: Major
status: Draft
size: S
parent_key: RFE-007
original_labels: null
---
## Summary

Data scientists working in Notebooks on Red Hat OpenShift AI need their training and evaluation runs to be automatically captured as experiments, so they have a complete record of their work without manually instrumenting each notebook cell with logging calls.

**Split from**: RFE-007

## Problem Statement

Notebook users must currently add explicit experiment tracking SDK calls to their code to log training runs, metrics, and model artifacts. In interactive notebook sessions, this is especially burdensome -- users iterate rapidly and often forget or skip logging, resulting in lost experiment history. Unlike structured pipeline or training job execution, notebooks have no clear "experiment start" or "experiment end" boundaries, making manual tracking error-prone. Platform-level instrumentation that activates framework auto-logging when supported ML libraries are used would provide automatic coverage for common workflows.

## Affected Customers

Data scientists and AI researchers using RHOAI Notebooks/Workbenches who iteratively develop and evaluate models in interactive sessions and need comprehensive experiment tracking without manually adding logging code to their notebooks.

## Business Justification

Notebook sessions are the most common entry point for experimentation, yet they are also where manual experiment tracking is most likely to be skipped due to the rapid, iterative nature of interactive development. Automatic tracking for notebooks ensures experiment history is captured by default, enabling data scientists to compare runs and reproduce results without changing their workflow. This supports the strategic objective of simplifying the AI experience by making experiment tracking seamless in the most-used development environment.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Notebook sessions support automatic experiment tracking, capturing training and evaluation metrics when supported ML frameworks are used
- [ ] Auto-logging requires minimal or zero user code changes -- users work in their notebook and training runs are tracked by default
- [ ] Automatically tracked notebook experiments appear in the experiment tracking UI alongside manually logged experiments
- [ ] Auto-tracked notebook runs are categorized by run type (Workbench) for filtering in the experiment UI

[RFE Creator] Split child 4 of 6: Automatic Experiment Tracking for KubeFlow Trainer Distributed Workloads
---
rfe_id: RFE-011
title: Automatic Experiment Tracking for KubeFlow Trainer Distributed Workloads
priority: Major
status: Draft
size: S
parent_key: RFE-007
original_labels: null
---
## Summary

ML engineers running distributed training via KubeFlow Trainer on Red Hat OpenShift AI need metrics and checkpoints from all distributed nodes/jobs to be automatically collected and associated with their experiment run, so they can evaluate distributed training outcomes in one place without manually instrumenting each training node.

**Split from**: RFE-007

## Problem Statement

Distributed training workloads via KubeFlow Trainer involve multiple nodes running in parallel, each producing metrics and potentially saving checkpoints. Manually instrumenting each node to log experiment data is complex and error-prone -- users must ensure every node reports consistently and that distributed results are correctly aggregated under a single experiment run. The Trainer controller already has progression tracking infrastructure that polls training pod metrics endpoints, providing a natural platform-level instrumentation point for automatic experiment logging.

## Affected Customers

ML engineers and platform teams using RHOAI KubeFlow Trainer for distributed training workloads who need comprehensive experiment tracking across distributed nodes without manually instrumenting training code on each node.

## Business Justification

Distributed training is where manual experiment tracking is most complex -- multiple nodes produce independent metric streams and checkpoints that must be correlated into a single experiment view. Automatic tracking for Trainer workloads eliminates this complexity, ensuring distributed training outcomes are fully captured and comparable. This supports the strategic objective of simplifying the AI experience by making distributed experiment tracking a platform capability.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] KubeFlow Trainer distributed workloads automatically collect metrics and checkpoints from distributed nodes/jobs and log them as experiment runs to the centralized tracking service
- [ ] Auto-logging requires minimal or zero user code changes -- users submit a training job and it is tracked by default as an experiment
- [ ] Automatically tracked distributed training experiments appear in the experiment tracking UI alongside manually logged experiments
- [ ] Auto-tracked training runs are categorized by run type (Training job) for filtering in the experiment UI

[RFE Creator] Split child 5 of 6: MLflow API Equivalency for RHOAI Experiment Tracking
---
rfe_id: RFE-012
title: MLflow API Equivalency for RHOAI Experiment Tracking
priority: Major
status: Draft
size: S
parent_key: RFE-008
original_labels: null
---
## Summary

Customers adopting RHOAI need confidence that its experiment tracking capabilities provide equivalency with core MLflow experiment tracking APIs, so they can use RHOAI as a drop-in replacement for their MLflow tracking workflows without losing critical functionality.

**Split from**: RFE-008

## Affected Customers

Organizations evaluating or adopting RHOAI who rely on MLflow experiment tracking workflows. This includes data science teams using MLflow's Python SDK (e.g., `mlflow.log_metric()`, `mlflow.start_run()`, `mlflow.search_runs()`) and CLI for day-to-day experiment management.

## Business Justification

MLflow is the most widely adopted open-source experiment tracking framework. Customers evaluating RHOAI need assurance that core MLflow experiment tracking capabilities are available before committing to the platform. Without a documented equivalency assessment and closure of any identified gaps, customers remain uncertain about whether RHOAI can replace their MLflow workflows, delaying adoption decisions. This directly supports Red Hat's strategic goal of growing the RHOAI customer base by removing a key adoption barrier for the largest segment of potential users.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A concrete API-by-API equivalency assessment is completed for core MLflow experiment tracking capabilities (experiments, runs, metrics, parameters, tags, artifacts, search/comparison APIs) against RHOAI's experiment tracking service
- [ ] Identified gaps in core experiment tracking API equivalency are closed, enabling customers to accomplish equivalent experiment tracking tasks in RHOAI

## Success Criteria

- Customers familiar with MLflow experiment tracking workflows can accomplish equivalent tasks in RHOAI without re-learning fundamentally different paradigms
- RHOAI experiment tracking passes a core MLflow API equivalency checklist covering the most commonly used tracking operations

[RFE Creator] Split child 6 of 6: MLflow Experiment Data Migration to RHOAI
---
rfe_id: RFE-013
title: MLflow Experiment Data Migration to RHOAI
priority: Major
status: Draft
size: M
parent_key: RFE-008
original_labels: null
---
## Summary

Customers with existing MLflow deployments need a supported way to migrate their experiment data (experiments, runs, metrics, parameters, artifacts) to RHOAI's experiment tracking service, so they can transition to RHOAI without losing critical experiment history.

**Split from**: RFE-008

## Problem Statement

Organizations with established MLflow deployments have accumulated significant experiment history -- runs, metrics, parameters, and artifacts that represent months or years of data science work. Without supported migration tooling, these customers must either abandon their experiment history when moving to RHOAI or manually recreate it, both of which are unacceptable for production environments. This creates a hard blocker for RHOAI adoption among customers with existing MLflow investments.

## Affected Customers

Organizations migrating from existing MLflow deployments (self-hosted or managed) to RHOAI. This includes customers with standalone MLflow installations as well as those transitioning from other platforms that use MLflow as their tracking backend.

## Business Justification

Customers with existing MLflow investments need a clear, supported migration path to justify a platform transition to RHOAI. Without migration support, these customers either stay on their current MLflow deployment (delaying RHOAI adoption) or face significant manual effort to recreate their experiment history. Providing migration tooling directly unblocks RHOAI adoption for this customer segment, aligning with Red Hat's strategic goal of growing the RHOAI customer base.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Customers can migrate existing MLflow experiment data (experiments, runs, metrics, parameters, artifacts) to RHOAI's experiment tracking service using supported tooling
- [ ] The migration process is documented with clear guidance on supported source topologies, what transfers, and any limitations
- [ ] Customers can verify migration completeness by comparing source and target experiment data

## Success Criteria

- Customers with existing MLflow deployments can migrate to RHOAI experiment tracking without losing critical experiment history
- Migration is a supported, documented process rather than a manual, best-effort exercise

## Scope

### In Scope
- Migration tooling for MLflow experiment data (experiments, runs, metrics, parameters, artifacts) to RHOAI
- Documentation covering migration scenarios, supported source topologies, and known limitations

### Out of Scope
- MLflow API equivalency assessment and gap closure (covered by RFE-012)
- The centralized experiment tracking service itself (covered by a separate RFE)
- Migration from non-MLflow experiment tracking systems

RHAIRFE-124.description:
The current platform's model experimentation metrics are distributed across various components, catering to both predictive and generative use cases. This feature will enhance existing experiment tracking capabilities to better support Generative AI (GenAI) use cases.
Initially, the goal is to establish experiment tracking as a centralized service for managing experiments and storing performance metrics, and evaluations. This will enable systematic tracking of foundation model performance as they get customized, ensuring reproducible validation and evaluation across all Red Hat AI components and services by storing all relevant data and artifacts.
Goals
- Develop visualizations that enable AI engineers and researchers to correlate run parameters and configurations with evaluations and key performance metrics. For the Minimum Viable Product (MVP), the following use cases should be included:
- Model compression

- Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

- Document preprocessing

- Evaluation of Models performance


- Enhance the usability of experiment tracking capabilities through:
- A single-page  summarized visualization of runs with filtering options and user-friendly configuration of metrics of interest.

- An interactive run comparison page.


- Support diverse run types for experiment tracking, including:
- Pipelines

- Notebooks

- Distributed Workloads (KubeFlow Trainer)


- Support low effort integration with the tracking service. With auto-logging of metrics customers just start a job that is tracked by default as an experiment.

- Enhance the metadata stored for a run
- User that started the run 

- environment metadata

- Infra specs{*}*


- Support various hardware profiles.

- Instrument a subset of Red Hat OpenShift AI (RHOAI) components for metric tracking:
- KubeFlow Pipelines

- Notebooks

- KubeFlow Trainer (collect the metrics and checkpoints from the distributed nodes/jobs).


- Provide MLFlow equivalency and support migration scenarios from MLFlow to facilitate adoption of RHOAI

Out of Scope
- Developing a new experiment tracking system from inception.

 
Requirements Functional
- Decouple metrics and evaluation tracking from AI pipelines. Experiment tracking should function as an independent service, compatible with various RHOAI components such as workbenches, training SDKs, and external components.

- Introduce new visualizations to facilitate improved comparisons of:
- Input parameters

- Metrics and evaluations

- Forecasting of metrics


- Implement filterable categories on the experiment runs page (MVP), including:
- Run type: (e.g., Workbench, Pipeline, Training job, Script)

- Run name: (e.g., Compressor, RAG)

- Owner

- Metrics


- Ensure filters are interactively applicable with dynamic updates to search results upon selection (MVP).

- Establish default sorting of search results and unfiltered lists by metrics (descending).

- Display metadata corresponding to filterable categories for each experiment listed in the catalog.

- Support queries on experiment data.

- Support the ability to publish to Model Registry the metadata and artifacts of the champion run

Data & Integration
- Integrate with Model Registry for storing metrics and evaluations.

Done - Acceptance Criteria
- A new left navigation option for experiments is available within RHOAI UI.

- Users are presented with a landing page displaying a table of available experiments (including runs and metrics) with filtering capabilities.

- The metrics displayed in the table are configurable, and the table is interactive.

-  Users can create a new experiment, then create a new run, select its type, and be directed to the specific run flow (e.g., pipelines).

- Upon selecting an experiment, users can view a table containing only the runs for that specific experiment.

- Users can compare multiple runs and view an interactive visualization of parameters and metrics of interest.

- Users can select different metrics or parameters for comparison.

Documentation Considerations
- Update RHOAI documentation with a new section on experimentation, encompassing metrics and evaluations, to explain the new capabilities.

Background & Strategic Fit
A significant challenge for customers adopting AI in production environments is the comprehensive evaluation and metric tracking. This process must consider the entire system, not solely the models. Therefore, a centralized service dedicated to systematically tracking and versioning this data is crucial. Currently, customers experience fragmented metric exploration across various AI components, with support limited to pipelines. This feature aims to expand support to include more components capable of tracking metrics and evaluations within a single, unified service.
Furthermore, this service will align with the new RHOAI GenAI Studio, contributing to the strategic objective of simplifying and centralizing the GenAI experience for Red Hat AI customers.

In practice, I was able to, with claude walking me through the guide, make a PR for multi-arch builds of Nemo guardrails yesterday that hermetically pulls AIPCC wheels (it’s not fully hermetic due to some other complications with model fetching). This makes me feel that the skill and the guide is in a good place.

RHAISTRAT-1113.description:
Hermetically build all downstream (and upstream?) workbench images by 2026-Jun-30.
We need not be hermetic in odh-io. There are both advantages and disadvantages to pursuing it, though. Advantages: midstream should be production-like, avoid doing the same work twice, and differently every time, to support odh and rhods. Disadvantages: getting anything new done in odh becomes more work, there is initial ramp-up work to even make the thing build, which would not be there otherwise. Instead of gradual increase of difficulty: make it work in odh, then spend additional effort to make it rhds ready, all is front-loaded to odh.
We currently (as of December 2025) believe that in the final state, this will encompass
- Transforming every git clone that we perform during container image builds into a git submodule (nods to @Vath Sok)

- Adding a dnf lock file, that means, for every image, having a file that lists all rpm packages that get installed during the workbench image build, and running a tool that generates a lock file from that

- Resolving any dependency on EPEL, or otherwise non-Red-Hat-internal packages we still have; currently we can install these into non-final stages of the build and that passes conforma, but jdanek is unsure whether we'd still be allowed by devops tooling (conforma) to have such packages in the dnf lock file at all after we start using the dnf lock files

- Use AIPCC base images and AIPCC-built wheels exclusively; avoid having to build python packages from source during our container image builds, which often needs the aforementioned EPEL -devel libs

- Resolve usage of any third-party software, be it RPMs or not; preferably have it be built by AIPCC for us in some manner, either RPMs, or built into the base image. For example, code-server. The mongodb cli is another good example, it is something that builds from source fast enough for us to take it on ourselves, but hundred nothings have brought down a camel...

- Request what we need from AIPCC, such as pandoc, texlive-tcolorbox

- Consider ways to build our own RPMs so that we don't depend on AIPCC for everything we may want to do. It still may be worth it to onboard CPaaS for us, if we are serious about this. Waiting for next-gen process to come along puts us into a passive role.

- Should workbench have their own RHEL Layered product? That may include the R language support. It would underscore the emerging Red Hat strategic investment into the R ecosystem.

- Avoid running from-source builds during container image builds. It takes time on every rebuild, which makes it harder to make modifications to the dockerfiles, because having to then spend 1h+ just to see if the thing builds kills productivity. Docker files should simply download and unpack already built binaries (from AIPCC, the allowed places), nothing computationally expensive.

- Make progress on the CLI, to hopefully make the restructurings that result from all the changes above more easily manageable, with fewer copy-paste mistakes.

- Enhance project toling, be it the new CLI, or Makefiles, to work with the git submodules and hermeto lockfiles, and generic fetcher, so we are still able to do local builds and github actions and we don't have to maintain a different logic for konflux hermetic build and non-konflux build. This is optional, but I believe reasonable, and not extremely difficult to accomplish. It can be accomplished progressively over time and improved as we move forward. If we are in situation where "local build passes but konflux fails on xyz", that would demotivate devs to ever perform local builds.

- Flipping the hermetic= switch from false to true in Konflux Tekton pipelines, the final step

Each of these steps with the exception of the final one (hermetic=true switch flip) can be tackled largely in isolation. For example, the AIPCC adoption is a complete stand-alone initiative for us already. Everything in the list above may not be strictly necessary to achieve hermetic builds, it is possible that things will fall in place naturally as we are working towards the goal.
The natural ways of dividing up the work seems to be going by a theme as exemplified by the bullet points above, or go image by image, or by theme and further subdivide the work by image. We should have multiple people on the team working on similar things at the same time, for example, it would be helpful to have multiple people working with git submodules or with dnf lock files in the same sprint, so that they benefit from listening to each other's updates at meetings and can see benefit from possible additional collaboration.

RHOAIENG-66462.description:
Summary
Achieve fully hermetic (disconnected/no-network) builds for the OGX component to comply with PSS.SBR.02.04 and eliminate the current hermetic build exception. This is driven by Chris Wright's directive requiring VP-level sign-off for any remaining exceptions and tracked on the risk register.
Background
- OGX (formerly llama-stack) currently builds non-hermetically, inheriting an exception from the odh-llama-stack-core-rhel9 component

- Non-hermetic builds mean incomplete SBOMs, unreliable CVE tracking, and supply chain risk

- Build failures can occur if external hosts (e.g. HuggingFace) are down or resources are removed

- Downstream builds already use RHAI package index, which partially addresses dependency sourcing

- See: Slack thread

Related Tickets
- RHOAIENG-63269 - Hermetic build blocker for 3.5

- PSX-1094 - PSX exception ticket for ogx rename

- AIPCC-1125 - Doug Hellman's hermetic build feasibility doc

Blockers to Hermetic Builds
1. Build-time network access in install-common.sh
- Source: install-common.sh

- Issue: Script downloads packages at build time, including tiktoken which is a strict dependency

- Fix: Vendor tiktoken and any other pip dependencies via RHAI package index or pre-built wheels included in the build context

2. Granite embedding model download from HuggingFace
- Source: Dockerfile.konflux L52

- Issue: Model binary downloaded from HuggingFace during image build. VLLM_EMBEDDING_URL is now configurable, but the download still occurs in the build.

- Fix options: a) Base container with model pre-baked (must itself be hermetic), b) Model stored as blob in build system/artifact registry, c) Remove model from image, require runtime download via config

3. Unknown additional network dependencies
- Issue: No full audit has been done yet

- Fix: Deep-dive audit of all build steps to identify every external fetch

Open Questions
- What is the timeline - does Chris Wright's directive apply starting 3.5 GA or earlier?

- What artifact storage options are available in the build system for vendored models/binaries?

- Can AIPCC base images be used for model hosting, and are those builds hermetic?

Stakeholders
- OGX team: @Artemy (volunteered for audit), @Eoin Fennessy, @derekh

- Release engineering: @Alex Fan, @ckodama

- Product security: @owatkins, @jkoehler, @Lindani LD Phiri

There is a section of the build docs for haskell that talks about how to generate and then save the intermediate files generated by ghc so you can bootstrap from source without needing ghc to be available in the build environment. We will want to do that, and save those artifacts to git. The use of the EPEL binary would then be limited to a developer updating the source in the git repo, and it would not be needed to actually build the image. That feels similar to the way we have other code generation tools that we use in developer settings to produce code that we review before pushing through the build pipeline.
Once we have the ghc source checked into git, we could build an image with haskell and all of the other tools hermetically in konflux, and the output image with pandoc in it would be viable as a base image for another image build pipeline to use as a source to copy the binary into the product image.

In order to avoid building all python packages from source we need to switch to using prebuilt aipcc wheels.
- Switch Dockerfile.konflux to use the image quay.io/aipcc/base-images/cpu:TAG@sha256<HASH>

- uv pip compile pyproject.toml \
        --index-url https://packages.redhat.com/api/pypi/public-rhai/rhoai/3.5-EA2/cpu-ubi9/simple/   \
        --python-version 3.12 \
        --emit-index-url \
        -o requirements-aipcc.txt

RHOAIENG-61427.description:
Convert the rhoai-upgrade-helpers shell/Python scripts into native Go actions within the odh-cli migrate command framework. This eliminates the /opt/rhai-upgrade-helpers/ container dependency, provides a consistent UX (dry-run, confirmations, structured output), and makes migration logic testable in CI. Context: RHAISTRAT-1519 requires "odh-cli helpers must be implemented in Golang." The migrate command framework (Action interface, registry, sequential executor) exists in pkg/migrate/ but was deliberately not wired into the CLI. The 21 shell/Python scripts across 9 component directories in rhoai-upgrade-helpers need to be converted to Go actions that register against this framework. These changes will additionally address the removal of binary wheel python dependencies in the odh-cli, as they are being ported to Go and the rhai-upgrade-helpers dependency is slated for removal.
Priority order: follows the component maturity tiering from RHOAIENG-60213: Tier 1 (GA) components first, then Tier 2 (TP).

AIPCC-11891.description:
Package 'pandoc' does not build as-is via the AIPCC self-service pipeline and requires builder repository onboarding.
Build Failure Summary
The log file only contains 6 lines showing the GitLab CI runner initialization — it doesn't include any actual build failure output. The log appears to be truncated and is missing the last 200 lines that should contain the build error details.
Analysis of available log for `pandoc`
What we can see:
- The CI job is running on GitLab with `gitlab-runner 18.2.0`

- It uses a `docker+machine` executor with a `podman-stable:v5.5.0` builder image

- The log cuts off immediately after executor preparation — no build output is present

What's missing
The prompt references "the last 200 lines from bootstrap-and-onboard.log showing the build failure," but the log file at `/workspace/bootstrap-and-onboard.log` only contains 6 lines of runner initialization. The actual build failure output — including the `pip install`, compilation errors, or dependency resolution failures for the `pandoc` package — is not present in the file.
General note on `pandoc`
The Python `pandoc` package on PyPI is a wrapper/binding for the Pandoc document converter, which is written in Haskell. Building it from source typically requires:
- A working Haskell toolchain (GHC + Cabal or Stack)

- The Pandoc Haskell source code and its dependencies

This is a common source of build failures since most Python build environments don't include a Haskell compiler.
To proceed with a proper root cause analysis, I would need the complete log file containing the actual build failure output. Could you provide the full log or verify the log file is complete?
Packaging Analysis Summary
The PyPI "pandoc" package is a pure-Python wrapper and *not* the Haskell-based Pandoc document converter (>=3.7) requested in the JIRA ticket. Building the real Pandoc is *10/10 complexity*, with static builds feasible for amd64/arm64 via ghc-musl but *blocked on ppc64le/s390x* due to missing GHC toolchain support. The key next step is to clarify the package identity with the requester and determine whether ppc64le/s390x architectures genuinely require Pandoc.

comments.author: Lalatendu Mohanty
comments.body:
Analysis: Stable index URL for hermetic prefetch
Problem summary
Hermeto (cachi2) reads the PyPI index URL exclusively from --index-url inside requirements.txt. It runs as a separate Tekton task before the build container starts, so it has no access to the base image's pip.conf, env vars, or labels. This forces every consuming repo to hardcode versioned AIPCC index URLs in requirements.txt, causing mass file churn on every release bump (e.g., the notebooks 3.4→3.5 commit touched 90 files).
Why a naive "latest" alias is dangerous
Each version (3.4, 3.5) is a distinct ABI-compatible wheel set with potentially different torch, CUDA, and RHEL versions. A latest redirect could silently switch torch 2.7→2.10 or CUDA 12.8→12.9, breaking builds.
Possible approaches
Option
Description
Pros
Cons
A. Version-series alias
Stable URL like .../rhoai/3/cpu-ubi9/simple/ resolving to latest 3.x
Simple server-side change
Even minor bumps (3.4→3.5) change torch versions — still risky
B. Base-image-coupled resolution
Hermeto extracts index URL from the base image (label com.redhat.aiplatform.index_url or pip.conf) instead of reading requirements.txt
Zero churn; index always matches base image; single source of truth
Requires upstream Hermeto changes
C. Pipeline-level parameterization
Pass index URL as a Tekton param in prefetch-input JSON, alongside BASE_IMAGE in build-args
Keeps explicit, reproducible URLs; one place to update per pipeline
Requires Hermeto to support index_url in prefetch-input JSON (not supported today)
D. MintMaker auto-bump
Automate --index-url updates in requirements.txt via MintMaker/Renovate when new releases publish
No upstream changes needed; works today
Still generates noisy PRs; doesn't solve the root cause

Recommendation
Option B (base-image-coupled resolution) is the cleanest long-term fix — the base image already has the index URL baked in as a label and in pip.conf. Option C (pipeline parameterization) is a smaller upstream change and could be a stepping stone. Option D (MintMaker auto-bump) is the only approach that works without Hermeto changes and could be implemented immediately to reduce toil while the upstream solution is pursued.
Next step: file an upstream feature request with Hermeto for index_url support in prefetch-input JSON (enables Option C) and/or base image index URL extraction (enables Option B).

AIPCC-15143.description:
Goal
Eliminate hardcoded PyPI index URLs from requirements.txt files and PipelineRun definitions across downstream RHAI repos. Teams should not need to chase version bumps when the RHAI package index version changes.
This  would benefit all RHOAI/RHAI teams that use the RHAI Python index to build their components  that's 20+ teams. Without this, each team has to hardcode the index URL in their requirements.txt or PipelineRun files and manually update it whenever the index version changes (which happens almost every month) . Having it as an official task lets all these teams resolve the index URL automatically from the base image label.
How we achieve it
Layer 1: Hermeto + Task support (Done)
- Hermeto respects PIP_INDEX_URL env var as a fallback when --index-url is not in requirements.txt — AIPCC-20093

- prefetch-dependencies task accepts a pip-index-url parameter — AIPCC-20094

- Documented in Konflux user guide — AIPCC-21292

Layer 2: Automatic resolution from base image (Planned)
- Reusable Tekton task reads com.redhat.aiplatform.index_url label from the base image and passes it to prefetch — AIPCC-30371

- Document the automatic resolution approach — AIPCC-30374

End state
Downstream teams build FROM a fondue base image. The pipeline automatically reads the index URL from the base image label and passes it to Hermeto. No --index-url in requirements.txt, no pip-index-url in PipelineRun YAML. When fondue publishes a new base image with an updated index version, downstream picks it up automatically.
Note
Fondue itself also uses the Layer 1 task support to consume the RHAI index for its own base image builds. That work is tracked separately under AIPCC-30149 and AIPCC-30370.

AIPCC-14258.description:
Summary
Red Hat AI Inference currently delivers vLLM CPU wheels only for x86_64. Teams building downstream components (notably llm-d and KV cache) on IBM Power and IBM Z are forced to do source builds for vLLM CPU and its dependency chain, which is slow, fragile, and has become a blocker. This epic covers building and publishing pre-built wheel packages for all required components to the AIPCC pulp wheel index for both ppc64le and s390x.
Problem
No pre-built wheels exist today for vLLM CPU or several of its dependencies on Power and Z architectures. Every downstream component that needs vLLM CPU (e.g., llm-d KV cache) must compile from source on each build, adding build time, introducing reproducibility issues, and blocking integration work for RHOAI 3.5 EA1.
Scope
This epic is limited to building and publishing wheels to the AIPCC pulp index. It does not cover container image delivery, RHAII vLLM image enablement for Power/Z, or llm-d support on these platforms — those are tracked separately under their respective RFEs.
Components to build (ppc64le and s390x)
- numactl

- llvmlite

- opencv

- opencv-python-headless

- rust (build toolchain dependency)

- torchvision

- hf-xet

- outlines-core-builder

- numba

- vllm-cpu

Acceptance criteria
- All listed components are built as wheels for both ppc64le and s390x.

- Wheels are published to the AIPCC pulp wheel index (test index at code freeze, production index at GA).

- Downstream consumers (llm-d, KV cache) can pip install all components from the index without falling back to source builds.

- Wheels pass basic installation and import smoke tests on both architectures.

Note
We will probably need to use beaker to get access to some P/Z systems to complete some testing
References
- AIPCC-14258: Original Jira request

- RHAIRFE-1926: Associated RFE for vLLM CPU on Power/Z

RHAIRFE-1583.description:
Description
Title: Intelligent Request Routing Across Multiple vLLM Instances on IBM P/Z using LLMInferenceServiceConfig
Problem Statement
Large Language Model (LLM) inference workloads on IBM P/Z are currently constrained to single vLLM instance deployments, resulting in suboptimal resource utilization and throughput bottlenecks under concurrent request loads. As enterprise AI adoption grows on IBM P/Z infrastructure, there is a critical need for a scalable, intelligent routing layer that can distribute inference requests efficiently across multiple vLLM instances. Without this capability, IBM P/Z deployments cannot meet the performance and scalability demands of production-grade enterprise AI workloads.
Business Alignment
Enabling production-grade LLM inference on IBM P/Z is a strategic priority. IBM P/Z serves as a critical platform for enterprise workloads in industries such as banking, insurance, and healthcare — sectors with high demand for secure, scalable, and reliable AI inference. Enabling intelligent multi-instance routing on IBM P/Z directly supports:
- Red Hat OpenShift AI (RHOAI) roadmap for multi-architecture model serving

- IBM Z platform differentiation for enterprise AI workloads

- Customer adoption of AI on existing IBM P/Z infrastructure investments

- Open source community growth through validated llm-d support on IBM P/Z

Customer - Kyndryl - Kyndryl is planning to deploy WXA4Z product ( WXA4Z utilizes LLM-D capability ) into 20+ customer deployments.
Proposed Solution/Rationale
The llm-d project provides a proven architecture for high-performance LLM serving, combining vLLM's inference engine with Kubernetes orchestration and intelligent routing capabilities. However, this architecture has not yet been fully validated and enabled for IBM P/Z deployments, leaving a significant gap in the ability to serve production-grade, high-concurrency AI workloads on IBM P/Z.
LLMInferenceServiceConfig, built on the llm-d architecture, addresses this gap by providing a Kubernetes-native configuration layer that enables:
- Multi-instance vLLM deployment — multiple decode replicas running concurrently on IBM P/Z

- Intelligent request routing — configurable routing strategies via the llm-d scheduler and EPP (Endpoint Picker Protocol)

- Concurrent request distribution — load balancing across vLLM instances to eliminate single-instance bottlenecks

Business use case:
This enhancement delivers significant performance benefits by distributing inference requests across multiple vLLM instances instead of relying on a single serving endpoint. It increases overall throughput, enabling clients (eg: WatsonX Assistant for Z) to support more concurrent users and conversations. Intelligent routing reduces request queuing and balances workload efficiently, resulting in lower response latency and faster token generation. The solution also improves resource utilization across available AI hardware, ensuring consistent performance and scalability as demand grows
- Higher Throughput — Distributing requests across multiple vLLM instances enables near-linear throughput scaling, allowing IBM P/Z deployments to handle significantly more concurrent inference requests without degradation

- Lower Latency — Intelligent routing strategies such as load aware , prefix-cache-aware & context length aware routing ensure requests are directed to the most available instance, reducing TTFT and TPOT under production load conditions

- Better Resource Utilization — Multiple vLLM instances spread across IBM P/Z AIU hardware ensures full utilization of available compute, maximizing return on infrastructure investment

- Scalability — Horizontal scaling via replica count allows IBM P/Z deployments to scale inference capacity in line with growing AI workload demands without architectural changes

This solution leverages existing llm-d routing infrastructure, minimizing new development effort while delivering full multi-instance routing capabilities on IBM P/Z.

RHAISTRAT-2303.description:
Business Need (from RFE)
The full business need is maintained in the source RFE: RHAIRFE-1926

Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)
TL;DR
Onboard prebuilt CPU-only Python wheel packages for vLLM and its dependencies to the RHEL AI Python Package Index for IBM Power (ppc64le) and IBM Z (s390x), replacing source compilation during container image builds. This eliminates build fragility, aligns with the hermetic build mandate, and unblocks llm-d integration on Power and Z.
Components: RHEL AI Python Package Index (AIPCC), vllm-cpu, odh-model-controller (runtime templates)
Technical Approach
Artifact Type Clarification
The RFE's dependency list conflates three distinct artifact types. The strategy must address each through its appropriate packaging channel:
Python wheels (target: RHEL AI Python Package Index): llvmlite, opencv-python-headless, numba, pytorch (torch), pyarrow, torchvision, torchaudio (ppc64le only), hf-xet, outlines-core-builder, outlines_core (ppc64le only), blake3 (ppc64le only), cbor2 (ppc64le only), llguidance (ppc64le only), openai-harmony (ppc64le only), xgrammar (ppc64le only), vllm itself. These require cross-compilation or native builds on ppc64le/s390x builders. Wheels with native C/C++/Rust extensions (blake3, llvmlite, pyarrow, opencv, pytorch, xgrammar) are the highest-effort items due to architecture-specific build toolchain requirements.
System libraries (target: RHEL RPM repositories): numactl, OpenBLAS, LAPACK. These are C libraries consumed via system package manager, not pip. The vllm-cpu build scripts (build_vllm_ppc64le.sh, build_vllm_s390x.sh) currently compile OpenBLAS and numactl from source. If RPM packages for ppc64le and s390x exist in RHEL 9.6 repositories, the build can switch to microdnf install instead of source compilation.
Build toolchains (build-time only): Rust and LLVM are build-time dependencies required to compile certain Python wheels (tiktoken, blake3, llvmlite). These do not need to ship as runtime artifacts. RHEL 9.6 provides Rust and LLVM toolchains for both ppc64le and s390x via the CodeReady Builder repository.
Onboarding to RHEL AI Python Package Index
The primary deliverable is making each Python wheel available in the RHEL AI Python Package Index (packages.redhat.com/api/pypi/public-rhai/rhoai/) for both target architectures. Per the AIPCC onboarding process, each package requires: self-service pipeline submission, builder onboarding, probe tests across architecture variants, QE validation, and production promotion. Lead time is 1-3 weeks per package.
The June 2026 Jira comments indicate that most common wheels were already added to the RH Index for RHOAI 3.4, but several remain missing for ppc64le (blake3, cbor2, llguidance, numba, openai-harmony, opencv-python-headless, outlines_core, vllm, xgrammar). The strategy should first audit the current index state for both ppc64le and s390x before submitting new onboarding requests, to avoid redundant work.
Build Pipeline Alignment
The vllm-cpu Konflux Dockerfile (Dockerfile.konflux.cpu) currently does not use AIPCC base images. It builds on ubi9/ubi-minimal directly and sources packages from upstream PyTorch CPU index and IBM DevPI. Once all required wheels are available in the RHEL AI Python Package Index, the vllm-cpu build should migrate to the AIPCC CPU base image (quay.io/aipcc/base-images/cpu), which supports ppc64le, s390x, and x86_64 and pre-configures pip/uv to use the RHEL AI index. This migration is a prerequisite for fully hermetic builds but is a separate work item from wheel onboarding.
llm-d Readiness
The RFE identifies llm-d as a downstream consumer that depends on vLLM CPU wheels for KV caching and tokenizer components. The llm-d-inference-scheduler recently reverted ppc64le and s390x builds due to build issues (RHOAI 3.5-ea.2 release notes). Confirming whether the missing wheels are the root cause of the llm-d build revert is an open question that should be validated before prioritizing the package list.
Affected Components
- RHEL AI Python Package Index (AIPCC): Onboard missing ppc64le and s390x wheels for vLLM dependencies

- vllm-cpu (IBM Power/Z teams via red-hat-data-services/vllm-cpu): Consume prebuilt wheels from RHEL AI index instead of compiling from source; migrate build scripts

- odh-model-controller (Model Runtimes): No code changes; existing vllm-cpu-power-runtime-template and vllm-cpu-z-runtime-template already reference CPU variant images

Impacted Teams
- AIPCC (RHEL AI Python Package Index, base images): Onboard missing wheels, provide builder infrastructure for ppc64le/s390x

- IBM Power team (red-hat-data-services/vllm-cpu, ppc64le): Update build scripts to consume RHEL AI index wheels, validate ppc64le builds

- IBM Z team (red-hat-data-services/vllm-cpu, s390x): Update build scripts to consume RHEL AI index wheels, validate s390x builds

- Model Runtimes (opendatahub-tests): Validate CPU variant integration tests pass with index-sourced wheel builds

High Level Requirements
- [P0] All common Python wheels (llvmlite, opencv-python-headless, numba, pytorch, pyarrow, torchvision, hf-xet, outlines-core-builder) available in RHEL AI Python Package Index for both ppc64le and s390x

- [P0] All ppc64le-specific Python wheels (blake3, cbor2, llguidance, openai-harmony, outlines_core, xgrammar, torchaudio) available in RHEL AI Python Package Index for ppc64le

- [P0] System libraries (numactl, OpenBLAS, LAPACK) available as RPM packages for ppc64le and s390x in RHEL 9.6 repositories, or confirmed to be already present

- [P1] vllm-cpu build scripts updated to install from RHEL AI Python Package Index instead of compiling dependencies from source

- [P1] Hermetic build (Konflux) pipeline produces vllm-cpu container images for ppc64le and s390x using only AIPCC-sourced wheels

- [P2] vllm-cpu Dockerfile migrated from ubi9/ubi-minimal to AIPCC CPU base image (quay.io/aipcc/base-images/cpu)

Dependencies
- RHEL 9.6 RPM repositories (external, exists): Must provide numactl, OpenBLAS, and LAPACK RPMs for ppc64le and s390x architectures

- RHEL AI Python Package Index (internal, partially exists): Some wheels already onboarded for RHOAI 3.4; remaining gaps must be filled per AIPCC onboarding process (1-3 week lead time per package)

- IBM DevPI (external, exists): Currently provides some ppc64le wheels; will be superseded by RHEL AI index for hermetic builds

- Rust/LLVM toolchains (external, exists): Available in RHEL 9.6 CodeReady Builder repository for ppc64le and s390x; required at build time for native extension wheels

- AIPCC CPU base image (internal, exists): quay.io/aipcc/base-images/cpu supports ppc64le, s390x, x86_64 per overlay 0017; migration is a P2 dependency

Non-Functional Requirements
- Build reproducibility: All Python wheels must be hash-pinned in requirements files and sourced from the RHEL AI Python Package Index with SHA256 verification, per the platform hermetic build mandate (architecture context: AIPCC base images overlay, Model Runtimes overlay)

- Multi-architecture parity: Wheel versions for ppc64le and s390x must match x86_64 versions to avoid behavioral divergence across architectures (RFE: "feature parity with x86")

- Security: All wheels must pass Red Hat's secure build pipeline (AutoQA probe tests, source provenance verification) before production promotion (architecture context: AIPCC onboarding process)

Out-of-Scope
- vLLM CPU container image build for Red Hat AI Inference -- tracked separately in RHAIRFE-2136

- GPU-accelerated vLLM variants (CUDA, ROCm, Gaudi) -- owned by RHAII team, unrelated to CPU wheel packaging

- llm-d inference scheduler ppc64le/s390x build fixes -- dependent on this work but tracked separately

- AIPCC base image migration for vllm-cpu -- listed as P2 requirement but warrants its own strategy if scope expands

- vLLM engine feature development (multimodal, quantization, speculative decoding) -- RHAII scope per overlay 0015

- IBM Spyre accelerator variant -- separate build pipeline via red-hat-data-services/vllm-spyre

Acceptance Criteria (Proposed -- requires PM/Engineering validation)
- Given the RHEL AI Python Package Index for RHOAI 3.5,

   when querying for all packages listed in the RFE scope,    then prebuilt wheel files exist for both ppc64le and s390x architectures,    measured by pip index versions <package> --platform linux_ppc64le and --platform linux_s390x returning valid entries from the RHEL AI index.
- Given a vllm-cpu Konflux build targeting ppc64le,

   when the build pipeline executes,    then all Python dependencies are resolved from the RHEL AI Python Package Index without compiling from source,    measured by absence of build_vllm_ppc64le.sh source-compilation steps for packages that now have prebuilt wheels.
- Given a vllm-cpu Konflux build targeting s390x,

   when the build pipeline executes,    then all Python dependencies are resolved from the RHEL AI Python Package Index without compiling from source,    measured by absence of build_vllm_s390x.sh source-compilation steps for packages that now have prebuilt wheels.
- System libraries (numactl, OpenBLAS, LAPACK) are installed via microdnf install from RHEL RPM repositories rather than compiled from source in the Dockerfiles,

   measured by removal of source-compilation blocks for these libraries from build scripts.
- Given a completed vllm-cpu container image for ppc64le or s390x built with RHEL AI index wheels,

   when deployed as a KServe InferenceService using the existing CPU variant runtime templates,    then the vLLM server starts successfully and responds to /v1/completions and /health REST endpoints,    measured by Model Runtimes integration test markers vllm_cpu_power and vllm_cpu_z passing.
Effort Estimate
M (Medium) -- 3-5 sprints. Primary work areas: (1) Audit current RHEL AI index state and identify remaining gaps for both architectures (~0.5 sprint), (2) AIPCC package onboarding for missing wheels, accounting for 1-3 week lead time per package batch (~2 sprints, parallelized across packages), (3) Update vllm-cpu build scripts and Dockerfiles to consume index-sourced wheels and RPM-packaged system libraries (~1 sprint), (4) Integration testing with CPU variant runtime templates on Power and Z hardware (~1 sprint). Effort is moderate but calendar time may extend due to AIPCC onboarding lead times and cross-team coordination with IBM.
Risks
- AIPCC onboarding bottleneck: Multiple packages require onboarding, each with 1-3 week lead time; if processed sequentially, total calendar time could extend significantly -- Mitigation: Batch-submit all packages simultaneously and parallelize onboarding across independent AIPCC builder instances; prioritize packages blocking the vLLM wheel itself.

- Native extension build failures on ppc64le/s390x: Some packages (xgrammar, llguidance, blake3) have Rust or C++ extensions that may not compile cleanly on Power/Z architectures -- Mitigation: Engage IBM Power and Z teams early to identify architecture-specific patches needed for build success; fall back to IBM DevPI-sourced wheels as interim solution if AIPCC onboarding is blocked.

- Version drift between architectures: Wheels built for ppc64le and s390x may lag behind x86_64 versions if builders are not synchronized -- Mitigation: Pin all wheel versions in a shared requirements file and enforce version parity checks in CI.

- RFE declined by product management: Doug Hellmann's June 2026 assessment declined this RFE as "not aligned with current business priorities." Proceeding with the strategy requires re-engagement with product management to confirm prioritization -- Mitigation: Escalate the dependency chain (this blocks llm-d on Power/Z, which blocks RHOAI LLM serving on strategic IBM platforms) to product management for re-evaluation.

- llm-d build revert root cause uncertainty: The llm-d-inference-scheduler ppc64le/s390x build revert may have causes beyond missing wheels -- Mitigation: Validate whether missing vLLM CPU wheels are the root cause before committing to the full package list; engage llm-d team to confirm.

Assumptions
- RHEL 9.6 repositories provide numactl, OpenBLAS, and LAPACK as RPM packages for ppc64le and s390x -- needs validation

- AIPCC builders support cross-compilation or native builds for ppc64le and s390x -- confirmed (AIPCC CPU base image already builds for these architectures per overlay 0017)

- IBM DevPI (wheels.developerfirst.ibm.com) will continue to serve as an interim source for ppc64le wheels until RHEL AI index onboarding completes -- needs validation

- Rust and LLVM toolchains in RHEL 9.6 CodeReady Builder are sufficient versions to compile blake3, llvmlite, and other native-extension wheels for ppc64le and s390x -- needs validation

- The vllm-cpu build for s390x requires the same common wheel set as ppc64le (the RFE lists additional ppc64le-only packages but does not list s390x-specific packages) -- needs validation

Open Questions
- Are the missing vLLM CPU wheels the root cause of the llm-d-inference-scheduler ppc64le/s390x build revert? (Owner: llm-d team) -- Determines whether this strategy directly unblocks llm-d on Power/Z or if additional work is needed.

- What is the current state of the RHEL AI Python Package Index for ppc64le and s390x? (Owner: AIPCC team) -- Shafi Hussain's June 2026 comment identifies 9 missing packages for ppc64le; a full audit for both architectures is needed before scoping onboarding work.

- Has product management reconsidered the decline decision for this RFE? (Owner: Product Management) -- The June 2026 decline blocks this work; re-prioritization is required before engineering effort begins.

- Are numactl, OpenBLAS, and LAPACK available as RPMs in RHEL 9.6 for ppc64le and s390x? (Owner: RHEL team) -- Determines whether build scripts can switch to microdnf install or must continue source compilation for system libraries.

- Does the s390x build require additional architecture-specific packages beyond the common set? (Owner: IBM Z team) -- The RFE lists additional packages only for ppc64le; s390x-specific gaps may exist.

Supporting Documentation
- Source RFE: RHAIRFE-1926

- Architecture context: vllm-cpu component doc (RHOAI 3.5-ea.2), AIPCC Base Images overlay (0017), vLLM variant architecture overlay (0015), Model Runtimes team architecture overlay (0014)

- RHEL AI Python Package Index: RH Index

Prerequisites & Process Gates

- ODH/RHOAI Build Onboarding: _Pending human review_ -- AIPCC package onboarding is the critical path

- Licence Validation: _Pending human review_ -- all listed packages are open source but license compatibility with RHEL AI distribution must be confirmed

- Accelerator/Package Support: _Pending human review_ -- CPU-only; no accelerator hardware required

RHAIRFE-2157.description:
Summary
Customers deploying on Intel Xeon need a clear way to discover which Red Hat AI models are validated and optimized for Xeon hardware. Today, validated Xeon models lack the appropriate label in the model catalog, there is no curated Xeon collection on Hugging Face, and models already shipped have not been rescanned to surface Xeon compatibility metadata. This limits discoverability for Intel joint customers and undermines a published blog that references the Xeon collection URL.
Problem Statement
Red Hat AI has completed validation of a set of models for Intel Xeon (documented in the "Model-List-April-9th-2026" spreadsheet, "Validated Models - Yes Only" tab). However, customers cannot currently identify these models as Xeon-validated through the model catalog because:
- The Xeon label has not been affixed to the validated models.

- Models that have already shipped were not scanned for Xeon compatibility, so the catalog does not reflect their Xeon readiness.

- There is no curated Xeon collection on Hugging Face (the expected URL https://huggingface.co/collections/RedHatAI/xeon-models does not resolve), which breaks a published blog post that links to it.

Affected Customers
- Intel partnership: Joint go-to-market customers deploying RHOAI on Intel Xeon infrastructure who need to identify compatible, validated models.

- Red Hat AI users on CPU-based deployments: Users running inference on Intel Xeon who need confidence that selected models are validated for their hardware.

Business Justification
This is driven by the Red Hat–Intel partnership. Xeon model discoverability is a joint go-to-market commitment. A published blog post references the Hugging Face Xeon collection URL, which currently does not resolve — creating a broken experience for customers and partners following the blog's guidance. The validated model list is ready; the catalog and collection need to reflect it.
Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Validated models from the final provided list have the Xeon label affixed in the model catalog

- [ ] All previously shipped models from the validated list are rescanned so the Xeon label is pulled into the catalog

- [ ] A Xeon collection exists on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/collections/RedHatAI/xeon-models containing the validated models

- [ ] The final model list is attached to or referenced in this ticket before work begins

Success Criteria
- Customers browsing the Red Hat AI model catalog can filter or identify Xeon-validated models by label.

- The Hugging Face Xeon collection URL resolves and displays the curated set of validated models.

- The published blog post's link to the Xeon collection functions correctly.

RHAIRFE-1470.description:
Problem Statement
Current experiment configuration (AutoML KFP pipeline input parameters) relies primarily on system-selected defaults for:
- Training configurations (e.g., model quality vs. speed trade-offs) 

- Evaluation metrics used for optimization

While this simplifies the experience for new users, it introduces limitations.

Business Justification
Strategic Value: Provides advanced experiment control in AutoML through presets and metric override. Enables power users to optimize for specific business objectives (accuracy vs speed, custom evaluation metrics) while maintaining AutoML ease-of-use.
Customer Use Case: Enterprises have diverse optimization goals - some prioritize model quality for critical decisions, others need fast turnaround for rapid experimentation. Regulated industries may require specific evaluation metrics aligned to compliance requirements. Without presets, users waste time manually tuning configurations to achieve common trade-offs. Custom metric override enables domain-specific evaluation (e.g., false negative cost weighting in fraud detection).
Value Delivered:
- Common optimization presets (quality vs speed)

- Custom evaluation metric override for domain-specific needs

- Faster configuration for common use cases

- Flexibility for regulated industry requirements

Sovereign AI Alignment: User-controlled experiment configuration ensures training objectives align with business requirements without external constraints.

RHAISTRAT-1066.description:
Enable AutoML
Outcome Overview
Deliver an open source AutoML capability in RHAI based on the experience of AutoML from WXAI (https://www.ibm.com/products/watson-studio/autoai)
AutoML is the process of automating the manual tasks data scientists must perform when building and training machine learning models (ML models). These tasks include feature engineering and selection, choosing the type of machine learning algorithm, building an analytical model based on the algorithm, hyperparameter optimization, training the model on datasets, and running the model to generate scores and findings. Researchers developed AutoML to help data scientists build predictive models without having deep ML model expertise.
Red Hat AI AutoML applies intelligent automation to the steps of building predictive machine learning models. These steps include preparing data sets for training; identifying the best type of model for the given data, such as a classification or regression model; and choosing the columns of data that best support the problem the model is solving, known as feature selection. Automation then tests a variety of hyperparameter tuning options to reach the best result as it generates, and then ranks, model-candidate pipelines based on metrics such as accuracy and precision. The best-performing pipelines can be put into production to process new data and deliver predictions based on the model training.
 
(From discussion in Dec 2025) MVP Backend for AutoML functionality: 
- AutoGluon as an AutoML framework

- KServe as serving engine

- KF Pipelines as an integration/execution engine (from data reading to best model serving).

Success Criteria
A user can
- Create an optimized machine learning model for their use case, providing a dataset and identifying the use case

- Automatically build machine learning and AI models without deep data science expertise.

- Experiment, train and deploy models more rapidly at scale.

Problem Statement
Red Hat AI Inference (RHAII) targets non-OpenShift Kubernetes environments (AKS, CKS, EKS, GKE), but MaaS - a key component of the RHAII product definition - has no validated deployment path or user management strategy for xKS.
Current State:
- MaaS is in Dev Preview on RHOAI 3.0 with OpenShift-specific dependencies

- No validated deployment of MaaS on xKS environments exists

- User management relies on Kubernetes RBAC identity mapping - unavailable on xKS

User Scenario:
A platform team wants to deploy RHAII on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) with MaaS capabilities for multi-tenant inference API management. They need user authentication, subscription management, and rate limiting - but these depend on identity infrastructure that doesn't exist on xKS the way it does on OpenShift.
—
Business Alignment
What is the Business Value and/or Impact?
- Enables RHAII adoption on xKS - the primary target platform for the new product

- Blocking dependency for Dashboard/UI scope decisions

- Competitive Positioning: Enterprise-grade inference API management on any Kubernetes

- User Management Strategy for xKS:
- Define authentication approach without k8s identity mapping

- Evaluate OIDC/OAuth2 integration options

- Document user identity flow for xKS deployments


- MaaS xKS Deployment Validation:
- Deploy current MaaS on AKS/CKS test environment

- Document what works vs. what breaks

- Identify engineering delta to make it functional

comments.body:
Assessment: Accepted  
Primary component: RHOAI Dashboard / Platform
Impacted components: MaaS, 'Observability team'
High-level architecture plan:
MaaS UI is a microfrontend (modular architecture) with the 'maas API' as its backend, so it should be straightforward to reuse in xks.
For Observability, at the first iteration, I recommend that we don't invest in 'integration with the xKS providers' observability stack', but instead use our current solution based on Perses, based on Prometheus data. Currently, our Perses 'architecture' is based on Observability Operator. If this is not available  on xks, we would need to sort out how to fetch Perses data sources. Also, is 'MaaS team' responsibility to generate this data.
With our migration to the Gateway API and the addition of BYOIDC support in Dashboard, we should be in a good position from an authz perspective.  The quickest way to find out is to try things out via a POC
During the STRAT/POC phase, we also need to explore our strategy: whether to build a new Kubernetes-native data plane or adapt RHOAI to run on xks. Both approaches have their pros and cons, which I can elaborate on in the refinement phase with the platform folks.

RHAIRFE-1056.description:
Problem Statement
Red Hat AI Inference as a SKU must exist because enterprise customers adopting "neo-cloud" strategies require a certified, supported application layer to manage production-grade distributed inference—such as tensor parallelism and llm-d—without the complexity and brittleness of manual setup on vanilla Kubernetes.
A dedicated UI is essential to this SKU, starting with providing a complete MaaS consumer experience for MVP, allowing developers to discover assets and manage keys through a streamlined interface while abstracting the underlying infrastructure. Future additions to the UI like model serving, full observability (cluster, gpu-aas), and model catalog should be expected.
Business Alignment 
- Business Value of Red Hat AI Inference: unblocks revenue from customers who will not migrate their infrastructure to OpenShift by offering a "workload-first" product.

- Driver of UI: Helps position Red Hat AI as top of the line Inference Stack, with MaaS showback, llm-d observability OOTB
- Acts as "neutral territory," providing a consistent UX whether the model runs on AKS, EKS, or GKE.


Proposed Solution/Rationale Develop a dedicated UI for Red Hat AI Inference (RHAII) that abstracts the K8 complexity for new ITOps/MLOps admins in setting up services for their users. For MVP, the primary focus is a UI that enables MaaS model discovery and self-service API key management, and BYOIDC access for users without OpenShift credentials. 
Core Capabilities:
 MaaS:
- Admin:
- Create and manage policies/subscriptions/tiers. 

- Able to manage users and user groups assigned to tiers

- Observe MaaS and showback

- Create and manage keys of all users with API Key management


- Consumer:
- Create and manage user keys with API key management

- Discover available models and endpoints via AI Asset Endpoints


Observability:
- MaaS Observability (see above for showback)

- llm-d observability

- vllm Model observability (kserve-vllm metrics) [Stretch]

- cluster observability [Stretch]

User Authentication: 
- Consumers of MaaS should be able to log into the UI without having an Openshift login
- BYOIDC: integrate with external OIDC


Acceptance Criteria
- UI functions consistently across certified 3rd party Kubernetes engines. For RHAII TP, this is AKS, EKS and OpenShift.

- MVP feature set: includes MaaS (Consumer/Admin) and Observability. 

- Documentation: UI installation, configuration

- User authentication with external OIDC must be secure, enabling external consumers to access the MaaS portal without an OpenShift login.

Affected Customers/Partners & Scope
- Target Audience: Enterprise customers adopting multi-cloud strategies who need a certified MaaS layer to govern and distribute AI Assets on their own infrastructure.
- Platform Engineers (Admin): Focus on multi-tenant governance—managing subscription tiers, usage policies, and global API keys while using "showback" metrics to justify AI spend.


- 
- AI Consumers (Developers): Focus on rapid integration—requiring a secure, OIDC-based login to discover model endpoints and independently manage API keys without needing Kubernetes expertise or OpenShift credentials.


- Scope: This initiative prioritizes the Consumer-facing UI and Admin policy management for the Summit timeframe, while technical optimizations for distributed serving (llm-d/vLLM) are supported via code-based templates and documentation.

Alternatives Approaches Considered
- No UI: Rejected as the full inference stack offered includes MaaS, and MaaS customers are requesting a UI (lite-maas like experience), which is also considered for MaaS GA in RHOAI as well. See RHAIRFE-1002. POCs would also be improved with a UI for showing llm-d metrics. 

- Status Quo (OpenShift AI Enterprise UI): Rejected for this SKU because it is tied to the full OpenShift stack; the RHAII SKU targets customers who require a lightweight, portable solution on other K8s engines.

Reference Documents/Links
- RHAII Delivery Plan

RHAISTRAT-1680.description:
Outcome
RHAII adds distributed inference on any Kubernetes to the existing standalone inference on any Linux. Both paths use the same engine, so a model optimized in standalone serves in distributed without modification.
This initiative delivers a single product with two distinct deployment values:
Non-Kubernetes/Any Linux: a "hardened, supported distribution of vLLM" paired with "LLM Compressor" and a "Validated Model Repository." This allows users to deploy vLLM and LLM Compressor directly on hardware.
Any Kubernetes: A comprehensive "AI Platform" installation for enterprise customers on Kubernetes. This path consists of: Distributed inference with llm-d with vLLM as an Engine, "Model as a Service" as AI/API Gateway, User Interface (UI), Observability—to manage AI at scale.
Customer Problem
Standalone inference gets a model running on one node. Production workloads outgrow that: the model needs more GPU memory than one node has, request volume exceeds what one instance can serve, or latency requirements demand dedicating resources to different phases of inference. Today, going from single-node serving to multi-node production is custom integration tied to one Kubernetes distribution. 74% of organizations stall between AI pilot and production due to scaling and ROI gaps (BCG / Red Hat Summit 2025). Hardware lock-in compounds the problem: IDC projects 40% of organizations will run custom silicon by 2027, and a single-vendor GPU dependency is a commitment most enterprises are not ready to make permanently.
Done Looks Like
RHAII installs and serves models on standard Linux without Kubernetes dependencies. RHAII installs on any Kubernetes with llm-d, optional MaaS, observability, and web UI, and serves models across multiple nodes at production scale. A model optimized in the standalone environment serves in the distributed environment without modification. Customers select their deployment path from a single product entry point.

RHAISTRAT-1403.description:
Outcome Overview
We are consolidating our AI inference capabilities into a single product offering, "Red Hat AI Inference (RHAII)," to maximize market reach and simplify the customer journey. Currently, our core engine (vLLM) and optimization tools (llm-compressor) exist as Red Hat AI Inference Server offering, we are adding Distributed Inference with llm-d and Model as a Service capabilities to make Production grade Inference solution that can run on any Kubernetes.
This initiative delivers a single product with two distinct deployment values:
- Non-Kubernetes/Any Linux: a "hardened, supported distribution of vLLM" paired with "LLM Compressor" and a "Validated Model Repository." This allows users to deploy vLLM and LLM Compressor directly on hardware

- Any Kubernetes: A comprehensive "AI Platform" installation for enterprise customers on Kubernetes. This path consist: Distributed inference with llm-d with vLLM as an Engine, "Model as a Service" as AI/API Gateway, User Interface (UI), Observability—to manage AI at scale.

 
Success Criteria
Unified Product Experience:  The "Red Hat AI Inference" product is established as the parent offering. Customers can select their deployment path (Standalone vs. Kubernetes) from a single entry point.
Non-Kubernetes Installation
- Verification that the product can be installed on a standard Linux server without Kubernetes components.

-  The "LLM Compressor" tool functions correctly in this environment, allowing users to shrink models (quantization) locally.

- The vLLM engine successfully loads these compressed models and serves traffic

Kubernetes Installation
- The product installs successfully on Kubernetes clusters that includes llm-d with vLLM and optional MaaS

- Observability: Collection and Visualization of system health and performance metrics

- UI: Web based UI

- MaaS: 
- A unified entry point for all API requests.


Model Portability & Compatibility
A model optimized and saved in the "Standalone Runtime" environment must successfully load and serve in the "Kubernetes" environment without modification, ensuring a seamless promotion path from developer workstation to production cluster.
Strategic Business Context: Red Hat is positioning itself as the "unifying layer" for AI inference, like it did for Linux and Kubernetes. The goal is to bridge the gap between AI pilots and production—where 74% of organizations currently stall due to ROI and scaling issues (Source: BCG / Red Hat Summit 2025).
*IDC Prediction 2027*40% of organizations will use custom silicon (ARM/AI chips). llm-d's hardware-agnostic design is the only way to avoid lock-in.
NVIDIA-Red Hat Rubin Collab: Red Hat is moving to "Day 0" hardware support. llm-d must be ready for NVIDIA Rubin and Vera CPUs at launch (2026).
https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1B9qnXRgZ98ltA57BNdlfbYMceL3uniMfiw_9iSkrVO8/edit?usp=sharing

Testing out this strat-creator skill locally, awaiting the following feedback from PM & Architects: 
- I've listed persisting image + audio files in storage as a performance enhancement, but I feel fairly strongly that this is a must-have. Storing B64 content of these files on the client side will give us problems. Do you know if something like this has been discussed amongst the architects? Even just caching B64 contents with a short TTL on the server side would be OK.

- Per the RFE, image and audio files input ---> text output is in scope. Video input is not in scope (we've worked with this before but not seeing official support in vLLM docs & AFAIK the models that support this are lacking)

- As discussed in the call, ASR & Text to Speech are out of scope since the technical implementation differ quite a bit and this should be tracked in a separate RFE. Same goes for image/multi modal output.

- For file types I have JPG + PNG and MP3 + WAV for images and audio files respectively. Will open a spike to investigate what we can get for free, but are there any other high priority ones you can think of?

- Do you have a minimum file size in mind that should be supported for each modality? Want to define what we'll enforce as the maximum in the UI and don't want it to be too low.

- Seems like there is no audio support in Open AI's /v1/responses yet, only in /v1/chat/completions. Need confirmation on whether this might be coming or if we have to pivot. If it isn't supported, we may need to build out audio input support by using /v1/audio/transcriptions, which complicates the STRAT by quite a bit.
