RHAISTRAT-1527.description:
NOTE: THIS IS NOT THE REVIEWED STRAT DETAILS, FINAL VERSION HAS BEEN ADDED AS AN ATTACHMENT AS THE RHAISTRAT-1527.md FILE
Problem Statement
The current Gen AI Studio Playground supports text interactions only. As multimodal models become standard, users expect to work with images, audio, and mixed input types when exploring model behavior. Without multimodal capabilities, users cannot evaluate vision enabled or audio enabled models, test real world workflows, or build prototypes that rely on visual or auditory content.
This gap limits the usefulness of the Playground for early experimentation and prevents users from taking advantage of modern model capabilities. Users need a way to upload images, process visual content, handle audio input and output, and explore multimodal interactions within the same unified workspace.
Proposed Capability
Add multimodal support to the Gen AI Studio Playground so users can interact with models that handle more than text. At minimum, this should include:
- Image upload and processing

- Display of model vision outputs

- Audio input support including microphone capture or audio file upload

- Audio output from models that support speech generation

- Ability to mix text, images, and audio in a single conversational flow

Users should be able to:
- Switch between text, image, and audio inputs

- Provide multiple images in sequence for iterative reasoning

- Play back audio responses directly in the Playground

- Combine multimodal inputs when comparing different models

- Store multimodal interactions inside persisted chats once chat persistence is available

Why This Matters
- Enables realistic experimentation with models that support vision and audio

- Allows users to explore workflows such as document analysis, object recognition, image based prompt engineering, and spoken interaction

- Improves parity with modern commercial LLM interfaces

- Provides a foundation for agents that operate on visual data or use speech as part of a workflow

- Makes the Playground a complete testing environment for next generation AI applications

High Level Requirements
- Support image upload including JPG, PNG, and PDF where available

- Support audio upload and microphone capture where permissions allow

- Render images and audio inside the chat interface

- Provide clear input type selection inside the Playground

- Ensure the request payload is compatible with supported multimodal models

- Add UI feedback for processing status and large file handling

- Provide guardrails if a model does not support a given modality

Dependencies and Considerations
- Needs clear support boundaries for each model type

- Requires coordinated updates to model registry metadata to indicate capabilities

- Audio input may involve browser permission prompts that need thoughtful UX

- Future tie in with Configuration Persistence and Chat Persistence is expected

- Large file handling and cost implications need to be considered

MVP Scope
- Image upload and vision inference using supported models

- Audio file upload and basic speech to text or audio to text functionality where supported

- Text combined with a single additional modality in one session

- Simple UI selector for input type

- Display of results in the existing chat transcript format

Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)
TL;DR
Add multimodal input support (images and audio) to the Gen AI Studio Playground so users can interact with vision-capable and audio-capable models deployed on RHOAI. The implementation adds file upload, media rendering, and modality-aware controls to the gen-ai-ui frontend, routes multimodal payloads through the Gen AI Studio BFF, and extends the model-metadata-collection catalog with modality metadata.
Components: gen-ai-ui (frontend + BFF), model-metadata-collection, odh-dashboard (proxy config), kserve, vllm-cpu, vllm-gaudi
Technical Approach
This strategy delivers multimodal support (image and audio) to the Gen AI Studio Playground, enabling users to interact with vision-capable and audio-capable models through the existing RHOAI UI. The implementation builds on the existing Module Federation architecture: the gen-ai-ui plugin (port 8143) handles both the Playground frontend and its own backend-for-frontend (BFF), and vLLM already exposes OpenAI-compatible multimodal APIs that support image and audio content natively.
Per Staff Engineer direction, the BFF responsible for proxying multimodal inference requests is the Gen AI Studio BFF (`packages/gen-ai/`), not the main Dashboard BFF. The Gen AI Studio BFF runs within the gen-ai-ui container on port 8143 and is accessed via the /gen-ai/api/* path (architecture context: odh-dashboard.md, HTTP Endpoints and Module Federation Plugin Access sections). The main odh-dashboard backend proxies traffic to the gen-ai-ui container, which then handles inference routing internally. This means all body size configuration, payload forwarding, and multimodal-specific backend logic must be implemented in the Gen AI Studio BFF package, not in the core dashboard backend.
Image support leverages the OpenAI Chat Completions API convention where content array items can include image_url entries with base64-encoded data URIs or external URLs. vLLM v0.16.0 (shipped in RHOAI 3.4) already supports this format in /v1/chat/completions for vision-enabled models (architecture context: vllm-cpu.md, HTTP Endpoints section). The vllm-gaudi image already ships HPU-optimized implementations for multimodal models including Gemma3, Qwen2.5-VL, and Qwen3-VL (architecture context: vllm-gaudi.md, Supported Models section). The gen-ai-ui Playground must be extended with: (1) a file upload component for JPG, PNG, and PDF files, (2) client-side base64 encoding and payload construction, (3) inline image rendering in the chat transcript, and (4) a modality selector UI that adapts based on the served model's capabilities.
Audio support uses the /v1/audio/transcriptions endpoint for speech-to-text (architecture context: vllm-cpu.md, HTTP Endpoints section shows this endpoint exists on port 8000). The Playground UI must add: (1) audio file upload (WAV, MP3, FLAC, OGG), (2) browser microphone capture via the MediaRecorder API with appropriate permission prompts, (3) an audio player component for model-generated audio responses, and (4) a mechanism to pipe audio input to the correct vLLM endpoint based on whether the user wants transcription or conversational audio interaction.
Model capability detection is essential to prevent users from sending image or audio content to text-only models. The model-metadata-collection component ships YAML catalogs (models-catalog.yaml, validated-models-catalog.yaml) that are volume-mounted into the dashboard pod at /app/data (architecture context: model-metadata-collection.md, Integration Points section confirms the RHOAI Dashboard reads these catalogs via volume mount). These catalogs must be extended with a supported_modalities field (e.g., ["text", "image", "audio"]) for each model entry, driven by model card metadata and HuggingFace task tags. The gen-ai-ui Playground reads the catalog to conditionally show or hide modality input controls. As a fallback, the Playground should also support querying the model's /v1/models endpoint and inspecting the model's reported capabilities at runtime.
Mixed-modality conversations require the Playground to construct messages arrays where individual messages can contain a mix of text, image_url, and input_audio content parts, following the OpenAI API convention. The chat transcript component must render each content type appropriately: text as markdown, images inline with lightbox support, and audio with a playback widget. For MVP, the strategy supports text combined with one additional modality per session, with full multi-modality mixing as a P1 follow-on.
Large file handling requires client-side validation of file size before upload (enforcing configurable limits, defaulting to 20 MB for images and 25 MB for audio), progress indicators during base64 encoding and inference, and clear error messaging when files exceed limits or when the inference backend returns errors related to input size. PDF support is limited to single-page or first-page extraction, with the rendering pipeline converting the first page to a PNG before sending as an image content part.
The architecture routes all Playground inference traffic through the Gen AI Studio BFF via the /gen-ai/api/* path. The main dashboard backend proxies these requests to the gen-ai-ui container (port 8143), which handles authentication via the forwarded user token (x-forwarded-access-token header from kube-rbac-proxy) (architecture context: odh-dashboard.md, Authentication & Authorization section). Both the main dashboard proxy and the Gen AI Studio BFF must support the increased body size limits for multimodal payloads. No new backend services or CRDs are required. The inference payload is constructed client-side in the gen-ai-ui frontend and sent through its own BFF to the model's InferenceService endpoint.

Non-Functional Requirements
- Performance: No specific latency targets for image base64 encoding are specified in the RFE or architecture context -- encoding performance depends on file size and device hardware. The UI must display a processing spinner and not time out for at least 120 seconds during vision model inference, as vision models typically have higher latency than text-only models (RFE: "Add UI feedback for processing status and large file handling"). No performance target specified in RFE or architecture context for encoding speed -- needs PM/Engineering input (see Open Questions).

- Security: All multimodal payloads traverse the existing kube-rbac-proxy authentication path (architecture context: odh-dashboard.md, Authentication & Authorization section); no new authentication surfaces are introduced. The Gen AI Studio BFF receives the user's forwarded access token via the x-forwarded-access-token header and uses it to authorize inference requests (architecture context: odh-dashboard.md, Flow 2: Module Federation Plugin Access). Uploaded files are base64-encoded client-side and never stored on the server; they exist only in the inference request payload. File type validation must reject non-allowlisted MIME types to prevent injection of unexpected content. RHOAI platform is FIPS-compliant (GOEXPERIMENT=strictfipsruntime for Go components, architecture context: PLATFORM.md, Build & Security Compliance section); base64 encoding is not a cryptographic operation and does not introduce FIPS concerns.

- Backwards Compatibility: Text-only Playground behavior must remain unchanged. The modality selector defaults to text mode. Models without multimodal capabilities show no multimodal input controls. No existing API contracts or CRDs are modified.

- Scalability: File size limits (20 MB images, 25 MB audio as proposed defaults) constrain request payload size. Both the main dashboard proxy and the Gen AI Studio BFF must support request bodies up to 50 MB to accommodate base64 encoding overhead (33% expansion). The odh-dashboard pod is deployed with 2 replicas with pod anti-affinity across zones (architecture context: odh-dashboard.md, Deployment Spec section). This is a per-request concern, not a concurrent-load concern, since inference is already rate-limited by model serving capacity.

- Accessibility: Image upload and audio controls must be keyboard-navigable and screen-reader compatible per WCAG 2.1 AA (RFE: implied by RHOAI product standards). Audio playback controls must include visible time indicators and volume controls.

Out-of-Scope
- Video input/output: Video modality is not included in this strategy. Video inference requires streaming pipelines and significantly different UX patterns.

- Image generation / diffusion models: This strategy covers image input (vision), not image output (generation). Text-to-image models (e.g., Stable Diffusion) require a separate strategy.

- Server-side file storage: Uploaded files are not persisted on the server. They are base64-encoded in the browser and sent as part of the inference request. Persistent file management is out of scope.

- Custom model capability registration UI: Admins cannot manually tag models with modality support through the UI. Modality metadata comes from the model catalog or runtime model info.

- Audio streaming / real-time voice conversation: The WebSocket-based /v1/realtime API for continuous voice interaction is deferred to a future phase. This strategy covers file-based audio upload and playback only.

- Multimodal guardrails integration: Content safety scanning of uploaded images or audio via the fms-guardrails-orchestrator is a separate concern and not gated by this strategy.

- Cross-model multimodal pipelines: Chaining a vision model output to an audio model (or similar) is an agentic workflow pattern, not a Playground feature.

- Main Dashboard BFF changes beyond proxy body size: The core dashboard backend (odh-dashboard) requires no multimodal-specific logic. All inference proxying and multimodal handling is scoped to the Gen AI Studio BFF.

Acceptance Criteria (Proposed -- requires PM/Engineering validation)
- Given a user has selected a vision-enabled model in the Playground, when the user clicks the image upload button and selects a JPG file under 20 MB, then the image is displayed inline in the chat input area and the model returns a text response describing or analyzing the image, measured by the presence of a non-empty assistant message in the chat transcript within 120 seconds.

- Given a user has selected a text-only model in the Playground, when the Playground loads, then the image upload and audio input controls are not visible or are disabled, measured by the absence of active upload controls in the DOM.

- Given a user uploads a PNG file larger than the configured size limit, when the file is selected, then the UI displays an error message indicating the file exceeds the maximum allowed size, measured by the presence of an error notification and the file not being submitted to the inference endpoint.

- Given a user has selected an audio-capable model, when the user uploads a WAV audio file, then the model's transcription response is displayed as text in the chat transcript, measured by the presence of a non-empty transcription result.

- Given a user has selected an audio-capable model, when the user clicks the microphone capture button and grants browser permission, then audio is recorded and submitted to the model upon stop, measured by a transcription or audio response appearing in the chat transcript.

- Given a user uploads a PDF file to a vision-enabled model, when the file is processed, then the first page is rendered as an image and sent to the model for analysis, measured by an assistant response referencing visual content from the PDF's first page.

- Given a user sends multiple images in sequence within a single conversation, when each image is submitted, then the model receives the full conversation context including all prior images and text, measured by the model's ability to reference content from earlier images in its response.

- The model-metadata-collection catalog includes a supported_modalities field for all validated models, measured by a non-empty array value in the catalog YAML for each model entry.

- The Gen AI Studio BFF (/gen-ai/api/*) accepts request bodies up to 50 MB without returning 413 errors, measured by successful submission of a 20 MB image encoded as base64 through the full proxy chain (main dashboard proxy to Gen AI Studio BFF to inference endpoint).

Effort Estimate
L (Large, 6-9 sprints)
Justification: This strategy touches 2 components requiring code changes (gen-ai-ui frontend + BFF, model-metadata-collection), one component requiring minor configuration (odh-dashboard main proxy body size), and requires validation across 2 additional components (kserve, vllm). The primary effort is in the gen-ai-ui plugin, which needs substantial new UI components (file upload, media rendering, modality selector, audio capture), client-side file processing logic (base64 encoding, PDF-to-image conversion, MediaRecorder integration), conditional rendering logic driven by model capability metadata, and BFF updates for multimodal payload proxying. Since the Gen AI Studio BFF is owned by the same AI Studio UI team that owns the frontend, the BFF changes are coordinated within a single team, reducing cross-team overhead compared to modifying the main dashboard backend. The model-metadata-collection changes require schema extension and extractor updates, which are moderate effort. Cross-team coordination is needed between AI Studio UI, Dashboard Backend (minor proxy config only), Model Metadata, and Model Serving teams. End-to-end testing requires deploying actual vision and audio models, which adds validation time. The P0 image scope alone is likely 3-4 sprints; P1 audio features add 2-3 more sprints.

Assumptions
- vLLM v0.16.0+ in RHOAI supports the OpenAI-compatible multimodal chat completions format (image_url content parts with base64 data URIs) without additional configuration beyond model selection -- needs validation

- At least one vision-enabled model (e.g., Granite Vision, Qwen2.5-VL, or Gemma3) will be validated and available in the RHOAI model catalog by the 3.5 release -- needs validation (vllm-gaudi already ships HPU-optimized implementations for these models)

- The gen-ai-ui Module Federation plugin has access to the model catalog data (via the Gen AI Studio BFF or direct volume mount) to determine model capabilities -- confirmed (model-metadata-collection is volume-mounted in the dashboard pod at /app/data, architecture context: model-metadata-collection.md)

- The Gen AI Studio BFF (packages/gen-ai/) Fastify body size limit can be increased without architectural changes -- needs validation

- The main dashboard Fastify proxy body size limit for the /gen-ai/api/* forwarding path can be increased without architectural changes -- needs validation

- Browser MediaRecorder API is available in all supported browser targets (Chrome, Firefox, Edge) -- confirmed (supported since Chrome 47, Firefox 25, Edge 79)

- Base64 encoding of files up to 20 MB is feasible in-browser without exceeding memory limits -- needs validation (depends on device memory)

- Audio-capable models (speech-to-text) will be available on vLLM within the RHOAI 3.5 timeframe -- unknown

I don’t see this being an open question. Changes in this space will happen, but the data is already set for us via the OpenAPI: https://github.com/opendatahub-io/models-as-a-service/blob/main/maas-api/openapi3.yaml

UX mocks will produce this answer – we are actively working on this; shouldn’t block work as we navigate this

I don’t see this happening – this is a tech stack problem well away from UI – even if they deliver by time for us to use, I think given it’s a P1 we descope this immediately and follow up more holistically throughout the app to give real-time quota consumption.

RHAISTRAT-1547.description:
Problem Statement
Non-admin users consuming MaaS endpoints — AI engineers, developers — have no self-service view of their own subscription entitlements. To find out which models they can access, what their rate limits are, or which API keys they own, they must contact a platform administrator.
The 3.4 dashboard surfaces subscription management exclusively to admins. From a non-admin's perspective, MaaS is a black box: models appear in the AI Asset Endpoints page, but there is no view of subscription name, assigned quota, rate limit policy, or API key lifecycle.
At scale — deployments with dozens or hundreds of developers — this creates a persistent admin bottleneck and prevents autonomous developer workflows.
Business Alignment
As MaaS moves toward GA and broader enterprise adoption, the admin-only access model becomes an adoption friction point. Field SAs deploying MaaS for customers going live in Q2/Q3 2026 are already raising this gap — customers expect developers to manage their own access without involving platform admins for every key rotation or quota query.
Proposed Solution
A My Subscription page in the RHOAI dashboard for non-admin users, giving them a self-service view of what they are subscribed to and what credentials they hold.
User scenario: A developer onboarding to their organization's MaaS platform opens the RHOAI dashboard, navigates to My Subscription, sees they are on the "Engineering Team" subscription with access to two models and a rate limit of 10k tokens/minute — and generates their own API key — without filing a ticket or pinging an admin.
Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Non-admin user can view their active subscription(s) without admin access

- [ ] Subscription view shows: subscription name, models accessible under that subscription, configured rate limits/quotas

- [ ] User can view their own API keys: list, creation date, expiration, last-used timestamp

- [ ] User can generate and revoke their own API keys from this page (within the scope granted by their subscription)

- [ ] Page is accessible from the RHOAI dashboard to non-admin personas (AI Engineer, Developer)

- [ ] Admin-scoped subscription policy configuration is not exposed to non-admins

What This Is NOT
- Not usage metrics or token consumption — historical usage/showback is tracked in RHAISTRAT-1378 / RHAIRFE-1499

- Not admin subscription management — creation, editing, and deletion of subscriptions remains admin-only (RHAISTRAT-1117)

- Not rate limit editing — read-only view of assigned limits; admins set policy

Reference Documents / Links
- RHAISTRAT-1117 — Subscription Model Redesign (entity model foundation)

- RHAISTRAT-1201 — API Key Self-Service

- RHAISTRAT-1378 — MaaS Showback Dashboards for Non-Admin Users (adjacent, distinct)

- RHAIRFE-1499 — MaaS Showback Dashboards for Non-Admin Users (adjacent, distinct)

- MaaS 3.5 UX priorities — agreed Mar 31 2026 (Vince Conzola, Celestine Tan)

Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)
TL;DR
Add a non-admin subscription view to the RHOAI dashboard (via the maas-ui Module Federation plugin) that gives non-admin users a read-only view of their subscription entitlements, accessible models, configured rate limits, and their API keys in subscription context — without admin privileges. The backend uses the existing GET /v1/subscriptions maas-api endpoint (already user-scoped) with no new endpoint required; a new filter-by-subscription capability is needed in the API key endpoints to support grouping keys by subscription. Real-time quota display is out of scope for this strategy.
Components: odh-dashboard (maas-ui plugin), models-as-a-service (maas-api)
Technical Approach
Today, MaaS subscription management is admin-only — visible only in the Settings area of the RHOAI dashboard. Non-admin users (AI engineers, developers) see model endpoints on the AI Asset Endpoints page but cannot determine which subscription grants their access, what their rate limits are, or view their API keys in subscription context. At scale — deployments with dozens or hundreds of developers — this creates a persistent admin bottleneck.
1. Dashboard integration via maas-ui plugin. The subscription view is implemented within the maas-ui Module Federation plugin (port 8243 in the odh-dashboard pod). This is not a new application — it is a new view within the existing maas-ui plugin, accessible to non-admin personas. The maas-ui plugin already runs inside the dashboard pod and receives the user's access token via the x-forwarded-access-token header (architecture context: odh-dashboard.md). Authentication flows through the kube-rbac-proxy sidecar, which validates OpenShift credentials before forwarding requests to the dashboard backend. The surface (dedicated page, tab, or section integrated into an existing page) and navigation placement are UXD decisions; UXD mocks are actively being produced. The strategy uses design-agnostic language throughout.
2. Non-admin data access via existing endpoint. The view queries the existing GET /v1/subscriptions maas-api endpoint, which already returns the authenticated user's subscriptions as an array of SubscriptionListItem. This endpoint is user-scoped by design — Authorino enforces Bearer token authentication and the endpoint returns only subscriptions the authenticated user can access. The response includes subscription name, display name, description, priority, and per-model rate limits (model_refs[].token_rate_limits[].limit + .window). No new backend endpoint is needed; the team will extend this endpoint as needed based on UX requirements rather than creating a parallel consumer-specific route (Staff Engineer Input). The maas-ui BFF's /api/v1/subscriptions route is a passthrough to maas-api — no new BFF routes are required (Staff Engineer Input; verification item: confirm against codebase before sprint 1 to resolve the documentation gap between architecture context and Staff Engineer Input).
3. API keys in subscription context. The view shows the user's API keys grouped by subscription context. The last_used_at field is confirmed stored in the PostgreSQL api_keys database — no schema migration is needed for this field (Staff Engineer Input). API key CRUD (create, list, revoke) is already implemented by the existing /v1/api-keys endpoints and surfaced on the existing API Keys page — that functionality is not re-implemented here. The RFE's AC4 ("User can generate and revoke their own API keys from this page") is intentionally narrowed: the subscription view shows API keys in context and links to the existing API Keys page for management rather than re-implementing CRUD. This narrowing requires explicit PM sign-off, as the RFE user scenario describes a developer generating an API key directly from the subscription view; the navigation-to-existing-page approach is functionally equivalent but changes the user journey (see Open Questions). This strategy's new backend ask: the maas-api team adds a filter-by-subscription capability to the API key endpoints so the view can show keys associated with each subscription. The API contract for this capability (query parameter, POST body filter key, null handling for pre-migration keys, interaction with existing search filters) must be agreed before sprint 1 UI implementation begins — this is a sprint 1 gate, not a post-planning detail (see Open Questions).
4. RBAC for non-admin access. The maas-ui plugin and maas-api endpoints are accessible to non-admin users. The kube-rbac-proxy sidecar authenticates the user (OpenShift credentials required — this is the RHOAI dashboard, not the consumer portal). maas-api's GET /v1/subscriptions endpoint is Authorino-enforced with a Bearer token; the maas-ui BFF forwards the x-forwarded-access-token header to maas-api, which performs a KubernetesTokenReview to resolve the user's identity and group memberships, then returns only subscriptions matching those groups (architecture context: models-as-a-service.md — maas-api ClusterRole includes authentication.k8s.io/tokenreviews: create).
5. Admin field exclusion. GET /v1/subscriptions returns SubscriptionListItem objects — a purpose-built consumer response type defined in the OpenAPI spec (models-as-a-service/maas-api/openapi3.yaml) that does not include raw CR fields. No field-stripping logic is required in the backend (Staff Engineer Input). The endpoint returns: subscription_id_header, subscription_description, display_name, priority, model_refs (with token_rate_limits), organization_id, cost_center, and labels. The priority field is not admin-only — it may be displayed to users (Staff Engineer Input). The UI must not render any form controls (edit, delete, policy assignment) that imply write access.

High Level Requirements
- [P0] Non-admin user can view their active subscription(s) without admin access

- [P0] Subscription view shows: subscription name, models accessible, configured rate limits

- [P0] User can view their own API keys in subscription context: list with creation date, expiration, and last-used timestamp

- [P0] View is accessible from the RHOAI dashboard to non-admin personas (AI Engineer, Developer)

- [P0] Admin-scoped subscription policy fields (CEL group selectors, billing metadata, internal CRD resource identifiers) are not exposed to non-admins

Non-Functional Requirements
- Security: GET /v1/subscriptions returns only subscriptions where the authenticated user's groups match subscription group selectors — no cross-user or admin data leakage (architecture context: models-as-a-service.md — Authorino-enforced Bearer token, KubernetesTokenReview for group resolution). API key listing is scoped to the authenticated user's identity via Authorino + SAR checks (architecture context: models-as-a-service.md). Admin-scoped CR fields (CEL group selectors, billing metadata, internal CRD resource identifiers) must be absent from the SubscriptionListItem consumer response — confirmed by endpoint design (Staff Engineer Input).

- Backwards Compatibility: New view is additive. No changes to admin subscription management UI or endpoints. Extensions to GET /v1/subscriptions and API key endpoints must be additive (new fields/params only, no field removal or type changes).

- Performance: No performance target specified in the RFE or architecture context; the API key creation modal already uses this data pattern without performance issues (Staff Engineer Input).

Out-of-Scope
- Usage metrics or token consumption history — tracked in RHAISTRAT-1378 / RHAIRFE-1499

- Admin subscription management (create, edit, delete subscriptions) — admin-only capability

- Rate limit editing by non-admins — read-only view only

- API key CRUD (create, revoke) from this view — already fulfilled by the existing API Keys page (RHAISTRAT-1201); this view shows keys in context and links to the existing page for management

- Real-time remaining quota display — data flow prerequisites are not in place; requires a more holistic approach across the app (including AAE Quota) before it can be tackled; belongs in a separate strategy if revisited

- Consumer portal for external (non-OpenShift) users — tracked in RHAIRFE-1622 / RHAISTRAT-1545

Acceptance Criteria (Proposed — requires PM/Engineering validation)
Subscription visibility:
- Given a non-admin user with group "engineering-team" matching MaaSSubscription "Engineering Tier", when they access the subscription view in the RHOAI dashboard, then they see "Engineering Tier" with its associated models and configured rate limits, measured by the subscription list rendering with correct data from GET /v1/subscriptions.

- Given a non-admin user who belongs to no MaaS subscription groups, when they access the subscription view, then they see an empty state (no subscriptions), measured by the view rendering an empty state message rather than an error.

API keys in subscription context:
- Given a non-admin user with active API keys, when they access the subscription view, then they see their API keys grouped by subscription with creation date, expiration, and last-used timestamp displayed, measured by the API key list matching the user's identity in maas-api (no keys owned by other users) and the last_used_at field rendering a non-null timestamp for keys that have been used.

- Given a non-admin user is assigned to two subscriptions with different API keys, when they view the subscription view, then keys appear under their respective subscription sections, measured by verifying the filter-by-subscription query returns the correct key sets per subscription.

Admin field exclusion:
- Given a non-admin user viewing their subscription, then the consumer response from GET /v1/subscriptions does not include admin-only fields, measured by inspecting the serialized JSON response body against the SubscriptionListItem schema defined in models-as-a-service/maas-api/openapi3.yaml and verifying that CEL group selectors, billing metadata, and internal CRD resource identifiers are absent.

Cross-user security:
- Given User A and User B with different group memberships, when User A calls GET /v1/subscriptions (via maas-ui BFF), then the response contains zero subscriptions matching only User B's groups, measured by verifying the subscription IDs in User A's response do not include any MaaSSubscription whose group selectors exclusively match User B's groups.

RFE AC4 scope deviation (requires PM sign-off):
- The RFE states "User can generate and revoke their own API keys from this page." This strategy scopes the subscription view to showing API keys in context and linking to the existing API Keys page (RHAISTRAT-1201) for management. PM must explicitly confirm this navigation-to-existing-page approach satisfies the original intent. If PM requires inline key management on the subscription view, scope and effort must be re-estimated.

Edge cases:
- Given a non-admin user is assigned to two subscriptions that both cover the same model (e.g., "Engineering Tier" and "Platform Tier"), when they access the subscription view, then both subscriptions appear with their respective rate limits, and the model is listed under each subscription, measured by the UI rendering two subscription entries each containing the model.

- Given a non-admin user's group membership changes (added to or removed from a subscription group) while the subscription view is loaded, when they refresh the view, then the updated subscription list reflects the current group membership, measured by verifying the UI refreshes from GET /v1/subscriptions on page load.

- Given a non-admin user's OpenShift session token expires while the subscription view is open, when they attempt any action (page reload, navigation), then the UI redirects to the OpenShift login page or displays an authentication-expired error, measured by mocking a 401 from the kube-rbac-proxy sidecar and verifying the UI response.

- Given a subscription with an empty model_refs[] array (no models assigned), when a non-admin user views that subscription, then the subscription entry renders an empty model list (zero-model empty state) rather than erroring, measured by the UI displaying the subscription name and an empty model list.

- Given a non-admin user viewing a subscription with a display name or model name exceeding 100 characters, when they view the subscription view, then the text is truncated with a tooltip or wraps within the layout without overflowing its container, measured by visual regression or layout snapshot test.

Effort Estimate
Size: S (1-2 sprints)
Justification: The core work is a new UI view within the existing maas-ui plugin, backed by the existing GET /v1/subscriptions endpoint (no new backend endpoint). The API key filter-by-subscription capability is a bounded new backend feature within the MaaS team, with the subscription_id column already present in the database. The last_used_at field requires no schema migration (confirmed in DB). No CRD changes, no new components, single-team execution (MaaS + Dashboard). Real-time quota display is out of scope. UXD design is the primary lead-time dependency; mocks are in progress.

Staff Engineer Input
API Corrections
The strategy references /v1/tiers/lookup — this endpoint no longer exists. The current maas-api exposes GET /v1/subscriptions, which returns the authenticated user's subscriptions as an array of SubscriptionListItem. This endpoint already provides subscription name, display name, description, priority, and per-model rate limits (model_refs[].token_rate_limits[].limit + .window). No new /v1/subscriptions/me endpoint needs to be created; the existing endpoint is already user-scoped.
The implementation approach shall be: the UI consumes GET /v1/subscriptions and the team expands that endpoint as needed based on UX requirements, rather than creating a parallel consumer-specific route.
Quota Display
Real-time remaining quota display is potentially in scope depending on backend support, but is currently blocked by a RHCL dependency. If that dependency resolves in time, the backend may expose current usage and the UI should surface it. If it does not resolve, the UI shall display configured limits only (already available via token_rate_limits in the existing response). The strategy must not assume real-time quota is out of scope — treat it as conditional: implement if RHCL unblocks, otherwise degrade gracefully to limits-only display.
Review Corrections
The following findings from the automated feasibility review are incorrect and shall not be carried forward in refinement:
BFF routing split (incorrect): The review claimed the maas-ui BFF's /api/v1/subscriptions route only handles admin CRD management via the K8s API. This is wrong. The BFF has /api/v1/subscriptions as a passthrough to the MaaS API directly. No new BFF routes are required for the consumer-facing subscription view.
Admin field exclusion concern (incorrect): The review claimed GET /v1/subscriptions may return raw CR data with admin-only fields that need stripping. This is wrong. The endpoint returns SubscriptionListItem objects, which is a purpose-built consumer response type defined in the OpenAPI spec. Inspecting the schema confirms it contains no admin-only fields — only subscription_id_header, subscription_description, display_name, priority, model_refs (with token_rate_limits), organization_id, cost_center, and labels. None of these are sensitive or admin-gated. The UI will not display all of them, but there is no field-level security concern to address in the backend.
UX Design Flexibility
The strategy must not prescribe a specific page name or navigation location. The subscription view may be implemented as a new dedicated page, integrated into the existing API Keys page, or another UXD-determined surface. Use design-agnostic language throughout (e.g., "subscription view" or "subscription section") rather than hardcoding "My Subscription page." Navigation placement is a UXD decision.
API Key Scope and last_used_at
last_used_at is confirmed stored in the maas-api PostgreSQL database for API keys. Remove all speculation, conditional branching, and open questions about this field — treat it as always available.
API key CRUD (list, create, revoke) is already implemented and is not part of this strategy. This strategy covers showing a user's API keys in the context of their subscription. Remove all acceptance criteria about viewing, generating, and revoking API keys — those are already fulfilled by the existing API Keys page. The same applies to the high-level requirements for those capabilities.
New ask for the maas-api team: add the ability to filter API keys by subscription. This is a new backend capability needed to show keys grouped by subscription context.
RHCL Quota Display — Binary Decision
Real-time quota display is a binary decision made before development starts, not a runtime graceful degradation. Before development begins, determine whether the RHCL dependency has been unblocked by the maas-api team. If yes, implement real-time quota display. If no, implement limits-only display. Do not build the UI to handle both cases at runtime — code for whichever state is current when development starts. Update the P1 requirement and dependencies table to reflect this: the RHCL status column should describe when and how the decision is made.
Policy Priority Visibility
priority from the SubscriptionListItem response is not an admin-only field — users may see it. Remove policy priority from any list of admin-scoped fields that must be excluded from the non-admin view.
Subscription Model Redesign (RHAISTRAT-1117)
RHAISTRAT-1117 has shipped. The MaaSSubscription CRD will not change. Remove all references to this as a risk, scheduling concern, or open question. Remove the RHAISTRAT-1117 row from the dependencies table.
Risk and Open Question Cleanup
Remove the following risks — they are not valid concerns:
- Group membership resolution (KubernetesTokenReview handles this reliably — not a risk)

- last_used_at schema availability (confirmed in DB — not a risk)

- RHAISTRAT-1117 CRD instability (shipped — not a concern)

- RHAISTRAT-1201 API key page conflict (the two pages will work hand in hand, not conflict — remove)

Remove or resolve the following open questions:
- "Does the PostgreSQL api_keys schema include a last_used_at column?" — Answered: yes, confirmed in the DB. Remove.

- "Is RHAISTRAT-1117 scheduling aligned with this work?" — Moot: the redesign is shipped. Remove.

- "Do RHAISTRAT-1201 API key management UX designs conflict with this page?" — Not a concern. Remove.

Acceptance Criteria Cleanup

Real-time quota display is not happening for this TP — the data flow prerequisites are not in place and this work needs to be approached more holistically across the app (including AAE Quota) before it can be tackled. RHAISTRAT-1267.description:
Problem Statement
The 3.4 EA1 Tech Preview of Perses-based observability dashboards (RHAISTRAT-113) is restricted to Cluster Admins only. Data scientists and other non-admin users cannot access metrics dashboards – including dashboards designed specifically for them – because the current implementation requires cluster-admin privileges. This is the primary blocker for broader adoption and GA graduation. Additionally, while an initial pattern exists for component teams to contribute Perses dashboards, it needs to be refined, hardened, and documented as the supported strategy for team collaboration and dashboard embedding.
Goals
Unblock non-admin user access to metrics and mature the existing component team contribution patterns into a production-ready, supported workflow, building on RHAISTRAT-113 to move observability from Tech Preview toward GA readiness.
Primary Objective: Enable data scientists and other non-admin users to access relevant metrics and harden the dashboard contribution and embedding strategy by delivering:
- User-Scoped Metrics Access: Non-admin users can view metrics dashboards scoped to the namespaces and resources they have access to, without requiring cluster-admin privileges

- Refined Dashboard Contribution Pattern: The existing pattern for component teams to contribute Perses dashboards is refined, documented, and hardened as the supported strategy – including a clear specification repository, onboarding process, and evaluation of newer Perses features (e.g., tags) to improve dashboard discovery and organization

- Embeddable Dashboards for Feature Teams: Component teams can embed Perses-based metrics dashboards within their own feature pages, bringing metrics closer to the user's workflow context

Requirements
User Access:
- Non-admin users (data scientists, project users) can view metrics relevant to their work, scoped to their authorized namespaces

- Cluster-admin-only dashboards (e.g., Cluster Overview) remain appropriately restricted

- Dashboards are hidden for users who lack access to the underlying metrics, preventing confusing error states

Dashboard Capabilities to Enable:
- Data Scientist / Model Deployments Dashboard: Currently cluster-admin-only. Enable non-admin access so data scientists can view model performance metrics (latency percentiles, throughput, GPU utilization, endpoint availability) scoped to their authorized namespaces

- Embedded Dashboards: Component teams can surface Perses-based metrics within their own feature pages (tabs, detail panels) in addition to the central observability page

Dashboard Contribution Pattern:
- Refine and harden the existing contribution pattern into the officially supported strategy, with clear documentation and onboarding guidance

- Establish a specification repository location for Perses dashboard specifications with a collaborative workflow between component and dashboard teams

- Evaluate newer Perses features (e.g., tags) to improve how dashboards are discovered, categorized, and presented in the UI

- Component teams can independently author dashboards for their domains; dashboard team provides oversight, integration guidance, and UX review

Quality:
- Real-time metrics refresh within 30 seconds

- Dashboard load times under 3 seconds for typical workloads

- Graceful degradation if underlying metrics infrastructure is unavailable

Acceptance Criteria
- Non-admin users can access the Data Scientist / Model Deployments dashboard scoped to their authorized namespaces

- The dashboard contribution pattern is documented as the supported strategy with specification repository, onboarding guidance, and embedding instructions for component teams

- A Perses CRD-based dashboard is demonstrated embedded within a feature team's page

- Performance validation: dashboards load within acceptable thresholds for non-admin users

Scope Definition
In Scope:
- Non-admin user access to metrics dashboards

- Refinement and hardening of the existing dashboard contribution pattern, including specification repository and onboarding process

- Evaluation of newer Perses features (e.g., tags) for dashboard organization

- Perses dashboard embedding pattern for component teams

Out of Scope:
- Infrastructure metrics collection - covered by RHOAISTRAT-575

- New dashboard content creation (component teams own their own dashboards)

- Custom dashboard authoring by customers at runtime

- Perses upstream UI issues (legend readability, clipping) - tracked separately

- Non-Prometheus data source integrations

Business Impact
- Customer Value: Data scientists and project users gain direct access to metrics relevant to their work without requiring cluster-admin intervention, removing the primary adoption blocker for observability in RHOAI.

- Team Velocity: A hardened, documented contribution pattern enables component teams to independently deliver metrics dashboards for their domains, reducing coordination overhead and accelerating delivery of new observability capabilities.

- GA Readiness: Resolving the non-admin access limitation is the primary requirement for graduating observability dashboards from Tech Preview to GA.

- Competitive Advantage: Matches hyperscalers' built-in monitoring capabilities with role-appropriate access out of the box.

Technical Review Required for Starting:
- Investigation needed into COO next version of Perses capabilities

Team Ownership
Implementation Team: Dashboard team Approval Authority: Observability team lead (Roy Nissim - rnissim@redhat.com) Technical Review: Kevin Howell (@khowell@redhat.com) for infrastructure integration patterns
Dependencies: RHAISTRAT-113 (Perses integration Tech Preview), RHOAISTRAT-575 (centralized metrics), RHOAISTRAT-617 (platform dashboards), CO Operator Perses integration, Newer COO 1.4 release?
Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)
Note: The full strategy exceeds Jira's description size limit and is stored as an attachment: RHAISTRAT-1267-strategy.md. The TL;DR is shown below for quick reference.

TL;DR
Enable non-cluster-admin users (data scientists, project users) to access Perses-based metrics dashboards scoped to their authorized namespaces, and harden the existing dashboard contribution pattern into a production-ready workflow with onboarding documentation and embeddable dashboard support. The authorization mechanism leverages existing OpenShift cluster monitoring RBAC and COO 1.5's Perses datasource query parameter interpolation — this is primarily a configuration and UI integration task, not a backend proxy engineering effort. Effort: S (2 sprints).
Components: odh-dashboard (host + observability kustomize overlay), Perses server (via COO 1.5 / Cluster Observability Operator), Thanos Querier (web + tenancy endpoints)
Staff Engineer Input
Effort: S (2 sprints). The L-XL estimate is based on incorrect technical assumptions.
Authorization mechanism — correct the technical approach. The Path A/Path B framing is wrong. Neither path involves PromQL rewriting.
- Path A (preferred): COO 1.5 Perses datasource query parameter interpolation. The Thanos Querier tenancy endpoint already enforces namespace-scoped RBAC. The gap was Perses constructing queries with namespace metadata for the tenancy endpoint. Solved upstream: perses/perses#3940, perses/plugins#638, perses/shared#118 (all merged). COO 1.5 (June 9, 2026) adopts these changes. This is configuration, not code.

- Path B (fallback): prom-namespace-auth-proxy ([RHOAIENG-52100](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHOAIENG-52100)). A standalone reverse proxy between Perses and Thanos that parses PromQL namespace matchers, resolves authorized namespaces via OpenShift Projects API, and forwards scoped requests. Working POC exists. Heavier — requires deploying an additional service.

These are mutually exclusive. A spike on the pre-release COO 1.5 build is essential. COO releases quarterly — validating now ensures fixes land before June 9, avoiding a quarter-long wait.
Namespace enumeration is not a backend concern. The dashboard UI already fetches the user's project list from the Kubernetes API. That list is used as a Perses variable in dashboard queries. Remove the backend namespace enumeration design (OpenShift Projects API calls, per-session caching, etc.).
Two Thanos endpoints, two access patterns. Cluster dashboards use the Thanos "web" endpoint, gated by the cluster-monitoring-view ClusterRole — the UI checks this role and hides cluster dashboards accordingly. Namespace-scoped dashboards use the Thanos tenancy endpoint, which enforces RBAC per namespace. The RBAC permission gate open question is already answered by the cluster monitoring stack.
Current-state data flow: Perses datasource currently points to the Thanos Querier web endpoint, not the tenancy endpoint. The web endpoint provides cluster-wide access gated by cluster-monitoring-view. For non-admin dashboards, a new datasource pointing to the tenancy endpoint (with COO 1.5 query parameter interpolation for namespace metadata) will be added. Both datasources will coexist — web endpoint for cluster dashboards, tenancy endpoint for namespace-scoped dashboards.
No CI linting of PersesDashboard CRs. Remove CI linting from the contribution pattern exit criteria.
`/api/prometheus/query` is unrelated to Perses. Perses uses its own datasource configuration to connect to a service. Remove references tying Perses data flow to the dashboard's /api/prometheus/query route.
PatternFly/Perses styling is already done. MUI theme adjustments and CSS overrides are in place. No PoC, no shared npm package, no monitoring-plugin evaluation needed. Full PatternFly component adoption (once Perses supports component-level theming) is out of scope.
Embedded dashboards are simple. Embedding is a shared React UI component that takes a PersesDashboard CR reference. No BFF sidecar, no separate proxy configuration, no Module Federation architectural decision. Remove the BFF-sidecar vs host-backend discussion and echarts dependency concerns.
No Go SDK. Teams create YAML PersesDashboard CRs directly. Remove all Go SDK references, project templates, and programmatic authoring descriptions.
Perses tags: adopt if available in COO 1.5. Tags are implemented upstream (perses-operator PR #321). Validate during the COO 1.5 spike. If supported, use tags instead of naming conventions. Not a hard requirement.
Graceful degradation on the frontend is valid. The UI should not break if the monitoring stack isn't configured correctly. Keep this requirement.
PersesDashboard CR storage is the component team's choice. Not an open question.
Dismiss these open questions: P99 latency target (out of scope), BFF-sidecar vs host-backend (not applicable), RBAC permission gate (answered by cluster monitoring stack), specification repository location (component team's choice).

comments.body:
Staff Engineer Update — July 3, 2026
Per Adel's July 2 email: kagenti will not be productized. OpenShell is the anchor upstream project. This strat's architecture has changed:
What changed
- No AgentRuntime CRD. BFF creates Sandbox CR (agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1) + optional Route via k8s API directly.

- Fallback: If agent-sandbox CRD not installed, BFF creates Deployment + Service instead.

- Discovery: Label selector opendatahub.io/agent-type=agent on Sandbox CRs + Deployments. No operator-driven discovery.

- Agent card: BFF probes /.well-known/agent-card.json from agent pod at runtime (separate async endpoint). No CRD status.card.

- Dependency changed: KATA-4728 (Agent Sandbox TP, ships July 7) replaces RHAISTRAT-1599 (kagenti, not shipping).

API endpoints (renamed)
- GET /api/v1/agents — list agents

- GET /api/v1/agents/:ns/:name — agent detail

- GET /api/v1/agents/:ns/:name/card — agent card discovery (async)

- DELETE /api/v1/agents/:ns/:name — delete

Staff input corrections
- Module placement: genAi federated module (port 8143) → agent-ops module (port 8843). Corrected.

- No K8s API proxy. All agent data through BFF endpoints only. Unchanged.

- No WebSockets. Frontend polls. Unchanged.

- BFF proxies to Kagenti backend → BFF creates Sandbox CR + Service via k8s API directly. No operator dependency.

- No observability / MLflow tracing for 3.5. Unchanged.

- Quick actions: stop (operatingMode: paused), start (operatingMode: running), restart, delete. Not replica scaling.

Removing strat-creator-human-sign-off label to trigger pipeline re-refinement with updated staff input.

RHAIRFE-2220.description:
Summary
Users need the ability to deploy agent images directly from the AI Hub Agents Deployments page, providing a seamless, integrated deployment experience for agents that mirrors the existing model deployment workflow. Today, deploying an agent requires users to manually create and manage deployments through OpenShift primitives, which is error-prone, requires deep platform expertise, and creates friction for data scientists and ML engineers who want to operationalize their agents.
Problem Statement
RHOAI users who have built or packaged agent images currently have no built-in way to deploy those agents from within the AI Hub interface. To run an agent, users must leave AI Hub entirely, work directly with OpenShift primitives (Deployments, Services, Routes, ConfigMaps), and manage the full lifecycle of their agent deployments manually. This creates several problems:
- Expertise barrier: Data scientists and ML engineers who can build agents may not have the OpenShift/Kubernetes expertise to deploy and manage them in production.

- Inconsistent experience: Model deployment is a first-class experience in AI Hub, but agent deployment is not — forcing users into a fragmented workflow despite agents and models having similar deployment needs.

- Operational overhead: Without platform-managed deployments, users must handle scaling, health monitoring, and teardown themselves, increasing the risk of misconfigured or orphaned resources.

Affected Customers
Named accounts requesting agent deployment capabilities:
- Turkish Airlines

- Verizon

- TMX Group

- Dell

- Citizens Bank

- Defense contractors (multiple)

These customers represent enterprise segments actively building agentic AI applications on RHOAI and are asking how to deploy agents within the platform.
Business Justification
- Customer demand: Multiple named enterprise accounts are asking how to deploy agents on RHOAI. The absence of a built-in deployment path is a friction point in active customer engagements.

- Competitive gap: Competing AI platforms provide integrated agent deployment experiences. Without this capability, RHOAI risks losing agentic AI workloads to platforms that offer a more complete agent lifecycle.

- Strategic imperative: Agent deployment is a foundational capability for the RHOAI agentic AI strategy. Agents cannot be operationalized at scale without platform-managed deployment, making this a must-have for the platform's agentic vision.

Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Users can deploy an agent image from the AI Hub >> Agents >> Deployments page

- [ ] The agent deployment experience follows established patterns from model deployment (familiar UX for users already deploying models)

- [ ] Users can view the status of their agent deployments (running, failed, pending)

- [ ] Users can stop or delete an agent deployment from the Deployments page

- [ ] Users can configure essential deployment parameters (e.g., replicas, resource limits, environment variables) when deploying an agent

Success Criteria
- Users can go from an agent image to a running, accessible agent deployment entirely within the AI Hub interface, without needing to use OpenShift primitives directly.

- The agent deployment workflow requires no more steps or expertise than the existing model deployment workflow.

KATA-4728.description:
Feature Overview{*}*
 
 Productize the upstream https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox project as "Red Hat Build of Agent Sandbox",  a new operator under the OpenShift Sandboxed Containers (OSC) product umbrella, available via OperatorHub on OpenShift. The operator provides a control plane for managing ephemeral, sandboxed execution environments on OpenShift.
Agent Sandbox is a separate operator with its own OLM bundle and CRDs, but it is part of the OSC product,  not a standalone product with its own SKU. There are still discussions to make it only available via the Red Hat OpenShift AI SKU only but this discussion is a business discussion.
Having multiple operators under one product umbrella follows the pattern established by products like OpenShift Data Foundation (multiple operators under one product umbrella) and OpenShift Virtualization (multiple operators under one product, with shared product identity).
The OSC product scope naturally extends to agent-sandbox: the product is called "OpenShift sandboxed containers", not "OpenShift Kata Containers", deliberately leaving room for sandbox technologies beyond kata.
Agent-sandbox manages sandbox lifecycle; OSC manages runtime installation. They are complementary capabilities under one product mission: providing secure, isolated execution environments on OpenShift.
Integration between the two operators is via an opt-in feature gate (agentSandbox=true in the osc-feature-gates ConfigMap) that auto-creates an OLM Subscription for agent-sandbox. However, agent-sandbox can also be installed independently from OperatorHub without OSC - it works with any OCI runtime (runc, kata, gvisor), and only kata/kata-remote require OSC to be present. This flexibility is important: sandboxing is a general-purpose platform capability that benefits use cases beyond confidential containers, including agentic AI code execution, oc debug, CI/CD sandboxes, and development environments. 
Agent Sandbox addresses a foundational infrastructure gap in the enterprise AI landscape: as AI transitions from passive chatbots to autonomous agents that execute code, manipulate filesystems, and orchestrate tool chains, enterprises need deterministic, infrastructure-level isolation for workloads that are inherently probabilistic. Standard Kubernetes containers provide insufficient isolation - default syscall profiles allow arbitrary execution, network policies lack domain-level granularity, and credential exposure enables lateral movement. Agent Sandbox closes this gap by managing the lifecycle of isolated  sandboxes backed by Kata Containers (lightweight VMs), providing VM-level isolation that contains even kernel-level exploits.
The sandbox CRDs (Sandbox, SandboxTemplate, SandboxClaim, SandboxWarmPool) are runtime-agnostic and contain no AI-specific fields. AI-specific integrations (Kagenti, MCP tool servers, ISV partnerships) layer  on top via RHOAI. This separation ensures the broadest possible adoption across OpenShift customers while positioning Red Hat to capture the agentic AI infrastructure market.
 
Two deployment modes are supported:
  - Peer pods on cloud (ARO, ROSA, OCP on cloud);: sandbox pods run as cloud VMs via kata-remote
  - Bare-metal with Kata: sandbox pods run in lightweight VMs via kata RuntimeClass
 
Goals (Expected Outcomes){*}*
1. Secure agentic code execution at the platform layer. OpenShift customers can run untrusted, AI-generated code in VM-isolated sandboxes without risk of host compromise, credential theft, or lateral movement — directly addressing the "Natural Language Malware" threat vector where malicious instructions embedded in agent workflows cannot be detected by traditional signature-based security tools.
2. Enable the MCP code execution pattern on OpenShift. Red Hat's MCP Development Requirements identify sandboxed code execution as an emerging critical pattern for MCP Servers. Agent Sandbox provides the recommended sandbox technology (Kata Containers) required by those requirements, and is the designated integration point for the upstream MCP Lifecycle Operator (kubernetes-sigs/mcp-lifecycle-operator) "Code Mode" capability. This positions OpenShift as the only enterprise Kubernetes distribution with a native, production-grade sandbox for MCP tool servers.
3. Unblock ISV and partner agentic AI integrations. Provide the sandboxing substrate that LangChain agents, Kagenti workflows, and ISV agentic platforms need to safely execute code on OpenShift — supporting the SandboxClient SDK pattern for programmatic sandbox creation, code execution, and file I/O from within agent frameworks.
4. Deliver warm pool pre-allocation for low-latency agent responsiveness. The SandboxWarmPool CRD pre-provisions sandbox environments so that agent code execution requests are served from a ready pool rather than waiting for cold-start VM creation — critical for interactive agentic workloads where latency directly impacts user experience.
5. Provide HTTP routing to sandboxes for agentic network access. The Sandbox Router enables HTTP traffic routing to sandbox pods via X-Sandbox-ID header and OpenShift Routes, allowing agents and external systems to interact with running sandboxes over the network — a prerequisite for web-based agent tools (browsers, Jupyter, VS Code, API servers).
6. Maintain upstream alignment and community leadership. Ship as a standalone operator that cleanly rebases on the upstream kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox project. Contribute fixes found during OpenShift testing (RBAC finalizer permissions, SandboxClaim controller panic, WarmPool status reporting) back upstream. Red Hat's participation in the upstream project and the related MCP Lifecycle Operator reinforces our position in the Kubernetes agentic infrastructure community.
7. Zero disruption to existing OpenShift Sandboxed Containers users. The OSC operator integration is via an opt-in feature gate (agentSandbox=true) that defaults to off. Existing OSC users experience no upgrade risk, no new dependencies, and no behavioral changes.
Requirements: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TPVZbyCOjQRnvStEeFtQYQCIs25eo7cySep2af5sVHU/edit?tab=t.0 
Target Release: OpenShift sandboxed containers 1.13 (alongside OCP 4.22), Tech Preview, June 30, 2026
Dependencies: upstream kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox v0.1.0+, OSC operator 1.11+, OpenShift 4.19+ (peer pods) / 4.17+ (bare-metal kata), Konflux tenant and release pipeline

Problem Statement
Sprint 40 design specs (RHOAIUX-2694, RHOAIUX-2695) were produced against a Kagenti operator / AgentRuntime CR / AgentCard backend model. Engineering has since pivoted agent deployments to OpenShell (sandboxed agent runtime with policy enforcement, gateway integration, and OpenShell-native lifecycle).
The existing specs are no longer aligned with the updated technical approach in RHAISTRAT-1758 and RHAISTRAT-1742, which specify a BFF-abstraction over the sandboxed runtime (OpenShell Go SDK path) rather than Kagenti CR orchestration. UX must revise both deliverables before Razzmatazz engineering proceeds on stale assumptions.
Objective
Revise the Agent Deployments list & detail and Deploy agent image wizard design specs to reflect the OpenShell-backed runtime model, producing updated annotated specs ready for engineering handoff.
Supersedes (delta revision, not greenfield):

- Revise list columns, status indicators, and health semantics for OpenShell deployment phases

- Update detail page tabs (Overview, Capabilities, Configuration) to reflect OpenShell-sourced metadata and BFF contract

- Reconcile capability discovery: A2A AgentCard at runtime vs OpenShell-native card discovery (per eng direction)

- Retain STRAT constraints: polling (no WebSockets), quick actions (start/stop/delete only), no K8s API from UI

2. Deploy agent image wizard (RHOAIUX-2535 / RHAISTRAT-1742)

RHAIRFE-2984.description:
Summary
When agents are deployed on RHOAI (RHAIRFE-2220), they land in ungoverned execution environments with no policy baseline, no credential isolation, and no workspace scoping. Administrators have no way to configure the security posture of agent execution environments before agents are deployed into them, and no way to enforce organizational policy across the agent fleet after deployment. This RFE delivers the administration and governance layer for agent execution environments: workspace management, security policy configuration, credential provider binding, and fleet-wide policy compliance visibility.
Problem Statement
RHAIRFE-2220 enables deploying agents from the console. RHAIRFE-2143 enables seeing running agents in the dashboard. Neither addresses what happens between "I want to deploy an agent" and "the agent is running securely":
- No workspace scoping: There is no way to partition agent execution environments by team, project, or tenant. All agents land in a flat namespace with no isolation boundary between teams.

- No security policy configuration: Administrators cannot define what an agent is allowed to reach (approved egress domains, blocked endpoints), what binaries it can execute, or what filesystem paths it can access. There is no global policy baseline per namespace. There is no way to see which agents violate organizational policy.

- No credential governance: Agents that need access to external services (GitHub, AWS, Slack, cloud KMS) require credentials. There is no way to configure credential providers (Vault, K8s Secrets, cloud IAM) at the workspace level and bind them to execution environments so agents never see raw secrets.

- No execution environment types: When a harness creates descendant execution environments for tool calls or sub-agent work, these are indistinguishable from the primary agent environment. Administrators cannot filter "show me my agents" vs "show me tool execution environments" vs "show me sub-agent sessions."

- No administration interface: All execution environment management requires CLI commands. Operations teams who manage agent fleets at scale cannot configure, monitor, or govern execution environments without platform expertise.

Without this governance layer, agent deployments (RHAIRFE-2220) are unsecured by default. The deployment wizard can place an agent into a running state, but cannot ensure that agent operates within organizational security boundaries.
Affected Customers
- NVIDIA IT (customer zero): deploying secure agent workspaces across GPU clusters. Operations team needs workspace-level policy baselines and credential provider configuration without CLI access.

- IBM Watson X Orchestrate: evaluating governed execution environments for multi-tenant agent platform. Per-tenant workspace isolation and policy enforcement are prerequisites for production.

- Wells Fargo: liked the sandbox + governance architecture at EBC. Explicit gap: global policy management across the agent fleet.

- Enterprise customers in discovery (Citi, AT&T, UiPath, KPMG): every engagement surfaces "how do we govern agents at scale?" after the initial deploy question is answered.

- Internal Red Hat teams (ACP, Ansible AO): need governed execution environments for agents without deep platform expertise.

- NTT Data (1,000+ agents), UBS ("ending up with 100 agents"), BBVA: fleet-scale governance cannot be CLI-only.

Business Justification
- Security gap in the agent lifecycle: RHAIRFE-2220 delivers agent deployment. Without governed execution environments, every deployed agent is an ungoverned workload with no policy, no credential isolation, and no compliance visibility. This is the gap between "we can deploy agents" and "we can deploy agents safely."

- Competitive parity: Azure AI Agent Service, AWS Bedrock Agents, and Google Vertex AI Agent Builder all provide governance controls for agent execution. E2B, Modal, and Daytona ship workspace-level policy and credential management dashboards. RHOAI has none.

- Productization prerequisite: Red Hat does not ship platform components without an administration surface. The governance layer is required for supportability and for enterprise customers whose operations teams must manage agent security policy without developer expertise.

- Connects existing investments: Agent deployment (RHAIRFE-2220) and agent visibility (RHAIRFE-2143) become significantly more valuable when agents land in governed environments. This RFE multiplies the value of both without duplicating their scope.

User Scenarios
- Platform administrator provisions a governed workspace: A platform admin creates a workspace for a development team, sets a global security policy baseline (approved egress domains, blocked internal IPs, allowed binaries), registers credential providers (Vault for API keys, AWS STS for cloud access), and assigns workspace administrators. When agents are deployed into this workspace (via RHAIRFE-2220), they inherit the policy baseline and credential bindings automatically.

- Workspace administrator configures per-agent policy overrides: A workspace admin sees the agents deployed in their workspace. One agent needs access to a domain not in the global allowlist. The admin creates a per-agent policy override within the bounds of the platform baseline, and the agent can reach the new domain without weakening the global policy for other agents.

- Operations team identifies policy violations across the fleet: An ops engineer views all agent execution environments across workspaces. Each environment shows its policy compliance status. Environments violating the global baseline are flagged. The engineer can drill into the policy diff and remediate.

- Harness creates descendant execution environments: A harness running inside one execution environment creates additional environments for tool calls and sub-agent work. The administrator can filter the fleet view to distinguish primary agents from tool execution environments and sub-agent sessions, and can see which primary agent spawned which descendants.

Acceptance Criteria
- Administrators can create workspaces that scope agent execution environments by team, project, or tenant

- Administrators can configure global security policy baselines per workspace (approved egress, blocked endpoints, allowed binaries, filesystem restrictions)

- Administrators can register credential providers at the workspace level and bind them to execution environments so deployed agents never handle raw secrets

- Per-agent policy overrides are configurable within the bounds of the workspace baseline

- Agent execution environments carry metadata identifying their type (primary agent, tool execution, sub-agent session) so administrators can filter and govern them distinctly

- Policy compliance is visible across the fleet: which environments comply with the workspace baseline and which violate it

- The administration experience is accessible through a browser interface integrated into the RHOAI console, not CLI-only

Success Criteria
- When an agent is deployed via RHAIRFE-2220, it inherits workspace policy and credential bindings by default, with no additional configuration steps

- Operations teams can identify and remediate policy violations across the agent fleet without CLI access

- Time to provision a governed workspace (policy + credentials + membership) is under 10 minutes through the interface

Scope
In Scope
- Workspace lifecycle management (create, membership, roles, delete)

- Security policy configuration (global baselines, per-workspace, per-agent overrides, compliance views)

- Credential provider management (register, bind to workspaces and execution environments)

- Execution environment type metadata (primary agent, tool execution, sub-agent session)

- Fleet-wide policy compliance visibility

- Browser-based administration interface integrated into RHOAI console

Out of Scope
- Agent deployment workflow (covered by RHAIRFE-2220)

- Agent runtime visibility and status (covered by RHAIRFE-2143)

- Agent discovery and registry browsing (covered by separate RFEs)

- Policy authoring IDE or OPA/Rego editor

- Gateway installation or upgrade

- Billing or chargeback per workspace

Discussed Topology
The administration interface for this RFE will be built upstream in the OpenShell project and consumed downstream in RHOAI. The upstream UI exposes workspace, sandbox, policy, and credential management through the OpenShell gRPC API in a platform-neutral, module-based architecture. Any platform (RHOAI, standalone, third-party) can deploy and consume it. Red Hat's downstream integration adds RHOAI console navigation, PatternFly theming, and composition with agent deployment (RHAIRFE-2220) and agent visibility (RHAIRFE-2143) via the module system. The upstream UI is being contributed to a neutral GitHub org to enable community adoption and maintenance.
Relationship to Agent Deployment (https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-2220#icft=RHAIRFE-2220
)
This RFE does not duplicate agent deployment; it makes it easier and safer. Today, deploying an agent (RHAIRFE-2220) requires the user to configure security policy, credential providers, and workspace scoping manually for every deployment. With governed execution environments in place, the deployment experience simplifies: an administrator sets up workspace policy baselines and credential provider bindings once, and every agent deployed into that workspace inherits the configuration automatically. The deploy wizard (https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-2220#icft=RHAIRFE-2220
) can offer pre-configured policy profiles as a dropdown rather than requiring the user to author policy from scratch. The result is fewer steps to deploy, fewer misconfiguration errors, and a default-secure posture for every agent in the workspace.

comments.author: Gage Krumbach

[Update - July 7] 3.6 plan clarified:

- Direct Sandbox CR creation (3.5 approach) is DROPPED in 3.6
- BFF switches to OpenShell Go SDK for all deploys
- Agents deployed via direct CR in 3.5 require redeploy through the SDK to gain OpenShell security layers (supervisor, network policy, credential injection) - cannot upgrade in place
- OpenShell Go SDK availability is a hard dependency for the 3.6 deploy path
- Agent-sandbox CRD remains the underlying workload CR - OpenShell enriches the spec before creation"

comments.author: Gage Krumbach
comments.body:
[Architecture clarification - July 7] Sandbox and OpenShell are independent features, not a migration path.

Sandbox (3.5): BFF creates Sandbox CR directly via k8s API. Bare pod, container-level isolation only.

Sandbox + OpenShell (3.6): BFF calls OpenShell Go SDK, Gateway creates enriched Sandbox CR with supervisor, network policy, credential injection, filesystem lockdown.

Key points:
- No migration required. Sandbox is not replaced by OpenShell — OpenShell is a layer on top.
- 3.5 agents deployed as bare Sandbox CRs keep running indefinitely. No forced redeploy.
- 3.6 adds a second deploy path through the Gateway. Likely a toggle in the deploy wizard ("Enable OpenShell security") gated on Gateway availability.
- Dashboard discovers both bare and enriched Sandbox CRs the same way — same label selector, same list, same lifecycle.
- Detail page can distinguish: enriched CRs have openshell.io/sandbox-id annotation + supervisor init container.
- Same CRD (agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1/Sandbox) for both. Same controller manages the pod lifecycle.

Previous comment about "dropping direct CR creation in 3.6" is superseded — direct CR remains as the base path, OpenShell SDK is the enhanced path."

Status Update (May 13, 2026):

A sync meeting was held today with the team to align on next steps for productizing the kagenti operator. Two key decisions were made:

1. Upstream-First Implementation — All significant changes to the AgentRuntime CRD controller and mTLS code will go upstream first, not midstream. This avoids the permanent patch maintenance burden of midstream-first divergence. Midstream remains the fallback if upstream proves too slow or resistant.

2. Product Naming — Keep "Kagenti" in midstream/upstream. Customer-facing product will use a technology-neutral name ("Agent Operator" or similar). Label/CRD API group cleanup deferred to the TP-to-GA transition.

What happens next:
The team will continue working on refinement docs and implementation planning in parallel, so that work can start immediately once upstream agreement is reached. The immediate priority is syncing with the Kagenti upstream maintainers (primarily IBM) to get a decision on where to implement the architectural changes.
