comments.author: Roland Huss
comments.body:
Acceptance Criteria Review (May 15, 2026)
Reviewed the STRAT acceptance criteria against the parent RFE (RHAIRFE-1351), the attached bot review, and ADR ODH-ADR-AgentOps-0002. Found several gaps and inconsistencies that need correction before this STRAT can move past Refinement.
Corrected Acceptance Criteria
The following replaces the current AC section. Changes are marked with the reason.
- MUST A customer can make their AI agent discoverable on the platform by creating an AgentRuntime CR that selects their existing Deployment _(clarified: discovery is through AgentRuntime CR selection via targetRef, not via label queries on Deployments)_

- MUST Other platform users and agents can find running agents and see what each agent can do (skills, protocols, endpoints) through the console or API _(unchanged)_

- MUST Agent metadata is verified and updated on workload rollouts without manual intervention _(clarified: "stays in sync" was ambiguous given the ADR's move from polling to event-driven verification. This AC now reflects the actual mechanism.)_

- MUST The agent operator is enabled via the Data Science Cluster CR (DSC), following the standard component controller pattern _(fixed: original said "installable via OperatorHub" which contradicts both the RFE and the strategy section's own DSC integration design. The RFE says "enabled via the Data Science Cluster.")_

- MUST Documentation covers the minimal image contract for creating a discoverable agent (endpoint format, health check, card structure) _(restored to MUST: the RFE has this as MUST. If TP should ship with reduced docs, amend the RFE, don't silently downgrade in the STRAT.)_

- MUST When the operator is disabled in DSC (managementState: Removed), all operator-managed resources are cleaned up _(new: standard operator lifecycle behavior, flagged as missing by bot review)_

- MUST When an agent Deployment is deleted, the operator garbage-collects associated resources (AgentRuntime status, generated NetworkPolicies, etc.) _(new: standard operator lifecycle behavior, flagged as missing by bot review)_

- SHOULD When an agent's A2A endpoint is unreachable or returns malformed metadata, the operator sets a degraded condition on the AgentRuntime CR with a descriptive message _(new: failure-mode behavior for diagnostics)_

- COULD Agents running in sandboxed environments are automatically registered on the platform _(unchanged)_

Items under team discussion (not changed here)
Two items are being discussed with the team and are not addressed in this comment:
- OTEL tracing AC: The RFE has a 5th MUST ("The agent operator enables Agents to send their traces to a trace sink to OTEL compatible sink") that is completely absent from the STRAT ACs. Discussing scope with team.

- AgentCard vs. label-based discovery: The STRAT strategy section still references AgentCard CRD creation, but ADR-0002 deprecates AgentCard entirely in favor of AgentRuntime-based discovery + live A2A fetch. The strategy section needs updating once the team aligns on the ADR.

Other observations
- No human sign-off: This STRAT was auto-generated and auto-reviewed by the bot (score 6/8). It needs a human sign-off before implementation starts. Missing strat-creator-human-sign-off label.

- No fixVersion: If this is committed for 3.5 (not just a candidate), fixVersion should be set by engineering.

- No engineering epic linked: The action items doc references RHOAIENG-3601 but that issue is unrelated (dashboard unit test). An engineering epic for the operator implementation work needs to be created and linked.

- Konflux deadline: The strategy mentions May 22 as the Konflux onboarding deadline. That's next week. Current status was "Not started" as of April 25.

cc Dimitri Saridakis, Varsha Prasad Narsing

Reach: 8 (Large group, 30-70% of users)
Five named enterprise customers (BBVA, T-Mobile, AXA, NTT Data with 1,000 agents, Phoenix Technologies) have documented specific needs for agent lifecycle management on OpenShift AI. This is foundational infrastructure — every customer deploying AI agents on the platform benefits. Calibrated against sibling agent features: RHAISTRAT-1742 (Deploy agent images, R=8), RHAISTRAT-1758 (Agent Deployments View, R=8), RHAISTRAT-1436 (Agent Registry, R=8). As the operator that enables all of these, it shares the same user population. Not R=13 because as a Tech Preview, actual near-term users are early adopters in the agent space, not the full RHOAI user base.
Impact: 8 (High — major pain point solved)
Transforms agent onboarding from "reinvent from scratch per agent" to "one CR, platform handles discovery and observability." NTT Data's 1,000-agent scale makes manual onboarding untenable. Without this operator, there is no agent platform story on RHOAI — it unblocks RHAISTRAT-1697 (Agent Hub UI) and the broader agent ecosystem. Per-user impact is high: changes how teams deploy and manage agent workloads. Not I=13 because this is a Tech Preview enabler, not a hard compliance/legal mandate.
Confidence: 75% (Some evidence, still assumptions)
Strong customer evidence: 5 named customers with specific asks, approved RFE (RHAIRFE-1351, status Approved, priority Critical), human-sign-off label. Strategy review scored 6/8 — passed but feasibility reviewer recommended REVISE, flagging: CRD schema undefined, upstream kagenti operator unvalidated at review time, sizing likely XL not L. The "confidence-yellow" label confirms residual uncertainty. Per rubric: approved RFE with named customer demand supports 75%; strategy review at 6/8 supports 75%; feasibility concerns and unresolved dependencies prevent 100%.
Effort: 8 (Massive effort — matches existing Jira value)
Retaining the existing E=8 set in Jira, which aligns with evidence. The feasibility review flagged L (6-9 sprints) as optimistic and likely XL. Multiple teams involved (AgentOps, AI Core Platform). Dependencies: upstream kagenti operator, CRD schema finalization, A2A SDK image contract, DSC integration, dashboard UI, Konflux onboarding (now complete per June 2 status). June 2 comment confirms "current scope is too large for the EA2 window." Cross-team coordination across ODH, RHOAI, agent operator, and dashboard. New CRD design, new operator, and new dashboard views. Comparable to RHAISTRAT-1267 (Perses Dashboard Patterns, E=5) but with more teams and unresolved upstream dependencies, justifying the higher E=8.
Calibration Context
RICE = (8 × 8 × 0.75) / 8 = 6.0. This positions it in the lower-mid range alongside RHAISTRAT-1555 (MLFlow Prompt Template, RICE=6.0) and RHAISTRAT-1535 (YAML Editor GA, RICE=6.25). The high effort (E=8) significantly depresses the score despite strong reach and impact — this is the RICE formula working as intended to flag high-effort items. For comparison, sibling agent features with E=3-5 score 9.6-16.0.
Re-scoring Triggers
- If scope is split (June 2 comment discusses this), Effort could drop to 5, pushing RICE to 9.6

- If upstream kagenti operator proves mature and functional, Confidence could rise to 100% (RICE=8.0)

- If scope is formally reduced to operator-only (no dashboard views), Effort could drop to 5

- If the feature is promoted from TP to GA scope, both Reach and Effort would change

RHAISTRAT-1599.description:
Summary
Enterprise customers building AI agents on OpenShift AI need a way to register their agent workloads with the platform so that agents become discoverable, observable, and manageable without manual per-agent configuration. Today, each team reinvents onboarding from scratch.
Problem Statement
AI agents are different from regular web applications. They expose machine-readable capability descriptions, connect to tools dynamically, act autonomously, and communicate with other agents. A vanilla Deployment can run the container, but it cannot express that the container is an agent, what it can do, or how to find it.
Customers deploying agents today must manually wire observability, write custom discovery logic, and build their own onboarding workflows for every agent. This per-agent overhead blocks teams from scaling beyond a handful of agents.
What Makes an Agent Workload Different
An AI agent workload is a container image that:
- Exposes a machine-readable capability description at a well-known endpoint, declaring its name, skills, and supported protocols

- Connects to external tools dynamically (e.g., via MCP) rather than through hardcoded API endpoints

- Acts autonomously, making inference calls and communicating with other agents without a human in the request loop

Agents range from self-contained (tools and model config baked into the image) to platform-assembled (receiving tools and configuration at deploy time).
Affected Customers
- BBVA: Building their own agent platform, described the need as "CR-based agent lifecycle management with sidecar injection for identity, observability, tracing." Maps to their Q2 roadmap.

- T-Mobile: Agent prototypes as Python containers. Explicit gaps: no MCP server lifecycle tracking, no production readiness infrastructure.

- AXA: Formal RFI for "Agentic Platform" covering agent lifecycle management, versioning, registry, and monitoring.

- NTT Data (1,000 agents): "The full agent architecture matters now: control plane, governance, orchestration."

- Phoenix Technologies: Evaluating platforms for native agent deployment and lifecycle management with a portable specification.

User Journey
- Customer builds their agent image using any framework. The image exposes a capability description at a well-known endpoint.

- Customer deploys as a standard Deployment with one label to mark it as an agent.

- Customer creates one custom resource to onboard the agent to the platform.

- The platform automatically registers the agent, makes it discoverable, and wires observability.

- The agent is visible in the console, findable by other agents, and producing telemetry.

- Total effort beyond a vanilla Deployment: one label, one custom resource.

Acceptance Criteria
- MUST A customer can make their AI agent discoverable on the platform by creating an AgentRuntime CR that selects their existing Deployment (discovery is through AgentRuntime CR selection via targetRef, not via label queries on Deployments)

- MUST Other platform users and agents can find running agents and see what each agent can do (skills, protocols, endpoints) through the console or API

- MUST Agent metadata is verified and updated on workload rollouts without manual intervention

- MUST The agent operator is enabled via the Data Science Cluster CR (DSC), following the standard component controller pattern

- MUST Documentation covers the minimal image contract for creating a discoverable agent (endpoint format, health check, card structure)

- MUST When the operator is disabled in DSC (managementState: Removed), all operator-managed resources are cleaned up

- MUST When an agent Deployment is deleted, the operator garbage-collects associated resources (AgentRuntime status, generated NetworkPolicies, etc.)

- SHOULD When an agent's A2A endpoint is unreachable or returns malformed metadata, the operator sets a degraded condition on the AgentRuntime CR with a descriptive message

- COULD Agents running in sandboxed environments are automatically registered on the platform

Open: The parent RFE (RHAIRFE-1351) has a MUST for OTEL trace sink integration that is not yet reflected here. Under team discussion.
Success Criteria
- At least 3 early-access customers successfully register and discover agents through the operator during Tech Preview

- Time to make an agent discoverable drops from hours (manual wiring) to minutes (label  one CR)

Scope
In Scope
- Agent registration and discovery (operator watches labeled workloads)

- Agent metadata synchronization (capability descriptions kept current)

- Observability wiring (telemetry auto-configuration)

- Console visibility (agents visible in OpenShift AI UI)

- Operator productization (OLM, certification, downstream builds)

Out of Scope (covered by RHAIRFE-408)
- Agent identity and authentication

- Trust enforcement and network policy based on agent verification

- Agent-to-agent authorization and delegation chains

- Per-tool access control

- AgentCard signing and attestation

Open Questions
- What is the minimal image contract for Tech Preview? Do we require the A2A protocol format, or accept a simpler metadata format?

- How does the onboarding custom resource interact with OpenShell's Sandbox CR when both are present?

Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)
TL;DR
Onboard the kagenti-operator into RHOAI as a standard DSC-managed component at Tech Preview maturity. This covers Konflux build pipeline integration (operator + AuthBridge sidecar images), a new component controller in rhods-operator following the established 16-component pattern, OLM/CSV packaging with RELATED_IMAGE entries, and dashboard BFF plugin registration with a feature flag for agent views. The operator's runtime capabilities (agent registration, discovery, sidecar injection) already exist upstream and are not part of this strategy.
Components: kagenti-operator, AuthBridge (kagenti-extensions), rhods-operator, odh-dashboard
Technical Approach
This strategy productizes an existing upstream operator rather than building new functionality. The kagenti-operator provides three controllers (AgentRuntimeReconciler, MLflowReconciler, ClientRegistrationController), a mutating admission webhook for AuthBridge sidecar injection, and the AgentRuntime CRD (agent.kagenti.dev/v1alpha1). AgentRuntime is the single CRD for agent workload management; there is no separate AgentCard CRD. Agent metadata is fetched by the AgentRuntimeReconciler from the workload's /.well-known/agent-card.json endpoint via mTLS and stored inline in AgentRuntime.Status.Card. The work here is build pipeline onboarding, platform integration, and packaging.
Konflux Build Pipeline
Two image families need Konflux onboarding:
- kagenti-operator image: Go binary built from opendatahub-io/kagenti-operator (midstream fork of kagenti/kagenti-operator). Requires FIPS-compliant compilation (CGO_ENABLED=1, GOEXPERIMENT=strictfipsruntime) on UBI9 base, consistent with all other RHOAI Go operators. The Dockerfile must follow the multi-stage pattern used by rhods-operator, model-registry-operator, and others: builder stage compiles with FIPS flags, production stage copies the binary to ubi9/ubi-minimal.

- AuthBridge sidecar images: Go binary built from opendatahub-io/kagenti-extensions (midstream fork of kagenti/kagenti-extensions). Three image variants exist upstream: authbridge-proxy (full proxy), authbridge-envoy (Envoy ext_proc mode), and authbridge-lite (auth-only). For TP, the minimum viable set is authbridge-proxy (default mode). Each variant needs its own Konflux component with FIPS-compliant Go compilation.

All images must include rpms.lock.yaml for RPM lockfile pinning and go.sum for Go dependency locking. SHA256-pinned image references go into the CSV as RELATED_IMAGE_* environment variables for disconnected/air-gapped installation support.
DSC Component Controller Integration
Register kagenti-operator as a new component in the rhods-operator component registry (internal/controller/components/). This follows the established pattern with 16 existing precedents:
- Component CRD: Define a new KagentiOperator kind in the components.platform.opendatahub.io/v1alpha1 group, following the same pattern as ModelRegistry, Trainer, FeastOperator, and other component CRDs. This CRD manages the lifecycle of the kagenti-operator deployment within RHOAI.

- Component controller: Implement the standard action pipeline: initialize, releases, kustomize render, deploy, check deployments, garbage collect. The controller registers in internal/controller/components/registry/ and the DSC controller iterates the registry to manage it.

- ManagementState lifecycle: Support Managed (deploy operator + CRDs + RBAC + webhook) and Removed (clean up all operator-managed resources including the controller Deployment, RBAC resources, CRDs, and namespace-scoped resources). Default to Removed for TP (opt-in).

- Kustomize manifests: Pull upstream manifests from the midstream fork via get_all_manifests.sh at pinned commits. Store in prefetched-manifests/kagenti-operator/. Apply RHOAI-specific overlays for namespace, image references, and RBAC adjustments.

- Namespace: Deploy the kagenti-operator into redhat-ods-applications, consistent with all other platform component operators. The operator itself watches all namespaces for AgentRuntime CRs, deploying agent workloads into user-defined namespaces.

OLM/CSV Packaging
Add kagenti-operator images to the ClusterServiceVersion:
- RELATED_IMAGE_KAGENTI_OPERATOR: kagenti-operator image (SHA256 pinned)

- RELATED_IMAGE_AUTHBRIDGE_PROXY: AuthBridge proxy sidecar image (SHA256 pinned)

- Additional AuthBridge variants as needed for future modes

The CSV must declare the new KagentiOperator CRD and include RBAC for the component controller to manage kagenti-operator resources.
Dashboard BFF Plugin Registration
Register a kagenti dashboard plugin using the odh-dashboard Module Federation architecture. This involves:
- Feature flag: Add a disableKagenti flag (or equivalent) to the OdhDashboardConfig CR, gated by the DSC component state. When the kagenti-operator component is Removed in DSC, the dashboard hides all agent-related UI elements.

- BFF plugin: A new Go BFF container following the pattern of gen-ai-ui, maas-ui, and other federated modules. The BFF proxies requests to the Kubernetes API for AgentRuntime CR management. It runs as a sidecar container in the dashboard pod on a dedicated port (next available in the 8043-8743 range).

- TP scope: For Tech Preview, the dashboard integration provides basic agent visibility (list AgentRuntime CRs, show status, link to workload details). Full agent management UI is out of scope for this strategy.

High Level Requirements
- [P0] Operator images built via Konflux with FIPS-compliant Go compilation (GOEXPERIMENT=strictfipsruntime, CGO_ENABLED=1) on UBI9 base (RFE acceptance criterion)

- [P0] Operator enabled/disabled via DataScienceCluster CR following the standard component controller pattern with managementState: Managed/Removed (RFE acceptance criterion)

- [P0] When disabled (managementState: Removed), all operator-managed resources are cleaned up: controller Deployment, RBAC, CRDs, namespace-scoped resources (RFE acceptance criterion)

- [P0] Upstream-first policy: significant changes go to kagenti/* repos before being pulled into opendatahub-io/* midstream forks (RFE acceptance criterion)

- [P0] Tech Preview maturity level with explicit opt-in (disabled by default in DSC) (RFE acceptance criterion)

- [P1] Dashboard integration infrastructure: BFF plugin registration and feature flag for agent views (RFE acceptance criterion)

- [P1] OLM/CSV packaging with RELATED_IMAGE_* entries for disconnected installation

- [P1] AuthBridge proxy sidecar image built via Konflux with FIPS compliance

- [P2] Multi-arch builds (AMD64 required for TP; arm64 if pipeline supports it without additional effort)

Dependencies
Dependency

Cannot productize without a working upstream operator. If upstream is incomplete, the team must finish it first, increasing effort.

Well-established pattern; low risk.

Non-Functional Requirements
- FIPS compliance: All Go binaries must be compiled with GOEXPERIMENT=strictfipsruntime and CGO_ENABLED=1, matching the platform-wide FIPS posture. AuthBridge sidecar proxy handles TLS termination and must use FIPS-approved cipher suites (architecture context: rhods-operator.md, kube-rbac-proxy FIPS cipher suite list).

- Container security: Non-root execution (USER 65532:65532 for Go operators, following distroless convention), capability dropping (capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]), seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault (architecture context: PLATFORM.md container security patterns).

- Disconnected installation: All images referenced via RELATED_IMAGE_* environment variables with SHA256-pinned digests in the CSV. This enables OLM relatedImages for air-gapped operation with image mirroring (architecture context: PLATFORM.md).

- Backwards compatibility: As a new TP component, no backwards compatibility concerns. The component defaults to Removed (disabled), so existing clusters are unaffected by the RHOAI upgrade.

- Resource cleanup on disable: When managementState transitions to Removed, the component controller must delete: the kagenti-operator Deployment, all associated RBAC (ClusterRoles, ClusterRoleBindings, Roles, RoleBindings), the AgentRuntime CRD, the mutating webhook configuration, and any namespace-scoped resources (ConfigMaps, Secrets) in redhat-ods-applications. This follows the garbage collection pattern used by all existing component controllers (architecture context: rhods-operator.md component action pipeline).

Out-of-Scope
- Agent registration, discovery, and lifecycle management runtime behavior (tracked in RHAIRFE-2387). This strategy productizes the operator; RHAIRFE-2387 covers its runtime features.

- Agent metadata extraction and sync (RHAIRFE-2388).

- Agent Runtime Contract / ARC specification and injection (RHAIRFE-2389).

- Agent identity and authorization, including SPIFFE binding, agent attestation, and trust enforcement (RHAIRFE-408, explicitly separated per April 25 RFE revision).

- Full agent management UI in the dashboard. TP scope is read-only agent list with status display.

- Kagenti backend (FastAPI) and full React UI deployment. These are part of the kagenti Helm chart and may be addressed separately.

- Observability stack for agent workloads (PodMonitor/ServiceMonitor, agent-specific dashboards). The operator itself will be monitored via the standard platform monitoring pattern, but agent workload metrics depend on the ARC (RHAIRFE-2389).

- Keycloak deployment or OAuth2 client registration infrastructure. These are prerequisites managed outside this strategy.

Acceptance Criteria (Proposed -- requires PM/Engineering validation)
- Given a fresh RHOAI deployment with DSC configured with kagenti-operator managementState: Managed,

   when the DSC controller reconciles,    then the kagenti-operator Deployment is created in redhat-ods-applications with the Konflux-built image,    measured by kubectl get deployment -n redhat-ods-applications -l app=kagenti-operator returning a Ready deployment.
- Given the kagenti-operator component is Managed in DSC,

   when a user creates an AgentRuntime CR in their namespace referencing an existing Deployment,    then the operator's AgentRuntimeReconciler applies the kagenti.io/type: agent label to the target workload,    measured by kubectl get deployment <name> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels.kagenti\.io/type}' returning agent.
- Given the kagenti-operator component is changed from Managed to Removed in DSC,

   when the component controller reconciles the state change,    then all operator-managed resources (Deployment, RBAC, CRDs, webhook configuration) are deleted from the cluster,    measured by kubectl get deployment -n redhat-ods-applications -l app=kagenti-operator returning no results, and kubectl get crd agentrimes.agent.kagenti.dev returning "not found".
- The kagenti-operator container image passes Konflux build pipeline check-payload validation for FIPS compliance (binary linked against OpenSSL, no statically-linked Go crypto).

- The AuthBridge proxy sidecar container image passes Konflux build pipeline check-payload validation for FIPS compliance.

- Given the odh-dashboard is deployed with the kagenti BFF plugin enabled (feature flag active),

   when a user navigates to the agent views section,    then the dashboard displays a list of AgentRuntime CRs from the user's accessible namespaces,    measured by the dashboard rendering AgentRuntime data retrieved via the BFF API proxy.
- Given a disconnected RHOAI installation using image mirroring,

   when the kagenti-operator component is Managed,    then the operator and AuthBridge images are resolved from the mirrored registry via RELATED_IMAGE_* environment variables,    measured by the kagenti-operator Deployment running with images from the mirror registry.
Effort Estimate
L (6-9 sprints) - justified but at the higher end of L:
- Konflux onboarding (2-3 sprints): Two image families (operator + AuthBridge), each requiring Dockerfile conversion, FIPS build flag integration, RPM lockfile setup, and pipeline validation. This is procedural but has lead time.

- rhods-operator component controller (2-3 sprints): Well-precedented pattern (16 existing controllers), but includes CRD definition, kustomize manifest integration, garbage collection logic, and DSC schema extension. Testing the Managed/Removed lifecycle thoroughly adds time.

- OLM/CSV packaging (1 sprint): Adding RELATED_IMAGE entries, CRD declarations, and RBAC to the CSV. Straightforward with existing tooling.

- Dashboard BFF plugin (1-2 sprints): Module Federation is well-established (7 existing plugins), but a new BFF for AgentRuntime requires Go backend implementation and basic React UI for the agent list view.

- QE and documentation (1 sprint): Test plan, E2E tests for component lifecycle, disconnected validation, installation docs.

The L estimate assumes the upstream kagenti-operator is functional and the midstream fork is ready. If upstream gaps exist that require operator development work, the estimate shifts to XL. The CRD schema (AgentRuntime) is already defined upstream per overlay 0014, which removes a previously-flagged sizing risk. The removal of the AgentCard CRD simplifies the operator surface area (three controllers instead of six in earlier iterations), which supports the L estimate.
Risks
Risk
Impact
Mitigation
Konflux onboarding misses code-complete deadline
Operator images not available for 3.5 release, blocking the entire strategy
Submit Konflux onboarding request immediately. Track as P0 with weekly status checks against the deadline. If submission is delayed past 2 weeks before deadline, escalate to platform lead for expedited processing.
Upstream kagenti-operator has functional gaps
Additional development work needed, pushing effort to XL and potentially missing 3.5 timeline
Validate the upstream operator against the three controllers listed in overlay 0014 within the first sprint. Create a gap analysis document. If gaps exceed 2 sprints of work, negotiate scope reduction for TP (e.g., defer MLflowReconciler, defer ClientRegistrationController).
AuthBridge sidecar injection conflicts with platform webhook ordering
Pod creation failures or unexpected sidecar behavior when combined with other mutating webhooks (HardwareProfile, connection injection)
Test webhook ordering explicitly in E2E suite. The kagenti webhook uses reinvocationPolicy: IfNeeded, which handles ordering conflicts. If conflicts arise, set explicit webhookOrder annotations.
DSC component cleanup leaves orphaned resources
AgentRuntime CRs or webhook configurations persist after component is disabled
Implement explicit finalizer on the component CR that enumerates and deletes all owned resources. Test cleanup in E2E suite with resources in multiple namespaces.
Dashboard BFF plugin port collision
New BFF sidecar port conflicts with existing Module Federation ports
Allocate the next available port in the 8043-8743 range. Verify against current assignments (8043-model-registry, 8143-gen-ai, 8243-maas, 8343-mlflow, 8443-eval-hub, 8543-automl, 8643-autorag).

Assumptions
- A functional upstream kagenti-operator exists in the kagenti GitHub org with the AgentRuntime CRD and core controllers -- needs validation (critical, must validate in sprint 1)

- The midstream fork opendatahub-io/kagenti-operator is set up and synced with upstream -- needs validation

- The AgentRuntime CRD schema (agent.kagenti.dev/v1alpha1) is stable enough for TP -- needs validation (CRD field changes after productization require migration)

- The Konflux build pipeline supports Go 1.25 with GOEXPERIMENT=strictfipsruntime (same version used by rhods-operator) -- confirmed (architecture context: rhods-operator uses Go 1.25)

- The kagenti-operator can run in redhat-ods-applications namespace alongside other platform operators without RBAC conflicts -- needs validation

- AuthBridge proxy sidecar images can be built with UBI9 base following the same pattern as other Go sidecars -- confirmed (standard pattern)

Open Questions
Question
Why It Matters
Owner
Is the upstream kagenti-operator functional with all three controllers listed in overlay 0014?
If the operator is incomplete, effort estimate changes from L to XL. Validate against: AgentRuntimeReconciler (including metadata fetch from /.well-known/agent-card.json), MLflowReconciler, ClientRegistrationController.
Kagenti team
Which AuthBridge sidecar variants are needed for TP?
authbridge-proxy is the default. Are authbridge-envoy and authbridge-lite needed for 3.5, or can they ship in a later release? Each variant requires a separate Konflux component.
Kagenti team / PM

RHAISTRAT-1762.description:
Summary
Platform engineers and security teams need a governed registry that serves as the operational source of truth for MCP servers that have been operationalized — either deployed to the cluster (Red Hat or customer-created MCPs) or registered as remote endpoints (e.g., GitHub-hosted MCPs). The registry must track version, provenance, ownership, deployment or registration state, namespace/workspace scope, lifecycle status, and policy associations for every operationalized MCP — providing the governance layer that enables auditability, compliance, and lifecycle management across the organization. Governance begins at the point of deployment or registration; all MCP servers in use must be recorded in the registry regardless of how they entered the environment.
Problem Statement
MCP servers enter production through two distinct paths — cluster deployment (Red Hat-provided MCPs like the OCP MCP, or customer-created MCPs deployed to the cluster) and remote registration (MCPs hosted externally, such as on GitHub, that are registered as remote endpoints). In both cases, there is no centralized governance surface that tracks their operational state once they are in use. Platform engineers cannot answer basic governance questions: Which MCP servers are actively deployed or registered? Who owns them? What version is running? What namespace are they scoped to? What policies apply? When was the last lifecycle change, and who made it?
Without an operational registry, governance of in-use MCP assets relies on ad-hoc tracking — spreadsheets, tribal knowledge, or manual inspection of cluster state. This creates compliance gaps, makes auditing difficult, and prevents platform teams from managing MCP lifecycle (deprecation, retirement, version transitions) across the organization. The problem is compounded by the two entry paths: cluster-deployed MCPs may be visible in cluster tooling but lack governance metadata, while remote-registered MCPs may not appear in cluster state at all.
Affected Customers
- Enterprise platform teams managing MCP deployments across multiple namespaces, teams, and environments who need operational visibility and lifecycle governance

- Security and compliance teams who must audit which MCP servers are in production, trace their provenance, and verify policy compliance

- AI engineering teams who need to understand which MCP servers are available within their namespace scope, what versions are deployed, and what lifecycle state they are in

- Red Hat OpenShift AI customers with multi-team, multi-namespace environments where ungoverned MCP proliferation creates operational and security risk

Business Justification
MCP server adoption is accelerating, and enterprise customers require the same governance posture for MCP assets that they expect for model assets. The established RHOAI pattern — Catalog for discovery, Registry for governance — must extend to MCPs to maintain product consistency and meet enterprise compliance expectations. Without registry governance, MCP servers become shadow IT: deployed, modified, and retired without organizational oversight. This is the core governance component of the RHOAI MCP story and is required for the RHOAI 3.5 Tech Preview MCP Registry milestone.
User Scenarios
- Cluster MCP deployment: A platform engineer deploys a Red Hat-provided MCP (e.g., the OCP MCP) or a customer-created MCP server to a team namespace. Upon deployment, the registry records the server's version, provenance, the namespace it's scoped to, who deployed it, and its initial lifecycle state (active). The platform engineer can now see this server alongside all other operationalized MCPs in the organization.

- Remote MCP registration: An AI engineer wants to use a remote MCP server hosted on GitHub. They register the remote endpoint in the registry, which records the server's URL, version, owner, and namespace scope. Governance begins at registration — the remote MCP is now tracked, auditable, and subject to lifecycle management even though it runs outside the cluster.

- Direct deployment with registration: A platform engineer deploys an MCP server directly from a private source (not through the Catalog). They must still register it with the MCP registry, which captures the same governance metadata. The registry is the single governance surface regardless of how the MCP entered the environment.

- Lifecycle management: An MCP server has a known vulnerability in an older version. A platform admin marks the affected version as "deprecated" in the registry, with a note directing teams to upgrade. Teams running the deprecated version see a clear lifecycle signal. After a transition period, the admin moves the version to "retired," and downstream enforcement (Gateway) can block new connections.

- Audit and compliance: A compliance officer needs to produce a report of all MCP servers currently active in production — both cluster-deployed and remote-registered — who operationalized each one, what version is running, and when the last lifecycle change occurred. The registry's audit trail provides this without manual investigation.

- Scoped visibility: A business-unit admin configures the registry so that their department's engineers see only the MCP servers that have been deployed or registered for their namespace. Other teams' operationalized MCPs are not visible, maintaining RBAC-controlled boundaries.

Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] When a cluster MCP server is deployed (Red Hat or customer-created), or a remote MCP server is registered, it appears in the registry with recorded metadata: version, provenance, owner, namespace/workspace scope, deployment/registration type, and initial lifecycle state

- [ ] Platform admins can transition an operationalized MCP server's lifecycle state (active → deprecated → disabled → retired) with ability to audit via access logs

- [ ] Users see only the operationalized MCP servers they are entitled to based on RBAC and namespace/workspace scoping; unauthorized servers never appear in their registry views

- [ ] Every lifecycle state change, ownership update, and scope modification is logged in an audit trail with user, action, timestamp, and comment

- [ ] The registry supports search and filter by name, version, lifecycle state, namespace/workspace, and owner; response times < 1 second for 1,000+ entries

- [ ] Downstream consumers (Gateway, dashboard) can query the registry to determine whether an MCP server is active and authorized; lookups complete in < 200 ms p95 for 10,000 entries

- [ ] The registry can record MCP servers that are operationalized but not broadly discoverable in the catalog (team-specific, private, or namespace-scoped usage), including MCPs deployed directly without going through the Catalog path

- [ ] The registry distinguishes between cluster-deployed MCPs and remote-registered MCPs, recording the appropriate metadata for each type (e.g., cluster namespace and image for deployed; endpoint URL for remote)

Success Criteria
- Platform engineers can answer "which MCP servers are active in my organization, who owns them, and what version is running" from a single governed interface

- Compliance teams can produce audit reports of MCP lifecycle changes without manual investigation

- The MCP governance flow (Catalog → Register/Deploy → Registry → Gateway enforcement) mirrors the established model governance pattern in RHOAI

Scope
In Scope
- Registry as the operational source of truth for MCP servers that have been deployed to the cluster or registered as remote endpoints

- Two governance entry paths: deployment (cluster MCPs) and registration (remote MCPs), both resulting in full registry governance

- Registration requirement for directly-deployed MCPs that bypass the Catalog path

- Lifecycle state management for operationalized assets (active, deprecated, disabled, retired)

- RBAC-controlled visibility scoped to namespaces/workspaces

- Audit trail for all lifecycle and ownership changes

- Query interface for downstream consumers (Gateway, dashboard)

Out of Scope
- MCP ingestion, curation, scanning, signing, or approval workflows — these are Catalog-side concerns and should be addressed in a separate RFE

- Draft/quarantined/certified status transitions — these belong in the Catalog's approval flow, not the Registry's operational lifecycle

- MCP server authoring, editing, or development tooling

- Gateway deployment or policy enforcement logic — the Registry informs the Gateway but does not replace it

- Catalog discoverability experience — the Registry is not the browsing/discovery interface

Resolved Design Questions
These questions were raised during drafting and have been resolved:
- Handoff mechanism: Two paths — deployment triggers governance for cluster MCPs (Red Hat-provided or customer-created), and explicit registration triggers governance for remote MCPs (e.g., GitHub-hosted).

- When governance begins: At the point of deployment (cluster MCPs) or registration (remote MCPs). No pre-registration phase.

- MCPs bypassing the Catalog: Must still be registered with the MCP registry. The registry governs all operationalized MCPs regardless of entry path.

Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)
Note: The full strategy exceeds Jira's description size limit and is stored as an attachment: RHAISTRAT-1762-strategy.md. The TL;DR is shown below for quick reference.

TL;DR
Implement the MCP Registry as a new API domain inside the existing MLflow backend, using the community-agreed data model and REST API (/ajax-api/3.0/mlflow/mcp-servers). The data model comprises six tables -- mcp_servers (server identity and metadata), mcp_server_versions (immutable versioned payloads with lifecycle state), mcp_server_tags and mcp_server_version_tags (extensible key-value metadata), mcp_server_aliases (named version pointers like "production"), and mcp_access_bindings (approved direct endpoint URLs for remote/gateway access). MLflow's workspace isolation, database-agnostic ORM storage, and Kubernetes service account authentication provide governance scoping. Lifecycle states use MLflow's native states (draft, active, deprecated, deleted) at the version level. Audit trail is provided by MLflow access logs. The odh-dashboard provides the UI surface. No new CRDs, no new Kubernetes controllers, no new container images. This is a Tech Preview for RHOAI 3.5.
Components: mlflow (MCP Registry API, implemented by AI Hub team), odh-dashboard (MCP Registry UI), MCP Gateway (forward-looking downstream consumer, no v1 work)

RHOAIENG-73639.description:
Remove all Deployment/StatefulSet/Job code paths from agent-ops BFF. Agents are exclusively deployed, discovered, and managed as Sandbox CRs (agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1/sandboxes). If the agent-sandbox CRD is not installed on the cluster, deploy returns an error.
Why
Per July 7 alignment with PM: our product deploys sandboxed agents only. We do not discover or manage agents deployed outside our UI. Sandbox CR is the foundation for OpenShell security in 3.6.
Scope — every file that needs to change
deploy.go (BFF deploy path)
Current state: DeployAgent calls isSandboxCRDAvailable() — if true, calls deploySandbox(); if false, calls deployFallback() which creates Deployment + Service.
Change:
- Remove deployFallback() entirely (~80 lines)

- Remove isSandboxCRDAvailable() auto-detect logic — instead, check CRD availability and return error if absent: "agent-sandbox CRD (agents.x-k8s.io) is not installed — cannot deploy agents"

- Remove UseSandbox field from DeployAgentParams — it's always sandbox now

- DeployAgent only calls deploySandbox(): ServiceAccount -> Sandbox CR -> Route (optional)

- DeleteAgent: remove the Deployment+Service fallback branch. Only delete Sandbox CR + SA + Route.

- StopAgent: remove Deployment replica scaling fallback. Only patch spec.operatingMode: paused.

- StartAgent: remove Deployment replica scaling fallback. Only patch spec.operatingMode: running.

client.go (discovery/list/detail)
Current state: listAgentSummaries scans Sandbox CRs, Deployments, StatefulSets, and Jobs by label selector. getAgentDetail tries Sandbox CR, then Deployment, then StatefulSet, then Job.
Change:
- listAgentSummaries: remove Deployment, StatefulSet, Job listing. Only list Sandbox CRs via dynamic client.

- getAgentDetail: remove Deployment, StatefulSet, Job fallback lookups. Only get Sandbox CR.

- Remove workloadLookupError multi-kind logic — single resource type now.

- Remove unused mapper functions: deploymentToSummary, deploymentToDetail, statefulSetToSummary, statefulSetToDetail, jobToSummary, jobToDetail (in mapper.go).

manifests.go (resource builders)
Current state: has buildDeployment, buildService, buildSandboxCR, buildRoute, buildServiceAccount.
Change:
- Remove buildDeployment (~90 lines) and buildService (~30 lines) — no longer needed.

- Remove buildDeploymentLabels, buildServiceLabels, buildServicePorts, buildEnvVars helpers that were only used by Deployment path.

- Keep: buildSandboxCR, buildRoute, buildServiceAccount, buildEnvVarsForSandbox.

deploy_types.go
Remove UseSandbox bool field from DeployAgentParams.
agent_rbac.go (RBAC checks)
Current state: agentDeployChecks includes both apps/deployments/create and agents.x-k8s.io/sandboxes/create.
Change:
- Remove {"apps", "deployments", "create"} and {"", "services", "create"} from deploy checks — we don't create Deployments or Services anymore.

- Add {"agents.x-k8s.io", "sandboxes", "delete"} and {"agents.x-k8s.io", "sandboxes", "patch"} for lifecycle actions.

- CanListAgentsInNamespace: change from checking Deployment/StatefulSet/Job list permission to checking agents.x-k8s.io/sandboxes list.

- CanGetAgentInNamespace: change from checking Deployment/StatefulSet/Job get permission to checking agents.x-k8s.io/sandboxes get.

- Remove agentWorkloadResources and longRunningAgentWorkloadResources slices.

agent_runtime.go (Sandbox mappers)
Already has sandboxToSummary, sandboxToDetail, listSandboxes, getSandbox. No changes needed unless mapper functions need cleanup.
mock client (mock/client.go, mock/demo_client.go)
Remove any Deployment-based mock data. Mock deploy should create mock Sandbox CR entries only.
Tests
- deploy_test.go: remove TestDeployAgent_Fallback* tests, update remaining tests to assert Sandbox CR only

- client_test.go: remove Deployment/StatefulSet/Job listing tests

- manifests_test.go: remove TestBuildDeployment, TestBuildService tests

- agent_rbac_test.go / agent_enrichment_rbac_test.go: update SSAR expectations

Sandbox CR shape (what we create)
apiVersion: agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Sandbox
metadata:
  name: my-agent
  namespace: my-ns
  labels:
    opendatahub.io/agent-type: agent
    opendatahub.io/workload-type: sandbox
    app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: odh-agent-ops
    app.kubernetes.io/name: my-agent
  annotations:
    opendatahub.io/agent-description: "..."
    opendatahub.io/agent-protocol: "openai"
    opendatahub.io/agent-framework: "langchain"
    opendatahub.io/agent-image: "quay.io/..."
spec:
  operatingMode: running
  podTemplate:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: my-agent
      containers:
      - name: agent
        image: quay.io/my-agent:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
          name: http
        env:
        - name: PORT
          value: "8080"
        - name: HOST
          value: "0.0.0.0"
The agent-sandbox controller auto-creates:
- Service (from container ports, accessible via status.serviceFQDN)

- Pod (from podTemplate)

We only create: ServiceAccount + Sandbox CR + optional Route.

If the Sandbox CRD is not registered, the deploy endpoint returns HTTP 503:
{"error": "agent-sandbox CRD (agents.x-k8s.io) is not installed on this cluster. Install the OpenShift Sandboxed Containers operator to enable agent deployments."}
The list endpoint returns an empty list (not an error) when CRD is absent — user just sees no agents.

RHAISTRAT-1752.description:
Business Need (from RFE)
The full business need is maintained in the source RFE: RHAIRFE-2572

Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)
TL;DR
Productize the upstream OpenShell operator for RHOAI by onboarding it into the standard midstream/downstream build pipeline, packaging it for OLM/OperatorHub delivery, integrating it as a DSC-managed component in rhods-operator, and establishing CVE scanning, security certification, and support lifecycle coverage. This provides the certified, supported delivery vehicle that regulated customers require before adopting agent sandboxing capabilities.
Components: rhods-operator, OpenShell operator (new), OLM ClusterServiceVersion
Technical Approach
Midstream and Downstream Repository Onboarding
The upstream OpenShell operator repository will be forked into the opendatahub-io organization as the midstream repo (e.g., opendatahub-io/openshell-operator), following the same upstream-first pattern used by Kagenti (kagenti/* -> opendatahub-io/kagenti-operator) and other RHOAI components. The downstream release branch (rhoai-<version>) will be maintained in the red-hat-data-services organization. The midstream fork enables RHOAI-specific patches (distribution overlays, image overrides, FIPS build flags) while preserving the upstream contribution model. Changes flow upstream first, then are pulled into midstream via branch synchronization, consistent with the established component onboarding pattern.
Build Pipeline and Container Image Production
The downstream build will use the Konflux pipeline, producing container images built on UBI9 base images (ubi-minimal) with FIPS-compliant cryptography. For Go components, this means GOEXPERIMENT=strictfipsruntime with CGO_ENABLED=1, matching the standard applied to rhods-operator, KServe, and other Go-based operators. The Konflux Dockerfile will follow the multi-stage build pattern: a builder stage with Go toolchain and a minimal runtime stage. Multi-architecture support will target amd64 and arm64 at minimum, with ppc64le and s390x evaluated based on upstream build compatibility (following the precedent set by llm-d-inference-scheduler, which reverted Power/Z builds when build issues arose). RPM lock files (rpms.lock.yaml) and go.sum will provide build hermeticity. All container image references will be digest-pinned for supply-chain integrity.
OLM Packaging and OperatorHub Delivery
The OpenShell operator will be packaged as an OLM-managed operator with a ClusterServiceVersion (CSV) that declares all container images via the relatedImages field, enabling disconnected/air-gapped deployment through OLM's image mirroring mechanism. This follows the same RELATED_IMAGE pattern used across all 129 existing RHOAI container images. The CSV will be added to the RHOAI operator bundle, making the OpenShell operator available through the standard RHOAI installation flow in OperatorHub. The operator will not be a standalone OperatorHub listing; it will be delivered as part of the RHOAI operator bundle, consistent with how other component operators (DSPO, KubeRay, Model Registry Operator, MLflow Operator) are packaged.
DSC Integration as a Managed Component
The OpenShell operator will be integrated into the rhods-operator as a DSC-managed component, following the decomposed operator architecture introduced in RHOAI 3.5. This requires: (1) a new component CRD (components.platform.opendatahub.io/v1alpha1, Kind: OpenShellOperator or similar) defining the component's desired state and management state (Managed/Removed), (2) a component controller in rhods-operator that reconciles this CRD by rendering and applying the OpenShell operator's kustomize manifests with RELATED_IMAGE overrides, and (3) status conditions (Ready, ProvisioningSucceeded, Degraded, DeploymentsAvailable) propagated back to the DataScienceCluster CR. The workbenches-operator provides a direct template for this pattern — it reconciles a cluster-scoped component CR, manages namespace lifecycle, monitors deployment health, and reports status conditions. The component will deploy into the redhat-ods-operator namespace alongside other component operators, reconciling resources in user namespaces as needed.
CVE Scanning and Security Certification
Container images will be enrolled in Red Hat's standard CVE scanning pipeline, with vulnerability assessments integrated into the Konflux build process. Security certification will include container image scanning, FIPS compliance verification (via the check-payload gate for Go binaries), and supply-chain attestation. CVE response times will follow RHOAI's existing standards for productized operators — Critical CVEs patched within the established SLA windows. The operator's RBAC surface will be scoped to the minimum permissions required for its reconciliation loop, following the principle of least privilege applied across existing RHOAI operators.
Release Lifecycle and Upgrade Path
The OpenShell operator will follow the standard RHOAI release lifecycle: Early Access 1 (EA1) for initial validation, EA2 for broader testing, and General Availability (GA) for production support. Upgrade paths between releases will be managed through OLM's CSV replacement chain, with the rhods-operator's component controller handling any required migration logic (namespace changes, CRD version conversions, resource cleanup). The support lifecycle and SLA will be defined as part of the GA readiness criteria, aligned with the SLA standards already established for other RHOAI component operators.
Affected Components
- rhods-operator (Platform team): New component controller for OpenShell operator lifecycle management, component CRD definition, CSV relatedImages entries

- OpenShell operator (new midstream/downstream component): Midstream fork, Konflux build pipeline, UBI9/FIPS container images, kustomize manifests with RHOAI overlay

- OLM ClusterServiceVersion (Platform team): relatedImages entries for OpenShell operator container images, RBAC declarations

Impacted Teams
- Platform team (rhods-operator): Implement DSC component controller, CRD, and manifest integration

- Build/Release team (Konflux, OLM packaging): Midstream repo setup, build pipeline configuration, CSV packaging, container certification

- QE team (OpenShell): Test plan for installation, upgrade, and lifecycle verification

- Security team (CVE scanning, certification): Container image scanning enrollment, FIPS compliance verification

High Level Requirements
The orange bullet points below are blocked: we don't have an OpenShell operator to onboard yet. The one area we can push forward on now is FIPS compliance in the application code.
- [P0] OpenShell operator midstream repository onboarded to opendatahub-io with downstream release branch in red-hat-data-services

- [P0] Container images built on UBI9 with FIPS-compliant cryptography and digest-pinned references

- [P0] OLM packaging with relatedImages for disconnected deployment support

- [P0] DSC component controller in rhods-operator for managed lifecycle (Managed/Removed states)

- [P0] CVE scanning pipeline enrollment with response times meeting RHOAI standards → Done

- [P1] Multi-architecture builds for amd64 and arm64 → Done

- [P1] Security certification complete (container image scanning, vulnerability assessment, FIPS check-payload gate)

- [P1] Upgrade path documented and tested through OLM CSV replacement chain

- [P2] Multi-architecture support for ppc64le and s390x (contingent on upstream build compatibility)

Dependencies
- Upstream OpenShell operator (external, exists): Must be stable and feature-complete enough for midstream fork; upstream API surface drives CRD and RBAC definitions

- Konflux build infrastructure (internal, exists): Build pipeline for downstream container image production; already in use for other RHOAI components

- RHAISTRAT-1751 — OpenShell capability integration (internal, needed): Depends on this productization strategy for the certified operator delivery vehicle; capability integration cannot ship without a productized operator

- KATA-4728 — AgentSandbox CRD productization (external, needed): OCP Sandboxed Containers team owns the AgentSandbox CRD; OpenShell operator may depend on this CRD being available on the cluster

- rhods-operator module/component system (internal, exists): DSC component controller framework and manifest rendering pipeline; well-established pattern across 16+ existing components

Non-Functional Requirements
- Security: Container images built on UBI9 base with FIPS-compliant Go runtime (strictfipsruntime build tag, CGO_ENABLED=1), matching the build standard applied to rhods-operator and KServe (architecture context: rhods-operator FIPS Compliance). RBAC scoped to minimum required permissions.

- Disconnected Support: All container images referenced via RELATED_IMAGE environment variables in the OLM CSV, enabling disconnected deployment through OLM's relatedImages mirroring and oc-mirror tooling (architecture context: PLATFORM.md Disconnected Support).

- Backwards Compatibility: Component managed through DSC ManagementState (Managed/Removed), following the standard RHOAI component lifecycle. Removal cleans up operator resources without affecting other platform components. No backwards compatibility concerns for initial release — this is a new component.

Out-of-Scope
- OpenShell feature integration and capability enablement (covered by RHAISTRAT-1751)

- AgentSandbox CRD development and productization (covered by KATA-4728, OCP Sandboxed Containers team)

- Kagenti and OpenShell coexistence model (separate spike Feature per RFE)

- OpenShell upstream feature development — this strategy covers productization of the existing upstream operator, not new feature work

- Dashboard UI integration for OpenShell management — deferred to capability integration phase

Acceptance Criteria (Proposed — requires PM/Engineering validation)
- Given the RHOAI operator bundle is installed on an OpenShift cluster,

   when the cluster administrator sets the OpenShell component to Managed in the DataScienceCluster CR,    then the OpenShell operator Deployment reaches Ready state in the operator namespace,    measured by the component's Ready and DeploymentsAvailable status conditions on the DSC CR.
- Given the OpenShell component is set to Managed,

   when the cluster administrator sets it to Removed,    then the OpenShell operator Deployment and associated resources are cleaned up from the cluster,    measured by the absence of OpenShell operator resources in the operator namespace.
- Given a disconnected/air-gapped OpenShift cluster with mirrored images,

   when the RHOAI operator bundle is installed,    then the OpenShell operator container images resolve from the mirror registry via RELATED_IMAGE references,    measured by successful operator deployment without external registry access.
- Given the OpenShell operator container image is built via the Konflux pipeline,

   then the image passes the check-payload FIPS compliance gate,    measured by a passing FIPS verification result in the build pipeline.
- Given a Critical CVE is identified in the OpenShell operator container image,

   then a patched image is produced within the RHOAI CVE SLA window,    measured by the CVE response time tracked in the vulnerability management system.
- Given an existing RHOAI installation with OpenShell operator at version N,

   when the cluster administrator upgrades to version N+1 via OLM,    then the upgrade completes without manual intervention and the operator reaches Ready state,    measured by the OLM InstallPlan completion status and DSC component status conditions.
Effort Estimate
Size: M (Medium, 3-5 sprints). The productization pipeline is well-understood — RHOAI has onboarded 26+ operator-based components through this same process. The primary work areas are: midstream/downstream repo setup and Konflux build configuration (1 sprint), DSC component controller and CRD implementation in rhods-operator (1 sprint), OLM CSV packaging with relatedImages and RBAC (0.5 sprint), and QE validation including installation, upgrade, disconnected, and multi-arch testing (1-1.5 sprints). Cross-team coordination with Build/Release, Security, and QE adds overhead but follows established processes.
Risks
- Upstream OpenShell operator API instability: If the upstream OpenShell operator CRDs or APIs are still evolving, the midstream fork and DSC integration will need rework as the API stabilizes — Mitigation: Pin the midstream fork to a tagged upstream release; gate EA1 on a stable upstream API version. Establish upstream API freeze agreement before starting downstream work.

- FIPS compliance gaps in upstream code: The upstream operator may not be built with FIPS-aware cryptography, requiring patches to build flags, dependencies, or crypto usage — Mitigation: Audit upstream Go dependencies for non-FIPS-compliant crypto usage during midstream onboarding; contribute FIPS patches upstream before forking.

- Multi-architecture build failures for ppc64le/s390x: Some Go dependencies or C bindings may fail on Power/Z architectures, as seen with llm-d-inference-scheduler — Mitigation: Start with amd64 and arm64 only (P0); treat ppc64le and s390x as P2, deferring if build issues arise.

- AgentSandbox CRD dependency (KATA-4728) not ready: If the OCP Sandboxed Containers team has not productized the AgentSandbox CRD, the OpenShell operator may not have its required CRD available — Mitigation: Validate CRD availability status early; if blocked, decouple the operator install from CRD presence by supporting a degraded mode where the operator is installed but reports a missing-dependency condition.

Assumptions
- The upstream OpenShell operator is a Go-based controller-runtime operator that follows standard Kubernetes operator patterns — needs validation

- The upstream OpenShell operator has a stable tagged release suitable for midstream forking — needs validation

- The OpenShell operator will be delivered as part of the RHOAI operator bundle (not as a standalone OperatorHub listing) — needs validation

- The DSC component controller pattern (as used by workbenches-operator and other decomposed components) is the correct integration path — confirmed (architecture context)

- Konflux build infrastructure supports the OpenShell operator's build requirements without custom tooling — needs validation

- The OpenShell operator's RBAC requirements are compatible with RHOAI's security posture — needs validation

Open Questions
- What is the upstream OpenShell operator's current API stability status? (Owner: OpenShell team) — Determines whether midstream fork can begin immediately or must wait for API stabilization

- Does the OpenShell operator depend on the AgentSandbox CRD being present on the cluster at install time? (Owner: OpenShell team / OCP Sandboxed Containers team) — Impacts deployment ordering and degraded-mode design

- What is the target RHOAI release for OpenShell operator GA? (Owner: Product Management) — Drives release lifecycle timing (EA1/EA2/GA) and QE planning

- Should the OpenShell operator be a DSC-managed component or a module-based component? (Owner: Platform team) — The decomposed operator pattern (component CRD) vs. the module system (out-of-tree) have different trade-offs for release cadence independence

- What are the performance and scalability requirements for the OpenShell operator? (Owner: Product Management / Engineering) — No performance targets specified in the RFE or architecture context; needed for NFR definition

Supporting Documentation

- Parent strategy: RHAISTRAT-1585

- Related capability integration: RHAISTRAT-1751

- AgentSandbox CRD: KATA-4728

- Architecture context: PLATFORM.md (rhoai-3.5-ea.2), rhods-operator.md, agents-operator.md, workbenches-operator.md

- Overlay 0008: Platform policy — RHOAI does not auto-install external operator dependencies

- Overlay 0014: Kagenti agent operator manages agent workloads on RHOAI via AgentRuntime CRD

RHAISTRAT-1697.description:
Problem Statement
Platform engineers and AI developers have no unified UI to discover, inspect, and manage AI agents in RHOAI. Agent metadata lives in the MLflow Agent Registry (RHAISTRAT-1436) while runtime state lives in OpenShell sandboxes, but neither has a dashboard surface. Users must use CLI or API to interact with both systems, limiting discoverability and governance visibility.
Beyond agents, the platform manages multiple asset types (skills, MCP servers, models) across separate registries with no unified discovery experience. There is no composition layer that connects these assets to secure execution environments, forcing users to manually wire security policy, credentials, and infrastructure for every agent deployment.
Affected Customers
- Infineon: "MCP registry combined with model registry, one place everything"

- AXA: "Agent registry/versioning, promotion/quarantine, access control, drift detection, rollback" (formal RFI for Agentic Platform)

- UBS: "Ending up with 100 agents" – need consolidation and visibility

- T-Mobile: "No centralized location to host and lifecycle MCP servers with proper lineage tracking"

- NTT Data (1,000+ agents): "The full agent architecture matters now: control plane, governance, orchestration"

- Florida Blue: "MCP Registry, MCP Gateway, centralized control and governance"

- BofA: Building Model Catalog for discovery and Model Registry for governance

- GIC: Using Langflow, needs a low-code platform to empower business users

- Cisco: "Looking for the recipe" – finds current guidance fragmented

- Gruve.ai: Interested in quick onboarding solutions for Agentic AI

- Foxconn: Attended Roberto's AgentOps workshop (Atlanta 2026), wants agent lifecycle and catalog integrated into their AI service provider portal. Planning a customer-facing tech day (Oct 2026) showcasing agent services powered by RHOAI.

Goal
Deliver Agent Hub views in the RHOAI Dashboard that provide:
- Registry View – browsable, searchable catalog of all registered agents (metadata from MLflow Agent Registry). "What agents exist in our organization?"

- Deployments View – running agent instances with health, endpoints, and status (from OpenShell sandboxes). "What agents are running right now?"

- Deploy Action – secure agent onboarding: select an agent image, configure policy and credentials via OpenShell, and launch into a governed sandbox.

- Admin UI – workspace and policy management for OpenShell: create workspaces, configure providers, set network policies, manage interceptors.

- Starter Kits and Templates – surface agentic starter kits in Dashboard for quick-start discovery. (Shipped 3.5 EA1 via RHAISTRAT-1376.)

Personas
Persona
Responsibility
UI Surface
Platform Admin
Deploys OpenShell operator, configures org-wide interceptor policies, manages gateway integrations
Operator config, interceptor rules, gateway bindings
Workspace Admin
Controls tenant boundaries: which users access which sandboxes, credentials, and policies
Workspace management, provider configuration, user/role assignment
Developer
Brings an agent image, selects a profile or starter kit, launches securely. Does not manually wire security plumbing.
Agent catalog, deploy action, deployment status, traces

Composition Layer (Vision)
The north-star UX is a composition layer that connects three building blocks into governed agents:
- Asset Registries – agents, skills, MCP servers, models (backed by MLflow, AI Hub)

- Validated Harness Images – pre-built OCI images for supported agent frameworks (Claude Code, OpenClaw, etc.)

- Secure Execution Environments – OpenShell sandboxes with identity (SPIFFE/SPIRE), policy, credentials, and interceptors

The composition flow: developer picks an asset from the registry, picks a harness image (or brings their own), the platform resolves policy and credentials via OpenShell, and creates a governed sandbox. Interceptors allow workspace and platform admins to enforce defaults transparently, so the developer does not need to manually configure security for every deployment.
Agent Execution Archetypes
Different agent deployment modes imply different UI flows:
Archetype
Description
UI Implication
Headless (always-on)
Long-running agent processing events or queues
Observability-focused: traces, sandbox rejections, health dashboards
Interactive
User-facing session (e.g., coding agent, chat)
Agent playground or workspace launcher with live interaction
Event-driven
Triggered by external events (PR filed, alert fired)
Minimal UI footprint; may not appear in deployments until triggered
Orchestrated (multi-agent)
Multiple agents collaborating via A2A/MCP
Topology view showing agent-to-agent communication (future)

Key Clarifications

Metadata store for all agents (deployed or not): identity, versioning, governance status
MLflow Agent Registry (RHAISTRAT-1436)

Dashboard views that surface registries and deployments in a unified experience
odh-dashboard (this outcome)
Dashboard

Workspace and policy management: create sandboxes, configure providers, set policies
OpenShell upstream UI (consumed downstream)
AgentOps
Composition Layer
Connects asset registries + harness images + secure execution into governed agents
TBD (target 3.7)

- OGX/Praxis is the inference backend; OpenShell is agnostic to how inference endpoints are served (any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works)

- Dev Spaces will use OpenShell underneath for coding agent environments; UX boundary between RHOAI console and Dev Spaces is being defined separately

Phased Delivery
Release
What ships
3.5 (current)
Starter kits catalog (done). Read-only agent deployments view (reading AgentSandbox CRs).
3.6
OpenShell operator TP on RHOAI. Admin UI for sandboxes/policy (upstream-first). Skill registry UX. Proper deployment view via OpenShell SDK. Validated harness images for five agent frameworks.
3.7
Composition layer: drop-down selection of skills, MCP servers, models during agent creation. Full secure agent onboarding flow.

Acceptance Criteria
- Users can browse, search, and filter registered agents in a unified Agent Hub view

- Users can view agent detail pages with metadata (description, version, capabilities, endpoint, owner, status)

- Users can view running agent deployments (OpenShell sandboxes) with health status and endpoints

- Users can deploy an agent from the registry into a secure OpenShell sandbox with policy and credentials

- Workspace admins can create and manage workspaces, configure providers, and assign user access

- Platform admins can configure interceptors to enforce default policies across sandboxes

- Users can discover agentic starter kits and templates from the dashboard

- The UI pattern is extensible and aligns with the shared AI Hub discovery chassis (RHAIRFE-1647)

- RHAIRFE-2143 – Agent Deployments View: runtime agent visibility

- RHAISTRAT-1213 – AgentCard standard (provides capability metadata for both views)

- RHAIRFE-1647 – AI Hub Scalable Discovery (shared search/filter chassis)

- OpenShell operator and upstream UI – feeds Deployments View and Admin UI

RHOAIENG-88996.description:
Summary
kserve's imageParamMap (the mapping the operator uses to inject an image digest via OLM at reconcile time), in PR #1902, adds six RELATED_IMAGE_RHAII_VLLM_CPU_PZ_* entries for a vLLM CPU Power/Z image. AIPCC (the team building this multi-arch base image) hasn't published it to the registry yet, so the companion PRs already merged in opendatahub-operator and odh-model-controller carry a placeholder digest instead of a real one.
disconnected-readiness-scorer added a temporary exception (*VLLM_CPU_PZ* in config/config.yaml) so the placeholder doesn't block unrelated kserve PRs in the meantime. That exception expires 2026-08-31. If AIPCC hasn't published the image and Renovate (the bot that auto-updates image digests) hasn't merged the digest update by then, KServe carries a real disconnected-readiness gap into the 3.6 EA1 release: the CSV points at an image that doesn't exist in a disconnected registry.
Scope
This ticket blocks 3.6 EA1 from releasing with KServe until the real image and digests are in place. It does not own the image build or the digest wiring itself. That work is tracked in related tickets.
Acceptance Criteria
- AIPCC has published the vLLM CPU Power/Z multi-arch image to the registry.

- The RELATED_IMAGE_RHAII_VLLM_CPU_PZ_* entries in kserve, opendatahub-operator, and odh-model-controller resolve to that image's real digest, not the placeholder.

Yes, but manual — user must patch the ServingRuntime template with the correct image
Not acceptable as a permanent solution for GA.

- Is this issue a regression from previously working functionality?
Yes — the template was functional in prior releases with a valid image reference. The 3.6 EA1 build introduced quay.io/vllm/vllm:latest which does not exist.

Low. Fix is a one-line image tag/digest change in the template YAML. No logic changes involved.

This issue is a known gap during the vLLM CPU Power/Z AIPCC migration sequence (RHAI-121) and is already being resolved. The Build-Config PRs that add the missing RELATED_IMAGE entries to the CSV were created today and are now in review:
- RHOAI 3.6 EA1: https://github.com/red-hat-data-services/RHOAI-Build-Config/pull/30867

Root Cause
The migration was sequenced as follows:
- ✅ opendatahub-operator #3996 - Added RELATED_IMAGE_RHAII_VLLM_CPU_PZ_* environment variable declarations

- ✅ odh-model-controller #925 - Switched vllm-cpu-runtime-template from $(vllm-cpu-image) to $(vllm-cpu-pz-image)

Since step 4 hadn't been created yet when you tested the EA1 build, the $(vllm-cpu-pz-image) parameter resolved to a placeholder value, causing ImagePullBackOff. This is expected during the migration sequence.

Once the Build-Config PRs merge (expected before code freeze this Friday), the next operator build will include the RELATED_IMAGE entries in the CSV, and the template will resolve to the correct multi-arch image digest. The AIPCC image should also be published to the registry before code freeze, and Renovate will automatically update the digests.
Recommendation
Downgrade priority from Blocker to High or Major since:
- Fix is in review and will merge before code freeze

- This is a build-in-progress issue during migration, not a shipped bug

- No customer impact (EA1 not yet released)

CRCPLAN-372.description:
Summary: This initiative focuses on the initial step towards enabling multicluster tenant application integration by migrating core ConsoleDot platform workloads to a new, dedicated cluster. This move will improve resiliency, scalability, and security for ConsoleDot services and tenant applications, as currently, most HCC platform capabilities are limited to applications deployed in a single cluster. This initiative aims to address the limitations of a single, monolithic cluster, which include a larger blast radius for incidents, challenges with cluster operations like upgrades, and restricted flexibility for application deployment.
Goal: Our purpose in implementing this initiative is to decompose the monolithic CRC cluster by moving ConsoleDot platform workloads to a new, dedicated cluster. This will enable Red Hat associates to:
- Platform capabilities should be readily available across all clusters, without limitation to a single one.

- Operate ConsoleDot platform services from an isolated, dedicated environment, reducing the blast radius of incidents affecting tenant applications.

- Enforce better security practices by addressing design anti-patterns related to authentication and authorization within a single cluster.

- Facilitate future architectural modernizations and lay the groundwork for geo-redundancy and regionality of platform components.

Acceptance Criteria:
- ConsoleDot platform workloads (backend services, frontend deployments, supporting operators) are successfully migrated to a new, dedicated ROSA HCP cluster

- Existing tenant applications continue to function without disruption after the migration of ConsoleDot platform workloads

- A new contract for service-to-service communication is implemented for core ConsoleDot platform services and used for cross-cluster communication

- Communication between services in the new HCC cluster and tenant applications in the CRC cluster maintains low overhead (latency, cost)

- Observability for the new ConsoleDot platform cluster is established and integrated

- SOPs are created/updated to ensure this migration process is repeatable and can be done again solely by following the SOPs

CRCPLAN-392.description:
Description
This feature enables customers to integrate their existing Identity Provider (IdP) and leverage their Single Sign-On (SSO) credentials with the On-Premise Management Fabric (OPMF) Dev Preview. This is a crucial piece of the solution, as it allows customers to maintain their existing identity management workflows and security policies. The "why" is to reduce the friction of adoption by eliminating the need for customers to manage a separate set of user identities and credentials for the OPMF. By supporting industry-standard IdPs and SSO, we make the OPMF a more seamless and secure part of their existing infrastructure. This directly supports the broader Outcome of increasing customer retention and expansion by making the management experience more cohesive and less operationally complex.
Included
- Customer-Provided IdP Integration: The ability for an OPMF administrator to configure and connect the Management Fabric to a customer's existing Identity Provider.

- Role Assignment with IdP Groups: Support for assigning OPMF roles to users and groups defined within the customer's IdP.

- Industry Standard SSO Support: The OPMF will be able to authenticate users using industry-standard SSO credentials provided by the customer.

Excluded
- Custom IdP/Authentication Methods: This feature will not support proprietary or non-standard identity management systems.

- User Management within OPMF: The OPMF will not provide internal user management capabilities. All users and groups will be sourced from the customer's IdP.

- Full Productization: As a Dev Preview feature, this will not have the full level of polish, documentation, or robust error handling that would be expected in a General Availability release.

Estimated Effort
Large. The effort is considered large due to the complexity of integrating with various industry-standard IdP systems and ensuring a secure and reliable SSO process. This requires significant engineering effort to build a flexible and secure authentication framework.
Definition of Complete
This Feature will be considered complete when:
- A documented process exists for an OPMF administrator to successfully configure an industry-standard IdP and enable SSO.

- Users can successfully authenticate to the OPMF using their IdP credentials.

- OPMF roles can be successfully assigned to users and groups sourced from the IdP.

- Integration with a customer-provided IdP is tested and validated.

- The system is documented for the developer audience as part of the overall Dev Preview release.

RHCLOUD-43616.description:
Goal
Reimplement the existing /internal/userIdentity endpoint (currently in insights-3scale) as a standard OAuth2 token exchange flow (RFC 8693) in parsec. This is a breaking change for clients — they will use the standard token exchange API instead of the bespoke endpoint.
The initial consumer is the Scheduler service, which runs asynchronously and needs a way to verify that a user still exists and obtain a fresh identity object on behalf of a user. While the Scheduler is the initial consumer, the feature is designed to be generic and will support additional consumers in the future.
Transaction token (txn token) support is out of scope for this epic and will be addressed separately (see CRCPLAN-412).
Background
The current /internal/userIdentity endpoint in insights-3scale takes a username via the x-rh-user-id header, calls BOP (Back Office Proxy) to resolve the user, and returns a base64-encoded x-rh-identity JSON. It runs on dedicated internal-only ports (8891/8892/8893), requires no caller authentication, and relies on network-level access control only (Kubernetes Service + Istio mesh).
This endpoint bypasses the entire normal authentication pipeline — no JWT validation, no cert-auth, no compliance, no entitlements, no 3scale authorization. It trusts that the caller has already authenticated the user by other means.
Client API Change
Old (insights-3scale):
GET /internal/userIdentity
x-rh-user-id: jdoe
New (parsec):
POST /v1/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
&subject_token=jdoe
&subject_token_type=urn:redhat:params:oauth:token-type:username
&requested_token_type=urn:redhat:params:oauth:token-type:rh-identity
The response includes an access_token containing the base64-encoded rh-identity JSON.
Implementation Approach
- Zero Go changes in parsec — config and scripts only, leveraging existing building blocks (token exchange, Lua validators, Lua data sources, CEL claim mapper, unsigned issuer)

- A new Lua-based datasource calls BOP to resolve usernames to user data

- The CEL claim mapper is extended with a new branch for identity construction

- The new datasource is registered after the JWT validator so normal auth flows are unaffected (JWT tokens are tried first and don't trigger BOP calls)

- BOP lookup results are cached in-memory with a 5-minute TTL

- - 


Acceptance Criteria
- parsec supports token exchange producing rh-identity tokens from a username subject token

- A new data source (not a validator) calls BOP /v1/users?queryBy=userId and validates the response (exactly 1 user, org_id and id present)

- CEL builds the identity envelope from the data source result: User type, auth_type: "jwt-auth", cross_access: false, no auth_time, no entitlements

- BOP lookup results are cached in-memory (5-minute TTL)

- The Scheduler service can use the token exchange endpoint to obtain identity objects for its asynchronous job execution
