RHCLOUD-31140.description:
In ConsoleDot, all external communication passes through 3scale, an API gateway. After proper authentication, it adds to the request a header called x-rh-identity that contains a JWT with the identity of the requester.
However, many tenants within ConsoleDot doesn't validate that header and assume that the request is valid just because their location: they assume that any request they receive is legitimate because the protection in the perimeter of the API gateway and they trust anything that comes from the internal network.
Nowdays trusted zones are no longer considered a good practice. Based on defense in depth and zero trust principles, each ConsoleDot tenant should not trust other services and should validate each request. However, it is not needed that each tenant implements this validation by themselves, what would be inefficient, as this could potentially be done by the platform transparently for the services.
This issue is to request that the ConsoleDot platform evaluates and implements a solution to guarantee that each request that is received by a service is validated at its ingress in an efficient and secure manner and as transparantly as possible for the services.

Problem summary: Today, most of HCC platform capabilities are limited to applications deployed in a single cluster. Tenant teams who prefer to deploy their applications elsewhere have limited access to HCC platform capabilities. This limits flexibility of application teams and has a negative impact on resiliency and scalability of the Console.

- Applications can be fully integrated into the Console without coupling to specific clusters or infrastructure

- Applications can continue to leverage tooling provided by the ConsoleDot platform (bonfire, Clowder)

- Applications continue to integrate with Console in an efficient way (cost, latency)

- Flexibility in how Console applications are delivered, reducing time to market

- Reduced onboarding friction and minimized redundant efforts

- Improved user experience due to better integration and reuse among Console applications

- Enablement of strategic functionality (such as Fabric) to be adopted across all applications

- Improved resiliency due to reduced blast radius and decoupling of tenant applications from the ConsoleDot platform

AIPCC-17138.description:
Overview
Track all work required to achieve full compliance with the ProdSec Security Policy Compliance Directive issued by CTO leadership.
Directive Requirements
Two hard requirements, effective immediately:
- Major Incident response is mandatory — ProdSec Incident Commanders have full authority to direct response. This is not optional or negotiable.

- No more security policy exceptions — Products that do not meet ProdSec security requirements do not ship. Exceptions require VP-level sign-off and risk register tracking.

Additional Work Areas
- RHOAI platform adoption to reduce Conforma exceptions

- Licensing limitations for bundled components

- Incident response runbook updates for ProdSec Major Incident authority

- 3rd-party partner security contract audit


Source: AIPCC Response to Security Policy Compliance Directive
Coordination channel: #tmp-aipcc-security-policy-compliance

This Epic covers integrating these modelcars into the NeMo Guardrails server build, replacing the current approach of sourcing models from RH mirrors (established in RHOAIENG-69658 and RHOAIENG-83211). Adopting modelcars is the final step in achieving full hermetic build compliance for NeMo Guardrails, aligning with the platform-wide modelcar pattern.

RHAIENG-6973.summary: Use OCI artifacts for file storage
RHAIENG-6973.description:
Currently, we list files required in our distribution builds in a artifact lock file. This file gets used by Hermeto generic file pre-fetcher to pull these files before the hermetic build stage for our downsteam builds - midstream builds use the same lock file with a fetch script instead of Hermeto.
While this pre-fetch stage is necessary for hermetic builds, we require a Conforma exception because the sources of these files (Hugging Face, ModelScope, etc.) are not trusted sources in the Conforma system.
AIPCC, Model Validation, ProdSec, and Agentic API teams have been working on a solution that provides generic file storage that is suitable for both hermetic and Conforma-compliant builds (see #tmp-model-artifact-packaging for discussions on this work).
The solution landed on is to use a private Hugging Face repo in the RedHatAI org for all OGX file artifacts, and build & publish an OCI artifact containing these files that can be consumed in OGX image builds. The Agentic API (OGX) team will populate the repo with all required files. The Model Validation team will produce an OCI artifact containing all files, ensuring all files have been scanned in a ProdSec-approved manner, publishing the artifact to a Conforma-approved registry. The Agentic API team will pull the OCI artifact in their builds, copying the required files from the OCI artifact.
